scenarios.name: Customer Support Resolution Agent
scenarios.desc: An Agent SDK agent resolves support tickets end to end. It looks up customers and orders through MCP tools, issues refunds within policy, escalates to human agents, and keeps state across long multi-turn conversations.

scenarios.name: Code Generation with Claude Code
scenarios.desc: A product team uses Claude Code to build and change features in a large production codebase, relying on CLAUDE.md, plan mode, custom skills and commands, and tests as the feedback loop.

scenarios.name: Multi-Agent Research System
scenarios.desc: A coordinator agent breaks research questions into parts, delegates them to search, analysis and synthesis subagents, and assembles a cited report.

scenarios.name: Developer Productivity with Claude
scenarios.desc: A platform team gives engineers Claude-powered tooling: shared team configuration, MCP servers for internal systems, custom tools, and help exploring large, unfamiliar codebases.

scenarios.name: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
scenarios.desc: Claude Code runs non-interactively in the CI/CD pipeline to review pull requests, generate tests and propose fixes, under tight permission, reliability and cost constraints.

scenarios.name: Structured Data Extraction
scenarios.desc: A pipeline extracts structured fields from invoices, contracts and forms using JSON schemas, validation and retry loops, batch processing, and human review of uncertain results.

lessons.title: Agentic loops
lessons.summary: The exam checks that you know exactly how the tool-use loop runs and ends, how to bound it, and when a workflow or a single call is a better design than an autonomous agent.
keyPoints: The loop: call the Messages API with `tools` → if `stop_reason == "tool_use"`, run every `tool_use` block → append the **full** assistant `content`, then **one** user message with a `tool_result` per `tool_use_id` → repeat until `end_turn`.

Branch on every stop reason, not just `tool_use`: `max_tokens` means truncation (never execute a `tool_use` from that turn, its input may be partial), `refusal` must not be parsed as success, `pause_turn` is resent as-is.

All `tool_result` blocks for a turn go in a **single** user message; splitting them across messages breaks parallel tool use. A failed tool returns `is_error: true` with an actionable message instead of crashing the loop.

Bound every production run in the harness: iteration/turn caps (`max_turns` / `maxTurns`) and a spend cap (`max_budget_usd` / `maxBudgetUsd`, which also counts subagent spend). Check the result `subtype` (`success`, `error_max_turns`, `error_max_budget_usd`, `error_during_execution`) before reading `result`.

**Workflow vs agent** ("Building effective agents"): workflows run LLMs and tools through predefined code paths; agents let the LLM direct its own process and tool use. Start with the simplest thing (often one well-prompted call) and add autonomy only when it measurably helps.

Use an agent when the path can't be specified in advance, the task is valuable enough to justify cost and latency, and errors can be caught (tests, review, rollback). Fixed, auditable, high-volume processes stay workflows.

Agents need ground truth from the environment every step (tool results, test output) and explicit stopping conditions. Prompted effort guidance ("simple fact = one agent, few calls") plus harness caps prevents runaway loops.
Routing (classify, then dispatch to a specialized prompt/tool set/model) is a workflow, not an agent.
traps: Ending the loop on `stop_reason != "tool_use"` without checking `max_tokens`: truncated answers are reported as complete.
Appending only the assistant text: the `tool_use` blocks disappear and the next `tool_result` is orphaned (400 error).
Answering only the first of several parallel `tool_use` blocks.
Relying on a prompt ("stop when done") as the only termination control; caps must live in the harness.
Choosing a multi-agent design for a fixed, well-specified process. Over-engineering is the most common wrong answer.

docs.title: Agent SDK: how the agent loop works

lessons.drill: Write a 30-line manual tool loop with two fake tools. Force each stop reason: set `max_tokens` tiny to trigger truncation, return two parallel tool calls, and make one tool throw. Confirm the loop never runs a truncated tool call, returns both results in one message, and stops at an iteration cap. Then list one task from your own work that should be a workflow instead of an agent, and say why in two sentences.

lessons.title: Coordinator and subagent patterns
lessons.summary: Expect multi-agent design scenarios: what the coordinator owns, when subagents should run in parallel or in sequence, when evaluator-optimizer fits, and when a multi-agent design is over-engineering.
keyPoints: **Orchestrator-workers / hub-and-spoke**: a coordinator decomposes the task at runtime, routes subtasks to workers, and synthesizes their results. The subtasks are decided per input, which distinguishes it from fixed parallelization.
The coordinator owns **decomposition, routing, dependency ordering and synthesis** (including resolving contradictions between workers). Workers own narrow execution: searching, reading, extracting.

Keep information flowing **through the coordinator**: a worker that needs another worker's output gets it in its brief from the coordinator. This keeps the system observable and lets the coordinator control what each worker sees.
**Parallel** for independent subtasks (total time ≈ the slowest worker); **sequential** when one subtask's output is another's input (find the vendors, then fan out one worker per vendor).

Anthropic's research system: the lead launches subagents in parallel and each runs tools in parallel, which cut research time sharply on complex queries; but multi-agent runs used roughly 15× the tokens of chat, so they pay off only on valuable, parallelizable work.
Its synchronous design means the lead waits for each batch; one slow worker stalls the batch and the lead can't steer workers mid-task.

**Evaluator-optimizer**: one model generates, a separate one critiques against explicit criteria, looping with a cap. Use it only when criteria are clear and feedback measurably improves output. A dedicated verification step (e.g. a citation pass) is a common evaluator.
Prefer a single agent or a routing workflow when work is tightly coupled, needs shared state, or the categories are known in advance; subagents add tokens, latency and coordination cost.
traps: Letting workers coordinate among themselves to "save the coordinator work": you lose control of synthesis and traceability.
Launching dependent subtasks in parallel, so later workers guess at inputs that don't exist yet.
Evaluator-optimizer with a vague rubric ("make it better") or no iteration cap.
Asking the generator to "double-check itself" in the same context and calling that an evaluator.
Using a coordinator that spawns subagents for a classification problem with known categories; that's routing.

code.src:
Coordinator plan for: "Top 5 EU battery suppliers: capacity and regulatory exposure"
  Stage 1 (sequential): worker A -> identify the 5 suppliers, return names + sources
  Stage 2 (parallel):   workers B1..B5 -> one per supplier, same output schema
  Stage 3:              coordinator synthesizes, flags conflicts between workers
  Stage 4 (evaluator):  citation checker maps each claim to a source; 1 revision max

docs.title: How we built our multi-agent research system

lessons.drill: Take one research question you care about and draw the coordinator plan: which subtasks are independent (parallel), which depend on others (sequential), what the coordinator keeps for itself, and where an evaluator step adds value. Estimate the number of model calls and decide whether a single agent would be good enough.

lessons.title: Subagent invocation and context passing
lessons.summary: The exam's core fact: a non-fork subagent starts with a fresh, isolated context and sees only its own system prompt plus the task string it is handed. Questions test what to put in that brief, what to return, and how to define and restrict subagents.
keyPoints: A non-fork subagent receives its own system prompt (`AgentDefinition.prompt`), the Agent tool's prompt string, project CLAUDE.md (via setting sources) and its tool definitions. It does **not** receive the parent's conversation history, tool results or system prompt.

So the brief must carry everything: objective, scope boundaries, relevant file paths/IDs/prior findings, tools or sources to use, and the required output format. Vague briefs cause duplicated work, gaps and drift.

Only the subagent's **final message** returns to the parent. Ask for condensed, structured results (findings, sources, gaps), not transcripts; large artifacts go to files/storage and the parent gets references.

Agent SDK: define subagents in `agents` with `AgentDefinition` (`description` and `prompt` required; optional `tools`, `disallowedTools`, `model`, `maxTurns`, ...). Claude invokes them through the `Agent` tool. Claude Code: Markdown files in `.claude/agents/` (project) or `~/.claude/agents/` (user).
`description` drives automatic delegation: write when-to-use descriptions that clearly separate similar subagents. Naming the subagent in the prompt invokes it explicitly.
**Omitting `tools` inherits every tool available to subagents.** Restrict with an explicit list (e.g. `Read, Grep, Glob` for a reviewer); a tool left out isn't in the subagent's session at all.
Explicit context passing is also a **data-minimization** control: give a subagent with web access only the fields it needs, not the whole customer record.
Use a cheaper model tier (`model`) for simple, reading-heavy workers and a capable one for planning and synthesis.
traps: "The subagent will see what we discussed." It won't; pass it explicitly.
Omitting `tools` on a "read-only" subagent; it inherits Edit, Write and Bash.
Telling a subagent in its prompt "don't search the web" instead of removing the tool.
Having subagents return full transcripts or raw documents, which defeats context isolation.
Pasting the whole conversation history into every brief: it bloats context and leaks data the worker doesn't need.

docs.title: How we built our multi-agent research system

lessons.drill: Define two subagents with overlapping jobs (e.g. `web-searcher` and `paper-analyst`) using one-line vague descriptions and watch which one Claude picks for five prompts. Rewrite the descriptions with explicit when-to-use criteria and rerun. Then remove `tools` from one and check the init message: it now has every tool.

lessons.title: Workflow enforcement and handoff
lessons.summary: When a step or order is mandatory (verify identity before refund, validate before writing), the exam wants a deterministic control in code, not a stronger prompt. It also tests structured handoffs between agents and to humans.
keyPoints: Prompts are probabilistic; code is deterministic. If a step must happen every time, enforce it in the harness: tool-handler checks, hooks, tool gating, or a code-defined pipeline.

**Prerequisite gates**: the refund handler checks server-side session state (identity verified for this customer) and returns an actionable error otherwise. Or expose the refund tool only after verification succeeds.
Never let the model attest to its own prerequisite (an `identity_verified: true` parameter, a self-reported `tests_passed` flag); the check must read state the model can't fabricate.
Derive sensitive values server-side from IDs (fetch the order amount from the order ID) rather than trusting model-supplied numbers.
Take irreversible side effects away from the model when the sequence is fixed: the pipeline writes to the ERP only after validation passes; the CI script pushes only after its own test run passes.

**Structured handoff to humans**: a required schema (customer/case ID, verified facts, what was tried and the results, what the customer wants, why it was escalated, recommended next step) so the reviewer doesn't have to read the transcript.
**Agent-to-agent handoff**: a typed contract (fields, units, nulls for missing values, source references) validated in code between stages, not free prose.
Routing to human review is decided by code rules (validation failures, calibrated thresholds), not by asking the model whether it is confident.
traps: "Add IMPORTANT/ALWAYS to the system prompt" as the fix for a step that is skipped 3% of the time.
A PostToolUse hook or after-the-fact audit as the control for something that must be prevented.
Handing off a raw transcript (or a free-text summary) and calling it a handoff.
Gating on a field the model fills in itself.

docs.title: Best practices: enforce rules that can't have exceptions

lessons.drill: Take an agent with `verify_identity` and `issue_refund` tools. Write a red-team prompt that convinces the model it already verified the user. Then add a handler check against server-side session state and rerun. Finally design the JSON schema for an `escalate_to_human` tool and test whether a teammate can act on one handoff without opening the transcript.

lessons.title: Agent SDK hooks
lessons.summary: Hooks are your code running at fixed points in the agent loop, so they enforce policy deterministically. Know which event to use, how to block or modify a call, how to rewrite tool output, and how multiple hooks combine.
keyPoints: Events include `PreToolUse` (before a tool runs: allow/deny/ask, or rewrite input with `updatedInput`), `PostToolUse` (after: add `additionalContext` or replace output with `updatedToolOutput`), `PostToolUseFailure`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `Stop`, `SubagentStart`/`SubagentStop`, `PreCompact`, `Notification`, `PermissionRequest`. `SessionStart`/`SessionEnd` callbacks are TypeScript-only in the SDK.
`PreToolUse` deny: return `hookSpecificOutput` with `permissionDecision: "deny"` and a `permissionDecisionReason` (shown to the model so it can adapt).
Hooks run before permission rules and modes, so a hook deny blocks even in `bypassPermissions`. A hook `allow` doesn't override a matching deny rule.
Matchers match the **tool name** (`Write|Edit`, `^mcp__`), never arguments. Check file paths inside the callback, and remember Bash can write files too.
When several hooks match, they run **in parallel**; for permission decisions the most restrictive wins (deny > defer > ask > allow). Write each hook to stand alone.
`PostToolUse` can't prevent an action (the tool already ran) but is the right place to normalize or trim tool output before the model sees it.
SDK callbacks run in your process and use no context window. Async outputs (`async: true`) suit logging only; they can't block or modify.
In Claude Code shell hooks: exit 2 blocks (stderr goes to Claude); exit 1 is a non-blocking error; a `Stop` hook exiting 2 sends Claude back to work.
traps: Exit code 1 (or a thrown error) expected to block.
Using `PostToolUse` to stop something that must not happen.
`Write|Edit` matcher believed to protect a file from `echo > file` in Bash.
Assuming hooks run in registration order so one can depend on another.
Putting must-run checks only in `canUseTool`; calls already approved by rules or modes never reach it.
lessons.drill: Register two `PreToolUse` callbacks with no matcher: one that logs and returns `{}`, one that denies any Bash command containing `rm`. Add a `PostToolUse` callback that rewrites a tool's output. Ask the agent to delete a file and to read one; confirm the deny reason reaches the model and the rewritten output is what it quotes back.

lessons.title: Task decomposition
lessons.summary: Questions ask how to split work: a fixed prompt chain or dynamic decomposition, how to cut independent sub-questions, per-item then cross-item passes, and how to avoid splits that are too narrow or too fine to keep coherence.
keyPoints: **Prompt chaining** (fixed steps with programmatic gates) fits tasks whose steps are known in advance; **dynamic decomposition** (orchestrator decides subtasks per input) fits open-ended questions whose shape varies.
Split into sub-questions that are **independent** (no worker waits on another), **non-overlapping** (distinct scope) and share an **output format** so the coordinator can merge.
Order dependent work: do the shared core first (schema, interface, entity list), then fan out the independent pieces.

**Per-item then cross-item**: analyze each file/document/source in its own pass into structured findings, then run an integration pass across them (contradictions, interfaces, call sites). One giant pass dilutes attention; per-item passes alone miss cross-item issues.
**Avoid over-narrow decomposition**: a first scoping pass that maps the dimensions of the question, plus a coverage check of subtasks against the question, prevents whole angles from going missing.
**Avoid over-fine decomposition**: one call per field or per edit multiplies cost and breaks cross-field consistency. Group related items and validate relationships in code.
Parallelization comes in two forms: **sectioning** (different independent subtasks at once) and **voting** (same task several times, aggregate).
For large mechanical changes, generate the work list deterministically, pilot the prompt on a few items, then fan out (e.g. `claude -p` per file).
traps: A fixed template of subtopics applied to every question regardless of its shape.
Adding more workers on the same narrow subtopics to fix missing coverage.
Fanning out coupled edits in parallel (conflicting changes to shared code).
Running one pass over everything and expecting it to catch both local and cross-cutting issues.

code.src:
# Deterministic work list, piloted prompt, then fan out
git grep -l 'legacyLogger' -- 'services/*/src' > targets.txt
head -3 targets.txt | while read f; do      # pilot first
  claude -p "Migrate $f to structuredLogger per MIGRATION.md" \
    --allowedTools "Read,Edit,Bash(npm test *)" --output-format json
done

docs.title: How we built our multi-agent research system

lessons.drill: Pick a broad research question and write two decompositions: a fixed four-section template and a scoped dynamic plan produced after a one-paragraph mapping of the question's dimensions. Compare which angles each misses. Then take a 10-document set and design the per-document schema and the cross-document comparison prompt.

lessons.title: Session state, resumption and forking
lessons.summary: Know when to continue, resume, fork or start fresh, what each one carries over, and why durable state belongs outside the context window when runs are long, distributed or interrupted.
keyPoints: **Continue** picks the most recent session in the current directory (`--continue`, `continue_conversation=True` / `continue: true`). **Resume** targets a specific session ID (`--resume <id>`, `resume=`) and is required whenever several sessions exist, e.g. one per user or parallel CI runs.

**Fork** (`fork_session=True` / `forkSession`, `--fork-session`, `/branch`) creates a new session ID that starts with a copy of the history; the original stays unchanged. Forks branch the **conversation, not the filesystem**: a fork's file edits are real and visible to anything using that directory.
Capture `session_id` from the result message (present on success and error results).

Sessions are local transcript files (`~/.claude/projects/...`). To resume on another host, use a `SessionStore` adapter or move the file, or skip resume and pass the captured results into a fresh session, which the docs call often more robust.
Resuming restores the conversation, not every launch flag: re-pass things like `--mcp-config`, `--settings`, `--plugin-dir` and `--add-dir` (settings files are re-read automatically).

**Start fresh with a summary** when the old context is stale (sources or files changed since), very long, or full of failed attempts. After two failed corrections, `/clear` and a better prompt beat a third correction.

Persist plans, progress and case facts outside the context window (files, memory, a database). Anthropic's research lead saves its plan to memory so it survives context truncation, and long runs should checkpoint so they resume where they failed instead of restarting.
`/compact` and compaction keep going on the same task within a session; they are not cross-session memory.
traps: Using `continue` in a multi-user or parallel setup: it grabs whichever session was most recent.
Believing a fork snapshots files, or that it starts with empty context.
Resuming a week-old session and trusting tool results that are now out of date.
Expecting `--resume` in CI to bring back an MCP config passed on the first run's command line.
Restarting a long multi-agent job from scratch after one worker fails.

code.src:
out=$(claude -p "Analyze failing tests" --mcp-config ci-mcp.json --output-format json)
sid=$(echo "$out" | jq -r .session_id)

# Same conversation, flags passed again
claude -p "Apply the fix you proposed" --resume "$sid" --mcp-config ci-mcp.json

# Try an alternative without touching the original history
claude -p "Try a different approach" --resume "$sid" --fork-session

docs.title: How we built our multi-agent research system

lessons.drill: Run `claude -p` twice in parallel in one directory and capture both session IDs. Send a follow-up with `--continue` and see which one it hits; redo it with `--resume <id>`. Then fork one session, have the fork edit a file, and check that the original session's working tree sees the change.

lessons.title: Tool interface design
lessons.summary: The exam checks whether you can design tools an agent picks correctly and uses efficiently: descriptions that say what a tool does and when to call it, schemas that make bad input hard to express, clean boundaries between similar tools, and outputs that return only high-signal fields. Expect symptoms (wrong tool picked, wasted tokens, invented IDs) and ask for the design fix.
keyPoints: The **description is the main selection signal**. State what the tool does, what it returns, and **when to call it** (and when not to). Vague one-liners ("Order tool.") make Claude skip the tool or pick the wrong one.

Schema hygiene: describe every property with units and format ("amount in cents, integer"), use `enum` for fixed value sets, mark only truly required fields in `required`, and give params unambiguous names (`customer_id`, not `id`).

**Boundaries between similar tools**: if two tools overlap (`search_customers` / `find_customer`), either merge them or rewrite both descriptions so each says what it covers and when to prefer it. Namespacing by service or resource (`kb_search`, `web_search`) also helps.

**Consolidate multi-step chains** the agent always runs together (`schedule_event` instead of `list_users` + `list_events` + `create_event`), and prefer **search over list** so the agent never pages through everything.

**Return high-signal fields only**: readable names and the few fields the next step needs, not raw API dumps or bare UUIDs. A `response_format` option (concise / detailed) lets the agent ask for IDs only when it needs them.
Large results: filter, paginate and set sensible default limits; when you truncate, **say so** and tell the agent how to narrow the query. Silent truncation makes the agent reason from partial data.

**Narrow, purpose-built tools beat generic power tools** (`get_order_status(order_id)` over `run_sql(query)`): the backend can enforce ownership and read-only access, and the harness can gate and log a typed call.
Promote an action out of `bash` into a dedicated typed tool when it must be approved, audited or rendered (`send_email(to, subject, body)` rather than `curl` in a shell).
Tool design is a context-engineering decision: every definition and every result costs context. Fewer, better tools usually beat many thin wrappers around REST endpoints.
traps: Fixing wrong tool selection with `tool_choice` or a system-prompt rule when the real problem is overlapping or vague descriptions.
Adding more granular tools (`get_x_by_id`, `get_y_by_id`) when the agent is already drowning in calls; consolidate instead.
Returning every field "so Claude has maximum information"; it dilutes attention and burns context.
Silently truncating large outputs or silently mapping invalid input to a default value.
Giving the model a free-form `run_sql` / `bash` tool and relying on prompt rules to keep it safe.
lessons.drill: Take three tools from a real agent you run. For each, rewrite the description to answer: what it does, what it returns, when to call it, when NOT to call it. Then look at one real tool result and cut it to the fields the next step actually uses, adding a `response_format` switch. Re-run five transcripts and compare tool-selection errors and tokens per task.

lessons.title: Structured errors for MCP tools
lessons.summary: Questions here test whether a failed tool call gives the agent enough information to recover: reported in-band as an error result (`isError` in MCP, `is_error` on the API `tool_result`), classified so the agent knows whether retrying can help, and phrased as an actionable next step. The classic wrong answers are empty success, thrown exceptions, and generic failure text.
keyPoints: MCP has two error channels. **Protocol errors** (JSON-RPC `error`) are for unknown tools, malformed requests and server faults. **Tool execution errors** (API failures, invalid input data, business-logic failures) go in the tool result with `isError: true` so the model sees them and can adapt.

On the Messages API the equivalent is a `tool_result` with `is_error: true`, keeping the same `tool_use_id`, in the same user message as the turn's other results. Never throw out of the loop and never drop the result.
**Never return an empty or "success" result on failure.** The agent will treat it as real data ("no orders found") or retry the same call in a loop because nothing told it what went wrong.

Classify errors so the agent can choose a strategy: **transient** (timeout, rate limit: retry later, maybe with a `retry_after`), **validation** (bad argument: fix the input and call again), **business rule** (policy forbids it: don't retry, take another path such as escalation), **permission** (not authorised: don't retry, escalate or ask).

Make errors machine-readable as well as human-readable: a small consistent envelope such as `{error_category, retryable, message, suggested_action}` across all your MCP servers lets prompts and hooks react uniformly.

Error text should be **actionable**: name the field, the accepted format and an example ("`start_date` must be YYYY-MM-DD, got '3/4'"), or the alternative path ("refund exceeds the $500 agent limit; escalate with reason `over_limit`").
Distinguish **"no results"** (a valid, successful empty answer) from **"could not check"** (an error). Downstream agents and coordinators make very different decisions on each.
Handle cheap deterministic recovery (a bounded retry on a transient timeout) inside the tool or server; surface the error to the model when judgment is needed or retries are exhausted.
Keep stack traces, internal hostnames and secrets out of error text; they waste context and can leak. Log the detail server-side and give the model the actionable summary.
traps: Returning `""` or `[]` as a normal result when the backend call failed.
Letting an exception become a JSON-RPC error for a business-rule failure, so the client shows only a generic failure and the agent retries blindly.
Marking a business-rule or permission error as retryable, which produces identical retries until the loop cap.
Fixing a retry loop by rewriting the system prompt ("don't call the same tool twice") instead of fixing the error result.
Dumping the raw stack trace into the tool result as the "most informative" message.
lessons.drill: In a small MCP server, make one tool fail four ways: timeout, bad date format, policy refusal, missing permission. Return each as `isError: true` with a shared envelope (`error_category`, `retryable`, `message`, `suggested_action`). Connect it to Claude Code and watch how the agent's next move differs per category. Then change one to an empty success and observe the agent's behaviour.

lessons.title: Tool distribution and tool choice
lessons.summary: This task is about who gets which tools and how strongly you steer the call. The exam rewards giving each agent or subagent a small, role-scoped tool set, using tool search when a catalog is genuinely large, and choosing the right `tool_choice` mode, including knowing that forced modes are not available on every model.
keyPoints: **More tools degrade selection.** Anthropic's tool search docs note selection accuracy drops once an agent has more than about 30 to 50 tools available, and definitions alone can cost tens of thousands of tokens.

**Scope tools per role**: a coordinator gets delegation and synthesis tools; a search subagent gets search/fetch; a refund subagent gets refund tools. Least privilege also limits blast radius (an extractor should not hold `update_erp`).
Claude Code / Agent SDK subagents: `tools` lists exactly what the subagent gets; omit it and it **inherits every tool**; `disallowedTools` removes tools and wins if a tool is in both lists.

Allow vs restrict: `allowedTools` / `--allowedTools` only **pre-approves** tools; unlisted tools still exist. To restrict availability use `--tools` (built-ins), or a bare name in `disallowedTools` / `--disallowedTools`, which removes the tool from context. `--tools` does not affect MCP tools (`--disallowedTools "mcp__*"` does).

Large catalogs on the API: add the **tool search tool** and mark most tools `defer_loading: true`; keep the 3 to 5 most-used tools loaded; at least one tool must stay non-deferred. Claude Code applies MCP tool search by default.

`tool_choice` modes: `auto` (default: Claude decides) and `none` (no tool calls; the definitions stay in the request) work on every model. Changing `tool_choice` does not invalidate the cached tools and system prefix.
`disable_parallel_tool_use: true` caps Claude at **one** tool call per response; by default it may request several in parallel.

Forced modes (`any`, `{"type":"tool","name":...}`) existed for guaranteeing a call, but **current models (e.g. Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5) reject them with a 400**, including in Batches. For guaranteed structured output use **structured outputs** (`output_config.format`); to steer toward a tool use `auto` + a prompt naming the tool + `strict: true` on the tool.

Because `auto` never guarantees a call, the harness should **check that the expected tool was called and retry if not**; add `disable_parallel_tool_use: true` when exactly one call per turn is required.
traps: Giving every agent every tool "for flexibility": the coordinator starts doing subagent work and selection accuracy falls.
Thinking `allowedTools: ["Read", "Grep"]` makes an agent read-only. It only auto-approves those; Bash and Edit are still there.
Omitting `tools` on a subagent meant to be read-only; it inherits Edit and Bash.
Designing around forced `tool_choice` (`any` / named tool); current models return a 400. Use structured outputs or `auto` + strict + verify.
Deferring every tool, including the tool search tool, which is a 400.
lessons.drill: Build a coordinator with two subagents. Give the coordinator only the Agent tool, one subagent only search tools, the other only Read. Run a task and confirm in the transcript that each stays in its lane. Then remove `tools` from one subagent and watch it inherit everything. Finally, get the same extraction two ways (`output_config.format`, and `auto` + prompt + `strict: true` + a check that the tool was called) and compare.

lessons.title: MCP server integration
lessons.summary: Expect configuration and placement decisions: where a server is declared (project `.mcp.json` vs local or user scope), how secrets stay out of git, which transport fits, which MCP primitive fits a capability, and whether to adopt an existing server, write a custom tool, or build a new server.
keyPoints: Claude Code scopes: **local** (default, private to you, this project, stored in `~/.claude.json`), **project** (`.mcp.json` at the repo root, committed and shared; Claude Code asks for approval before using project servers), **user** (all your projects, private).
Same server name in several scopes: Claude Code uses the **whole entry** from the highest-precedence source (local, then project, then user); fields are not merged.
Secrets: `.mcp.json` supports `${VAR}` and `${VAR:-default}` in `command`, `args`, `env`, `url` and `headers`. Commit the file with placeholders; each developer or CI job supplies the value.
Transports: **stdio** for local processes the client launches; **Streamable HTTP** for remote, shared servers (with OAuth for per-user auth). The older SSE transport is deprecated.

Primitives: **tools** are model-controlled (Claude decides to call), **resources** are application-controlled context (in Claude Code, `@server:protocol://path`), **prompts** are user-controlled templates (in Claude Code, `/mcp__server__prompt`).

Build vs adopt: use an existing, maintained server for a common system (GitHub, Jira, a database) before writing your own; write a custom in-app tool when one application owns the capability; build an MCP server when several clients must reuse the same integration.
CI / scripted runs: `--mcp-config <file>` loads servers from a file and `--strict-mcp-config` ignores every other MCP configuration, so a pipeline gets exactly the servers it declares.
Claude Code warns on MCP tool output over 10,000 tokens and caps it at 25,000 by default (`MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS`). Design tools to paginate rather than raising the cap.
MCP tool names in permission rules and hook matchers take the form `mcp__<server>__<tool>`; `mcp__<server>__*` matches all of one server's tools.
traps: Committing tokens in `.mcp.json` because the repo is private.
Expecting a local-scope override and the project entry to merge (e.g. keep the project's auth header). The whole entry from one scope wins.
Choosing stdio for a server thousands of users reach remotely, or the deprecated SSE transport for a new remote server.
Building and hosting an MCP server for one function used by one app.
Mapping a user-picked template to a resource or a tool instead of a prompt.
lessons.drill: In a scratch repo, commit a `.mcp.json` with one stdio and one HTTP server whose credentials use `${VAR}`. Open Claude Code, approve the project servers, and check `/mcp`. Add a local-scope server with the same name and confirm the whole entry is replaced. Finally run `claude -p --mcp-config ci-mcp.json --strict-mcp-config` and confirm only the CI file's servers load.

lessons.title: Built-in tools
lessons.summary: The exam expects you to know what each Claude Code / Agent SDK built-in tool is for and how it behaves at the edges: content search vs path matching, Edit's exact unique-match rule and what to do when it fails, Write's full overwrite, what WebSearch and WebFetch actually return, and how tool names are used in permissions and subagent tool lists.
keyPoints: **Grep searches file contents** (ripgrep regex syntax, so escape metacharacters like `{`; output modes `files_with_matches` (default), `content`, `count`; filter with `glob` or `type`). **Glob matches file paths** by pattern (`src/**/*.ts`), returns paths sorted by modification time. Find files by name with Glob, find code by content with Grep. (On macOS/Linux Claude Code may run these searches as `grep`/`find` via Bash; the decision is the same.)
Exploration pattern for large codebases: Glob/Grep to locate, then **targeted Read** of the relevant files or line ranges, not reading whole directories.

**Edit is exact string replacement**: `old_string` must match exactly (whitespace included) and appear **exactly once**. If it matches several times, add surrounding context to make it unique, or set `replace_all: true` when every occurrence should change. No regex, no fuzzy matching.
**Write creates or fully overwrites** a file; it never appends or merges. Use Edit for partial changes; use Read then Write when a file needs a full rewrite or Edit cannot anchor a unique match.

**Read** returns file contents with line numbers; large files are read in pages with `offset`/`limit`; it also reads images, PDFs (page ranges for long ones) and notebooks. It refuses binary formats like `.xlsx` (use a skill or a script) and does not list directories.
**Bash** runs each command in a separate process: the working directory carries over inside the project, but **environment variables do not persist** between commands.

**WebSearch** returns result titles and URLs only (it does not fetch pages); scope with `allowed_domains` or `blocked_domains`. **WebFetch** fetches one URL and runs your extraction prompt over it, so the result is **lossy by design**; it refuses `localhost` and dotless intranet hostnames (use `curl` via Bash).
**Agent** (formerly Task) spawns a subagent with its own context; the parent sees only the final result. Restrict subagents with `tools` / `disallowedTools`.

Tool names are the strings used in permission rules, `--allowedTools`/`--disallowedTools`, subagent `tools` and hook matchers. Path rules for writing are `Edit(path)`, which also covers Write and NotebookEdit; a `Write(path)` rule matches nothing.
Before building a custom tool, check whether a built-in covers it; to use a different search backend than WebSearch, add an MCP server with a search tool.
traps: Using Glob to find where a function is called (that is a content search: Grep).
Retrying the same Edit after "found N matches"; the fix is more context or `replace_all`.
Using Write to "append" a line and wiping the rest of the file.
Assuming WebSearch results contain page text good enough to quote; fetch the page.
Exporting an env var in one Bash call and expecting the next call to see it.
Writing a deny rule as `Write(/infra/**)`; path rules for file writes use `Edit(...)`.
lessons.drill: In a repo you know, ask Claude Code to (1) find every file named `*.config.*` and (2) find every call to one function; note which search it uses for each. Make an Edit whose `old_string` appears three times and watch the failure, then fix it once with context and once with `replace_all`. Finally `export FOO=1` in one Bash call and `echo $FOO` in the next.

lessons.title: CLAUDE.md hierarchy
lessons.summary: The exam tests where an instruction should live so that the right people (and the CI runner) actually get it, how the files load, and what CLAUDE.md can and cannot guarantee. Most items are a diagnosis: a teammate or a pipeline doesn't get an instruction because it sits in the wrong scope or never loads.
keyPoints: **Scopes, broad to specific**: managed policy CLAUDE.md (deployed by IT, all users on the machine) → user `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` (you, every project) → project `./CLAUDE.md` or `./.claude/CLAUDE.md` (committed, the team) → local `./CLAUDE.local.md` (you, this project; add it to `.gitignore`).

Files in the working directory **and every ancestor** load at launch and are **concatenated**, not overridden; content closer to the launch directory is read last, and `CLAUDE.local.md` comes after `CLAUDE.md` at each level.
CLAUDE.md files in **subdirectories load on demand**, the first time Claude reads, writes or edits a file in that subdirectory (a single-file `cat`/`head` counts as a read).

`@path` imports: relative paths resolve from the importing file, recursion up to four hops, code spans are not imports, and an import outside the project triggers a one-time approval dialog. Imports organize; they **don't reduce context**, because they load with the parent.

Keep each file short (the docs target **under 200 lines**): build/test commands, conventions, 'always do X' rules written concretely enough to verify. Move procedures to **skills** and area-specific rules to **path-scoped `.claude/rules/`**.
CLAUDE.md is delivered as context after the system prompt: **guidance, not enforcement**. For 'must never happen', use permission `deny` rules (managed settings for org-wide) or a PreToolUse hook.
`claudeMdExcludes` (glob on absolute paths, any settings layer, arrays merge) skips irrelevant ancestor or other-team files in a monorepo; it **cannot** exclude the managed CLAUDE.md.

After `/compact`, the project-root CLAUDE.md is re-read from disk; instructions given only in conversation survive only as whatever the summary kept. Nested CLAUDE.md files and path-scoped rules reload on demand.

**CI**: only committed files exist on the runner, so `CLAUDE.local.md` and `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` don't apply there. `claude --bare` skips CLAUDE.md discovery entirely; pass what the run needs with `--append-system-prompt(-file)` or drop `--bare`.
Debug with `/context all` (Memory files list) and `/memory`; the `InstructionsLoaded` hook logs which instruction files load and why.
traps: Putting team conventions in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` or `CLAUDE.local.md`: teammates and the CI runner never see them.
Expecting a 'NEVER edit X' line in CLAUDE.md (even the managed one) to block an action. Only permissions and hooks enforce.
Splitting a long CLAUDE.md into `@imports` 'to save tokens'. Imports load with the parent.
Assuming every CLAUDE.md in the repo loads at launch. Subdirectory files wait until Claude touches a file there.
Adding `--bare` to a CI job for speed and then wondering why repo conventions are ignored.
lessons.drill: In a scratch repo create `CLAUDE.md`, `CLAUDE.local.md`, `pkg/a/CLAUDE.md` and an `@docs/extra.md` import. Start `claude` at the root, run `/context all`, then ask Claude to read a file in `pkg/a/` and watch the `Loaded` line. Finally run `claude --bare -p "what are this project's conventions?"` and compare.

lessons.title: Slash commands and skills
lessons.summary: The exam tests when to package knowledge or a procedure as a skill instead of CLAUDE.md, where skills live (shared vs personal vs plugin), and how frontmatter controls who can invoke a skill, what it may use and whether it runs in isolation.
keyPoints: A skill is a folder with `SKILL.md` (YAML frontmatter + instructions) plus optional supporting files and scripts. Custom commands in `.claude/commands/*.md` have been **merged into skills**: both create `/name`; prefer skills for new work.

**Locations**: project `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` (commit it to share), personal `~/.claude/skills/`, enterprise (managed), plugin (`/plugin-name:skill-name`). Nested `<subdir>/.claude/skills/` load the first time Claude touches a file in that subdirectory.
**Name clash**: enterprise beats personal, personal beats project; a skill beats a same-named `.claude/commands/` file; plugin skills don't clash because they are namespaced.

**Progressive disclosure**: only the description (plus `when_to_use`, truncated at 1,536 characters) sits in context each turn; the body loads on invocation; supporting files load only if Claude reads them; scripts run and only their output enters context.
The **description drives auto-invocation**: say what the skill does and when to use it, key use case first, in the words users actually type.

`disable-model-invocation: true` = only the user can run it (description not even in context; good for side-effecting `/deploy`). `user-invocable: false` = only Claude can load it (hidden from the `/` menu).

`allowed-tools` pre-approves tools for the turn that invokes the skill; `context: fork` (+ `agent`) runs the skill as an isolated subagent whose prompt is the skill body. It needs an actual task; a skill of bare guidelines returns nothing useful when forked.
`` !`command` `` runs a shell command **before** the skill content reaches Claude and splices in the output (e.g. `` !`gh pr diff` ``); a failing command aborts the invocation.
In `claude -p`, user-invoked skills and custom commands work: put `/skill-name args` in the prompt. `--bare` skips skill discovery (except skills in an `--add-dir` directory).

**Which mechanism**: always-true facts → CLAUDE.md; area-specific conventions → path-scoped rules; repeatable procedures or bulky reference → skill; distribution across many repos → plugin; guarantees → hooks/permissions.
traps: Confusing `disable-model-invocation: true` (user-only) with `user-invocable: false` (Claude-only).
A vague description ('helper utilities') and then wondering why Claude never auto-loads the skill.
Putting a team skill in `~/.claude/skills/`: it never reaches teammates or CI.
Using `context: fork` on a reference-only skill, or expecting a non-forked skill to keep its content out of the main context.
Believing skills and slash commands can't run in `claude -p`.

code.src:
---
name: pr-summary
description: Summarize a pull request's changes and risks. Use when asked to summarize, describe or explain a PR.
context: fork
agent: Explore
allowed-tools: Bash(gh *)
---
## Pull request context
- Diff: !`gh pr diff`
- Comments: !`gh pr view --comments`

Summarize what changed, why, and the riskiest hunks.

lessons.drill: Convert one multi-step procedure from your CLAUDE.md into `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`. Write two descriptions (vague vs specific) and test whether Claude auto-invokes each from a natural request. Then add `disable-model-invocation: true` and confirm only `/name` runs it, and run it once via `claude -p "/name arg"`.

lessons.title: Path-specific rules
lessons.summary: The exam tests scoping conventions to the files they govern with `.claude/rules/*.md` and `paths:` frontmatter, so they load only when Claude works on matching files, and diagnosing rules that load too often or never.
keyPoints: Rules live in `.claude/rules/` (discovered **recursively**, one topic per file). Rules **without** `paths` load at launch with the same priority as `.claude/CLAUDE.md`.

`paths` is the **only** frontmatter field Claude Code reads from a rule (YAML list or comma-separated string). Any other field (`globs`, `description`, ...) is ignored silently, so a rule with only an unrecognized field behaves as unconditional.
If the frontmatter YAML doesn't parse, it is ignored and the rule loads as if it had no `paths`; `claude --debug` shows the parse error.

A path-scoped rule loads when Claude uses **Read, Write or Edit** on a matching file (or a Bash single-file read such as `cat`). Content that arrives some other way, such as a diff piped on stdin, triggers nothing.

Patterns are relative to the rule's **base directory**: the directory containing the rule's `.claude` folder (for `~/.claude/rules/`, the session's primary working directory). Examples: `**/*.test.ts`, `src/api/**/*.ts`, `src/**/*.{ts,tsx}`.
**Rules vs subdirectory CLAUDE.md**: a nested CLAUDE.md covers one directory tree; a rule's globs can cut across the tree (all test files, all migrations, all `.tf` files) without duplicating files.
**Rules vs skills**: rules load automatically when matching files are touched; skills load when invoked or when Claude judges them relevant to the prompt. Task procedures belong in skills.
User-level rules in `~/.claude/rules/` apply to every project and load before project rules; neither overrides the other, so conflicts make behaviour unpredictable.

Excluding `project` from `--setting-sources` skips project rules. With `--add-dir` (and `CLAUDE_CODE_ADDITIONAL_DIRECTORIES_CLAUDE_MD=1`) the extra directory's unconditional rules load but its `paths` rules do not.
traps: Writing `globs:` or `applyTo:` (other tools' syntax) instead of `paths:`. The rule silently becomes always-on.
Writing patterns relative to the repo root for a rule that lives in a nested package's `.claude/rules/`.
Expecting a path rule to apply in a CI review that only sees a piped diff.
Solving context bloat with `@imports` instead of path scoping.
Creating 30 identical subdirectory CLAUDE.md files for a convention one glob could cover.

code.src:
---
paths:
  - "src/api/**/*.ts"
  - "tests/api/**/*.test.ts"
---
# API rules
- Validate every request body with the shared zod schemas
- Return errors via `apiError(code, message)` only

lessons.drill: Add `.claude/rules/tests.md` with `paths: ["**/*.test.ts"]`. Start a session, run `/context all` (the rule is absent), ask Claude to open a test file, and confirm it now loads. Then rename `paths` to `globs` and observe that it loads at launch.

lessons.title: Plan mode vs direct execution
lessons.summary: The exam tests choosing between planning first and just doing it: plan mode for large, ambiguous, multi-file or architectural changes; direct execution for small, well-scoped fixes; and subagents to keep discovery output out of the main context.
keyPoints: **Plan mode** (`Shift+Tab`, a `/plan` prefix, or `--permission-mode plan`): Claude reads files, runs exploratory commands and writes a plan, but **source edits stay blocked until you approve**.

On approval you pick how to continue (for example auto mode/auto-accept edits, or manually approve edits) or **No, keep planning** with feedback. `Ctrl+G` opens the plan in your editor so you can fix it before any code changes.
Plan mode keeps its blocks in non-interactive runs: `claude -p --permission-mode plan` is a safe way to have CI produce a proposal without touching code.

Use plan mode when the approach is uncertain, many files or modules are involved, the code is unfamiliar, or a wrong direction is expensive. Skip it when the fix is small and well located (a one-line bug with a failing test, a rename in one file).
Correcting a plan is cheap; correcting a half-implemented wrong approach is expensive. Review the plan for the decisions that matter (data model, migration order, API shape) before approving.

The built-in **Explore** subagent (read-only; Write/Edit denied) does searches in its own context window, and the **Plan** subagent does research during plan mode, so only findings return to the main conversation.
Explore and Plan start **without CLAUDE.md**; put anything they must respect into the delegation prompt.
For long efforts, write the approved plan or spec to a file and start the implementation in a fresh session from it, rather than dragging a compacted, noisy exploration context along.
In automation, separate 'propose' from 'apply': a plan-mode job produces the plan, a human approves, then an edit-capable job implements it.
traps: Using plan mode for every trivial fix (slow, no benefit) or skipping it for a cross-cutting migration.
Asking for 'a plan first' in normal mode and assuming nothing will be edited. Only plan mode blocks edits.
Approving a flawed plan and planning to fix it during implementation.
Reading hundreds of files into the main conversation instead of delegating exploration.
Assuming the Explore subagent knows your CLAUDE.md conventions.

code.src:
# CI: propose, don't apply
claude -p "Propose an implementation plan for issue #412" \
  --permission-mode plan --output-format json > plan.json

docs.title: Common workflows: plan before editing, delegate research

lessons.drill: Pick a cross-module change. Run it once in plan mode: edit the plan with `Ctrl+G`, then approve. Run a one-line bug fix directly. Then ask 'use a subagent to investigate how X works' and compare the main context size (`/context`) with reading the files yourself.

lessons.title: Iterative refinement
lessons.summary: The exam tests how to get Claude Code to converge on the right result: concrete examples instead of adjectives, a pass/fail check it can run (tests first), interview-style clarification when requirements are fuzzy, and deciding whether to give interacting issues together or one at a time.
keyPoints: **Concrete input/output examples** beat descriptions ('make dates nicer'): show 2-3 exact before → after pairs, including edge cases.
**Give Claude a check to run**: a test file, build exit code, linter or fixture diff. With pass/fail feedback Claude closes the loop itself; put the exact test command in CLAUDE.md.

**Test-driven iteration**: write (or have Claude write) tests from the spec, confirm they fail, commit them, then have Claude implement until green **without changing the tests**. A deny rule on the test path makes that deterministic.

Enforcement ladder for 'done': prompt ('keep going until tests pass') → `/goal` → a **Stop hook** that exits 2 to send Claude back to work. Always ask for evidence (command + output), not 'all tests pass'.
**Interview first** when requirements are fuzzy: 'interview me until you could write the spec, then write SPEC.md', then build from it in a fresh session.
Issues that **interact** (they touch the same calculation or code path) go in **one message** so fixes are designed together; independent issues can go one at a time.
After two failed corrections, `/clear` and write a better prompt that folds in what you learned; `Esc` early when Claude drifts; `/rewind` to try a bolder approach safely.
Unattended runs can't ask questions: state what done looks like, what it may touch, what stops it (`--max-turns`, `--max-budget-usd`) and who signs off.
For legacy code without tests, write characterization tests first, then refactor in small steps.
traps: Adding 'IMPORTANT' or capital letters instead of an example or a test.
Letting Claude edit the tests it is supposed to satisfy.
Feeding three interacting bugs one at a time so each fix breaks the previous one.
Retrying a failed headless run with the identical prompt and no failure details.
Trusting 'done' without a check whose output you can read.

code.src:
Fix formatDuration(). Expected:
  formatDuration(59)    -> "59s"
  formatDuration(3600)  -> "1h"
  formatDuration(3661)  -> "1h 1m 1s"
  formatDuration(0)     -> "0s"
Add these as cases in duration.test.ts first, run `pnpm vitest run duration`,
confirm they fail, then fix the function until they pass. Don't edit the tests.

docs.title: Best practices: give Claude a check to run

lessons.drill: Take a small function with a known bug. Prompt once with a vague description, then with four concrete input/output pairs written as failing tests. Compare the number of correction rounds. Add a project deny rule on the test file and observe Claude fixing the source instead.

lessons.title: Claude Code in CI/CD
lessons.summary: The exam tests running Claude Code unattended: `claude -p` with machine-readable output, permissions that neither hang nor over-grant, the committed repo config as CI context, an independent review session, and keeping review cost proportional to what changed.
keyPoints: `claude -p "..."` runs non-interactively; exit code is 0 on success. `--output-format json` returns `result`, `session_id`, usage and `total_cost_usd`; `stream-json` streams events.
`--json-schema '<schema>'` (print mode) adds a validated `structured_output` field. If the run ends without valid structured output the field is absent, so check for it.

**Permissions**: `--allowedTools` pre-approves (e.g. `"Read,Edit,Bash(npm test *)"`; the space before `*` matters); `--tools` restricts which built-ins exist; `--permission-mode dontAsk` denies anything not pre-approved. Never `bypassPermissions` outside an isolated container.

Permission rules merge across scopes and evaluate **deny → ask → allow**; a local allow can't override a project deny. Bash rules match command text only, so pair them with **sandboxing** for network/file isolation.
**Caps**: `--max-turns`, `--max-budget-usd` (client-side estimate; leave headroom), plus job `timeout-minutes`/concurrency in GitHub Actions (`claude_args` carries CLI flags).

Only committed config reaches the runner: project `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/settings.json`, `.claude/rules/`, `.claude/skills/`, `.mcp.json`. `--bare` skips all of that for reproducibility; pass needs explicitly (`--append-system-prompt-file`, `--settings`, `--mcp-config`).
Without `--bare`, `-p` runs the repo's hooks and MCP servers with no trust dialog. Be careful with untrusted PRs.
**Independent review**: review generated code in a separate session that never saw the generator's reasoning, not via `--continue` or a fork of the generating session.
**Incremental review**: on new pushes review only the commits since the last reviewed SHA and pass prior findings so only new or unresolved issues are reported.
Sessions: capture `session_id` from JSON and `--resume` it; `--continue` picks the most recent session and is unsafe with parallel jobs.
traps: `bypassPermissions` 'so the job doesn't hang'. Use narrow `--allowedTools` + `dontAsk` (+ sandbox).
Asking the generating session to review its own diff.
Re-reviewing the whole PR on every push and re-posting the same comments.
Scraping text output instead of `--output-format json` / `--json-schema`.
Relying on CLAUDE.md lines like 'never push' as a CI control.

code.src:
claude -p "Review the diff in diff.patch against CLAUDE.md criteria" \
  --allowedTools "Read,Grep,Glob" \
  --permission-mode dontAsk \
  --max-turns 15 \
  --output-format json \
  --json-schema "$(cat review.schema.json)" | jq '.structured_output'

lessons.drill: Write a script that runs `claude -p` on a diff with `--output-format json --json-schema` for `{findings:[{file,line,severity,message}]}`, `--allowedTools "Read,Grep,Glob"` and `--permission-mode dontAsk`. Make it exit non-zero when `structured_output` is missing or contains a `high` finding.

lessons.title: Prompts with explicit criteria
lessons.summary: The exam tests whether you replace vague adjectives ("be conservative", "flag anything important", "high quality") with concrete, checkable criteria: what to act on, what to skip, and how to grade severity. Expect scenarios where a reviewer or classifier produces too many false positives or inconsistent judgments and you must pick the prompt change that fixes the cause.
keyPoints: **Be clear and direct**: state the goal, audience, output format and constraints. Anthropic's test: if a colleague with minimal context would be confused by the prompt, Claude will be too.

Vague qualifiers ("be careful", "only important issues", "be conservative with refunds") leave the threshold to the model, so results drift between runs and inputs. Replace them with **observable conditions** ("flag only if the change can cause data loss, a security hole or a crash on a reachable path").

Define **what to flag AND what to skip**. Explicit exclusions (style, naming, pre-existing code, speculative issues without a concrete trigger) are the main lever for cutting false positives in review and triage prompts.
A reviewer told to find problems will always find *something*. Scope it ("report gaps that affect correctness and skip style") or you end up acting on noise.

**Severity levels need definitions and an example each**, e.g. `critical` = exploitable or data-corrupting in production; `minor` = correct but harder to maintain. Undefined labels collapse into "everything is high".

**Give the why**: the reason behind a rule ("findings are posted as PR comments that block merge, so only report what a senior engineer would block on") lets Claude generalise to cases the rule did not list.
Current models follow instructions closely: old `CRITICAL: you MUST ALWAYS…` emphasis causes **over-triggering**. Use normal phrasing and say *when* the behaviour applies.

Criteria that must never be violated (refund limits, required steps) belong in **code** (hooks, validation, tool gating); explicit prompt criteria improve judgment but are not an enforcement boundary.
Prove a criteria change with an **eval set** (labelled true and false positives), not by eyeballing one run.
traps: Adding "be more careful" or "only report real issues" to fix false positives. It restates the vague goal; define the criteria and exclusions instead.
Switching to a bigger model to fix inconsistent judgments that come from an undefined threshold.
Shouting (CRITICAL / MUST / ALWAYS) to make a rule stick. On current models it over-triggers.
Asking for a confidence score and filtering on it instead of defining what qualifies. Self-reported confidence is not calibrated against your criteria.
Relying on prompt criteria alone for a hard business rule such as a refund ceiling.

code.src:
<review_criteria>
Report a finding ONLY if it is one of:
- correctness: the changed code produces a wrong result on a realistic input
- security: injection, auth bypass, or secret exposure introduced by this diff
- data: a migration or write path that can lose or corrupt data
Do NOT report: style, naming, formatting, missing comments, issues in
unchanged lines, or hypothetical problems without a concrete trigger.
Severity: blocker = must fix before merge (give the failing input);
warning = real but low impact. If nothing qualifies, return no findings.
</review_criteria>

lessons.drill: Take a review or triage prompt you use. Run it on 10 inputs and label each finding true/false positive. Rewrite it with explicit include/exclude criteria and defined severities (one example each), re-run on the same 10, and compare the false-positive count.

lessons.title: Few-shot prompting
lessons.summary: The exam tests when examples beat more instructions (ambiguous judgment calls, exact output format, edge-case handling) and how to build them: a few relevant, diverse examples in tags, ideally showing the reasoning for the hard cases. Expect symptoms such as inconsistent formatting, copied surface patterns or mis-handled edge cases.
keyPoints: Examples are **one of the most reliable ways** to steer output format, tone and structure. Anthropic's guidance: make them relevant, **diverse**, and structured; **3–5** is a good default.
Wrap each in `<example>` tags inside `<examples>` so Claude can separate them from instructions and from the real input.

Few-shot wins over more prose when the rule is hard to state but easy to show: ambiguous classifications, borderline cases, exact output shape (date format, how to write a missing field, null vs omitted).

Cover the **edge cases** that are failing: a document with a missing field, a conflicting value, an "other" category, a case that should produce no output. Examples that only show the happy path teach only the happy path.
For judgment calls, show **why**: an example with a short rationale ("flagged because the clause auto-renews without notice") teaches the decision boundary, not just the label.
Claude matches examples' length, phrasing and structure. Near-identical examples get copied; vary surface form deliberately and label them as illustrative.
Pair positive and **contrastive** examples near the boundary (one that should be flagged, a similar one that should not) to cut false positives.
Examples add input tokens on every call: keep the static examples block early in the prompt so it can be prompt-cached.
Worked examples also shape how Claude reasons in its thinking: present each as problem, method, answer.
traps: Adding a paragraph of extra rules for an ambiguity that two contrasting examples would settle.
Five examples from the same document type or author: the model copies their length and phrasing onto very different inputs.
Examples that never show the edge case (missing value, no findings), so the model invents a value or a finding.
Examples whose output format disagrees with the stated schema or instructions: the model follows the examples.
Treating more examples as always better. Relevance and diversity matter more than volume.

code.src:
<examples>
<example>
<clause>Either party may terminate with 30 days' written notice.</clause>
<output>{"risk": "none", "reason": "mutual, standard notice"}</output>
</example>
<example>
<clause>This agreement renews automatically for successive 3-year terms.</clause>
<output>{"risk": "high", "reason": "auto-renewal with no opt-out window"}</output>
</example>
</examples>

docs.title: Prompting best practices: use examples effectively

lessons.drill: Pick a classification prompt with a known confusing boundary. Write two pairs of contrastive examples (one flagged, one not, each with a one-line reason) plus one 'no output' example. Compare accuracy on 15 borderline inputs before and after.

lessons.title: Structured output with JSON schemas
lessons.summary: The exam tests how to guarantee machine-parseable output (structured outputs via `output_config.format`, or `strict: true` tools) and how to design the schema so it does not force bad data: required vs nullable fields, enums with an escape hatch, clear types and units. It also tests the difference between syntactically valid and semantically correct.
keyPoints: **JSON outputs**: `output_config: {format: {type: "json_schema", schema}}` constrains decoding so the response matches the schema. SDK helpers (`messages.parse()` with Pydantic/Zod) also return typed, validated objects.
**Strict tool use**: `strict: true` on a tool definition guarantees tool inputs match its `input_schema`. Every object needs `additionalProperties: false`.
Prompt-only "respond with JSON only" and assistant prefill are obsolete: prefill returns a 400 on recent model generations; use structured outputs.

**Required means the model must produce a value.** If the source can lack a field, a required non-null field forces fabrication. Make it nullable (or optional) and describe what null means ("not present in the document").
**Enums** for closed sets; add an `"other"` value plus a free-text `*_detail` field so unexpected inputs are captured instead of being forced into the nearest wrong category.
Describe each property: type, unit, format (ISO 8601 dates, amounts as numbers with a separate currency code). Schema descriptions are instructions the model reads.
Some JSON Schema features (e.g. numeric/length constraints, recursion) are not supported for constrained decoding; SDK helpers strip them and validate client-side.
**Schema-valid is not correct.** Constrained decoding guarantees shape, not truth: totals can still disagree, IDs can be wrong. Semantic checks belong in code (D4.4).
Check `stop_reason` before parsing: `max_tokens` (truncated) or `refusal` output may not match the schema.
traps: Making every field required "for completeness": the model invents plausible values for absent data.
A closed enum with no `other`: novel document types get silently forced into the wrong bucket.
Believing structured outputs make extracted values accurate.
Retrying parse failures in a loop when the response was truncated (`max_tokens`).
Keeping a JSON-forcing prefill when migrating to a newer model.
lessons.drill: Take an extraction schema and list every field the source documents can lack. Make those nullable with a description of null, add `other` + detail to each enum, then run 10 documents with missing data and count fabricated values before and after.

lessons.title: Validation and retry loops
lessons.summary: The exam tests the loop around the model: validate semantics in code, retry with the specific error fed back, cap retries, and recognise when retrying cannot help because the information is not in the source. Expect scenarios where a pipeline either retries blindly, gives up too early, or accepts schema-valid but wrong data.
keyPoints: Structured outputs give valid syntax; **semantic validation is your code's job**: totals equal the sum of line items, end date after start date, IDs exist, values fall in allowed ranges.

On failure, **retry with the specific error** ("line items sum to 1,180.00 but total is 1,280.00; re-read the totals section") plus the original document and the previous output. A bare "try again" repeats the same mistake.
**Cap retries** (often 1–2) and route persistent failures to human review or a fallback queue with the error attached.
**Know when retry can't help**: if the value is absent or illegible in the source, re-asking produces fabrication or the same failure. Return null/"not found" and route to review instead.

**Self-correction fields**: ask for both the value as stated in the document and the value computed from parts (e.g. `stated_total` and `calculated_total`), plus a flag for conflicts. Code compares them; mismatches become review items rather than silent errors.
Retry only the failing step or item, not the whole chain or batch.
Truncation (`stop_reason: max_tokens`) and refusals are not validation errors: retrying unchanged fails the same way; fix the cause or branch.
Log validation failures by type: recurring errors point to a prompt, example or schema fix rather than more retries.
traps: Retrying until the output passes validation, with no cap: an absent value eventually gets invented to satisfy the check.
Retrying with a generic message and no error detail.
Treating a schema-valid response as correct and skipping business-rule checks.
Asking the model to self-report whether its numbers are consistent instead of computing the check in code.
Restarting the whole multi-step pipeline when one step fails.
lessons.drill: Add two semantic checks (a sum and a date order) after an extraction call. Feed failures back with the exact numbers, cap at two attempts, and log which documents still fail; inspect whether those documents actually contain the data.

lessons.title: Message Batches API
lessons.summary: The exam tests when to move work to the Message Batches API (bulk, non-blocking, cost-sensitive) and when not to (someone is waiting, a deadline tighter than the processing window, or a multi-turn tool loop). It also checks the mechanics that affect design: `custom_id` correlation, unordered results, and resubmitting only failed items.
keyPoints: Batches are **asynchronous** and priced at **50%** of standard rates; the discount stacks with prompt caching.
Processing can take **up to 24 hours** and there is **no latency SLA**; requests not finished by then expire. Many batches finish much faster, but you cannot design on that.
Good fit: overnight extraction backlogs, re-classification of archives, eval suites, nightly reports—anything nobody is waiting on.
Bad fit: interactive or blocking paths (a user uploading one invoice and waiting, a pre-merge CI check), and any deadline shorter than the processing window.

Each batch request is a **single Messages call**: there is no multi-turn tool loop inside a request. Agentic work that needs tool results mid-task stays real-time, unless you restructure it (pre-fetch inputs so one call suffices).
Results are **not returned in submission order**: correlate with `custom_id` (use a stable business key such as a document ID).
Per-request outcomes: `succeeded`, `errored`, `canceled`, `expired`. Only succeeded requests are billed. Resubmit **only** failed/expired items; fix invalid requests before resending.
A common hybrid: real-time for the interactive path, batch for the backlog and for low-priority re-processing (e.g. validation retries that can wait until the next run).
traps: Moving a user-facing or merge-blocking step to batch to save cost.
Assuming a batch will finish in an hour because it usually does.
Mapping results back by array position instead of `custom_id`.
Trying to run a multi-step tool-using agent inside one batch request.
Resubmitting the entire batch because a few hundred requests failed.
lessons.drill: Split one of your workloads into 'someone waits' vs 'nobody waits'. For the second, write the batch submit + results loop keyed by `custom_id`, and a function that builds a follow-up batch from only the errored/expired IDs.

lessons.title: Multi-pass review
lessons.summary: The exam tests how to structure review so it actually catches problems: an independent reviewer instance that did not generate the work, per-unit passes followed by a cross-unit integration pass, and scoped criteria so the reviewer reports what matters. Expect scenarios where one model reviews its own output in the same context, or one giant pass over a large change misses issues.
keyPoints: A generator reviewing its own output **in the same context** is anchored on the reasoning that produced it. A **fresh instance** (separate session, subagent or `claude -p` call) that never saw that reasoning is a better reviewer.
Claude Code's `/code-review` reviews the diff in a fresh subagent that never saw the conversation; a second session reviewing a file without having watched it being written is the same idea.
Give the reviewer **fewer tools** where possible (e.g. a subagent limited to `Read, Grep, Glob`): it cannot "fix" what it should only report, and the limit is enforced, not requested.

**Attention dilution**: one pass over 40 files or 30 sources gives each item shallow attention. Run **per-file (or per-document) local passes**, then a separate **cross-file integration pass** over summaries/interfaces for issues no single file shows (contract mismatches, duplicated logic, inconsistent claims).
Review **against explicit criteria or a spec** (D4.1) and tell the reviewer what to skip; an unscoped reviewer always finds something.
In CI, review only what changed (the diff, or files changed since the last reviewed commit) rather than re-reviewing the whole repo every run.
Multiple independent reviewers (voting) raise recall for high-stakes checks, at extra cost; use it where a miss is expensive.
Delegating the same task to a subagent does not make the answer better by itself; the benefit comes from the reviewer's **independence** and focus.
traps: Appending "now review your work for bugs" to the generator's own conversation and calling it a review stage.
One mega-prompt reviewing an entire large PR or report at once.
Only doing per-file passes and missing cross-file contract breaks.
Giving the reviewer write access and letting it silently rewrite the code it reviews.
Using a bigger context window as the cure for a pass that misses issues.

code.src:
---
name: reviewer
description: Reviews changed files against the spec they were built from. Use after implementing a feature, before opening the PR.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob
---
You are reviewing code you did not write. Compare each changed file with the
spec you are given. Report only correctness gaps and missing tests for listed
edge cases, with file and line. Skip style.

lessons.drill: Generate a small feature in one Claude Code session. Review it (a) by asking the same session to review its work and (b) with a read-only reviewer subagent given the spec. Compare which real issues each found.

lessons.title: Context across long conversations
lessons.summary: Long conversations and long agent runs lose information in predictable ways: summaries paraphrase away exact numbers and dates, verbose tool output crowds out what matters, and details buried in the middle of a long context get less attention. The exam tests whether you keep critical facts in a durable, structured place instead of trusting the transcript to carry them.
keyPoints: Context is a **finite attention budget**. Recall of any one detail degrades as total tokens grow (**context rot**), even well below the window limit. A bigger window is not a fix.

**Progressive summarisation is lossy.** Compaction keeps the gist but turns `$46.80 refund for order #A-1182, promised by Friday` into 'a partial refund was discussed'. Exact amounts, IDs, dates and commitments are what gets lost first.

Keep a **persistent case-facts block**: a structured record (customer ID, verified identity, order IDs, amounts, dates, promises made, decisions taken) that your code updates from tool results and injects on every turn, **outside** the history that gets summarised.

**Trim tool output at the source.** Tools should return the fields the agent needs, keyed by ID, with parameters for more detail. Raw payloads cost tokens on every later turn and bury the relevant values.

**Position matters in long inputs.** Put long documents at the top and the question and instructions at the end; wrap documents in tags with source metadata. Information in the middle of a very long context is the most likely to be missed, so split very long inputs into sections and process each one.

In Claude Code and the Agent SDK, **auto-compaction** may drop instructions from early in the conversation. Put persistent rules in **CLAUDE.md** (re-injected on every request), not in the first prompt.
Steer what compaction keeps with a summary-instructions section in CLAUDE.md or `/compact <focus>`. A `PreCompact` hook can archive the full transcript before it is summarised.
Subagents return only their final message, so delegating noisy work keeps the parent's history short. Ask them for **condensed, structured** results.
For work that spans days, persist state externally (a store or notes file) and start a fresh session that loads it, rather than dragging one huge, stale transcript forward.
traps: Treating a larger context window as the cure. It delays the problem and makes the middle of the context easier to miss.
Telling the summariser to 'be accurate' instead of moving exact facts into a structured block that is never summarised.
Putting a durable rule in the opening prompt of a long session and expecting it to survive compaction.
Asking the model to ignore irrelevant fields in a huge tool result. The tokens are still in context; filter in the tool.
Letting the model maintain the facts block by free-text rewriting. Update it in code from tool results so values are copied, not paraphrased.

code.src:
case_facts = {
    "customer_id": "C-20931", "identity_verified": True,
    "orders": {"A-1182": {"total": "46.80", "status": "delivered_damaged"}},
    "commitments": ["Refund 46.80 to original card for A-1182"],
}
# Rebuilt by code after every tool call, injected each turn,
# never passed through the summariser.
system = BASE_PROMPT + "\n<case_facts>\n" + json.dumps(case_facts) + "\n</case_facts>"
