How the agent loop works (context window, compaction)
How Claude Code works: the context window

lessons.drill: Take a 30-turn support transcript that includes three order IDs, two amounts and a promised date. Summarise turns 1 to 20 with a plain 'summarise this conversation' prompt and list which exact values survived. Then add a case-facts dict that your code updates from tool results and injects each turn, rerun, and check that every value reaches turn 30 unchanged.

lessons.title: Escalation and ambiguity
lessons.summary: A reliable agent knows when to stop acting on its own. The exam tests the escalation triggers that hold up in production (an explicit request for a human, a policy gap, or no progress) against tempting ones that don't (sentiment, self-reported confidence), and whether the agent asks a clarifying question instead of guessing when the input is ambiguous.
keyPoints: **Escalate when:** the customer explicitly asks for a human; the request falls in a **policy gap** or needs an exception the agent isn't authorised to make; or the agent **cannot make progress** (repeated tool failures, required information unavailable after asking).
**Honour an explicit request for a human immediately.** Don't try one more fix first or argue the customer out of it. Hand off with a summary.

**Sentiment is not a trigger by itself.** An angry customer with a solvable, in-policy issue should get the issue solved, with a human offered if they ask. Escalating on tone sends easy tickets to humans and keeps hard, calm ones.
**Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated.** 'Escalate if confidence < 0.7' rests on a number the model makes up. Use explicit, observable criteria and check them against labelled transcripts.

**Ambiguity means ask, don't guess.** When a lookup returns several matching customers, or a request could refer to several targets, ask for a distinguishing identifier. Acting on the wrong account is worse than one extra question.
Write escalation criteria into the prompt **with examples of borderline cases** (few-shot), and enforce hard limits such as refund caps in code or hooks so they can't be talked past.

**Escalation handoff = structured summary**: customer and verified identity, the issue, what was tried, facts established, why it is being escalated, and a recommended next step. The human usually doesn't read the transcript.

In a non-interactive run (CI, batch) there is nobody to ask. Make 'needs a human decision' a **first-class output** (a status field, a label, a comment) instead of letting the agent pick an interpretation.
For a coordinator, a cheap clarifying question about scope **before** fanning out to subagents saves the cost of researching the wrong question.
traps: Auto-escalating on negative sentiment or caps-lock while calm customers with real policy gaps stay with the bot.
Thresholding on the model's own confidence score as the escalation trigger.
Picking the 'most likely' customer record (most recent, most active) when several match.
Trying to resolve the issue one more time after the customer has asked for a person.
Escalating with 'customer needs help, see transcript' instead of a structured handoff.

code.src:
## When to hand off (call escalate_to_human)
- The customer asks for a person, in any wording. Do it now.
- The request needs something policy does not cover
  (e.g. price matching, refunds on final-sale items).
- Two tool attempts have failed, or you still lack required
  information after asking once.
Do NOT escalate only because the customer is upset.
If a lookup returns more than one customer, ask for the
order number or account email before doing anything else.

lessons.drill: Write ten short support openers: two explicit human requests, two angry-but-in-policy, two policy gaps, two ambiguous customer lookups, two routine. Write an escalation section for a support system prompt, run all ten, and count how many land on the correct action (resolve, ask, or escalate). Rewrite until sentiment alone never triggers a handoff.

lessons.title: Error propagation
lessons.summary: In multi-step and multi-agent systems, how a failure is reported decides whether the final answer is honest. The exam tests whether subagents and tools return structured error context the coordinator can act on, whether the design tells 'could not check' apart from 'checked and found nothing', and whether one failure leads to a partial, clearly labelled result rather than a silent gap or a total abort.
keyPoints: A subagent's result should carry a **status** (complete / partial / failed), **what was attempted** (queries, sources, tools), the **error category** (transient, permission/access, not found, invalid input), **partial results**, and **suggested alternatives**. The coordinator then chooses to retry, reroute, or proceed with the gap marked.
**'Access failed' is not 'no results'.** A timed-out search returned as an empty list becomes 'no evidence exists' in the final report. Make the two cases different in the schema.
**Never swallow errors into an empty success.** `[]`, `null` or 'nothing found' on failure silently turns into false negatives downstream.
**Don't abort everything on one failure.** Continue with the remaining work and report coverage: what was done, what failed, what is unknown.
**Recover locally first.** The component closest to the error retries transient failures with a bound and backs off. It passes up only what it can't resolve, with context.

MCP: **tool execution errors** (API failures, invalid data, business-rule errors) go in the tool result with `isError: true` so the model sees them and can adapt; **protocol errors** (unknown tool, bad arguments) are JSON-RPC errors. In the Messages API the equivalent is `is_error: true` on the `tool_result`.

Agent SDK / `claude -p`: check the result **`subtype`** (`success`, `error_max_turns`, `error_max_budget_usd`, `error_during_execution`, ...) before reading `result`. `claude -p` exits non-zero on failure, and `structured_output` is absent when no valid output was produced, so check that it is present.

Long-running multi-agent systems should **resume from a checkpoint** where the error happened rather than restart, and tell the agent when a tool is failing so it can adapt (Anthropic's research-system write-up).
In extraction pipelines, keep a per-document **processing status** separate from field values: `null` should mean 'not in the document', never 'couldn't read the document'.
traps: Returning 'No relevant sources found' when the search tool timed out.
Aborting a 20-subagent research run because one source was paywalled.
Dumping a raw stack trace or full transcript to the coordinator instead of a structured, actionable summary.
Writing `jq '.structured_output.findings // []'`, which turns a failed run into 'no findings'.
Putting all retry logic in the coordinator so a transient blip reruns an entire subagent.

docs.title: How we built our multi-agent research system
How the agent loop works (handle the result)

lessons.drill: Build a two-subagent research script where one subagent's search tool randomly times out. Version 1 returns an empty list on timeout; version 2 returns the structured status above. Run each ten times and compare the final reports: count how often version 1 claims something 'does not exist' and confirm that version 2 always lists the gap.

lessons.title: Large codebase context
lessons.summary: On a large repository you can't load everything, so the exam tests how you pull in the right slice: search first and then read only the targeted files, isolate exploration in subagents, carry state across context boundaries in files, and use `/clear` and `/compact` at the right moments.
keyPoints: **Just-in-time retrieval**: CLAUDE.md loads up front, and Claude finds the rest with **Grep** (content search) and **Glob** (path patterns), then **Read**s only the files that matched. Paths are cheap references; file contents are expensive.
Delegate broad discovery to a **subagent** (for example the built-in Explore agent). Its searches and reads stay in its own context, and the main session receives a summary.
**`/clear`** between unrelated tasks. **`/compact <focus>`** to continue the same task with less history. A summary-instructions section in CLAUDE.md steers auto-compaction.

For work that spans sessions or people, keep a **notes or progress file** (checklist of migrated files, decisions, open questions) that Claude updates as it goes and reads at the start of each session.

**Summarise before changing phase**: when investigation ends, have Claude write findings (files involved, constraints, decisions) to a file, then start the implementation in a fresh context that references it.

Don't pull huge artifacts into context. Use `grep`, `head` or `tail` on a large log, or delegate the analysis. If one output is so big that context refills after every summary, Claude Code stops auto-compacting and reports an error instead of looping.
Run **`/context`** to see what is using the window. MCP tool definitions are deferred by default via tool search, and skills load their full content only when used.
Sessions start fresh. Durable conventions belong in CLAUDE.md; one-off investigation output does not.
traps: 'Read every file under src/ first so Claude has the full picture.'
Keeping one session running for days so Claude 'remembers everything', instead of a notes file and fresh sessions.
Using `/compact` between unrelated tasks (keeps irrelevant history) or `/clear` mid-task (throws away decisions you need).
Pasting or catting a multi-megabyte log into the conversation.
Putting investigation logs into CLAUDE.md, which then loads into every future session.

code.src:
# MIGRATION.md  (Claude updates this; read it first each session)
## Decisions
- New client: `httpx.AsyncClient`, one per service, in `core/http.py`
- Timeouts come from `settings.HTTP_TIMEOUT_S`, never hard-coded
## Progress (142 / 410 files)
- [x] services/billing/**
- [ ] services/search/**  (blocked: custom retry wrapper, ask Priya)
## Next
- services/notifications/*.py

Effective context engineering for AI agents

lessons.drill: In a repo you don't know well, ask Claude Code to find every caller of one function and explain the call graph, first directly and then delegated to a subagent. Compare `/context` after each. Then ask it to write the findings to NOTES.md, run `/clear`, and check that a fresh prompt can continue from the notes alone.

lessons.title: Human review and confidence
lessons.summary: Production extraction and classification systems decide which outputs a person checks. The exam tests calibrating confidence against labelled data rather than trusting raw model scores, routing at field level, breaking accuracy down by segment, and sampling the auto-accepted 'confident' outputs so silent errors are caught.
keyPoints: **Raw model confidence is not calibrated.** Whether a score is self-reported or from a classifier, measure what accuracy each score band actually delivers on a **labelled validation set**, then set thresholds from that.

**Field-level, not document-level.** One invoice can have a certain vendor name and an uncertain total. Route the uncertain **fields** to review, with stricter thresholds for high-impact fields (amounts, dates, legal terms).

**Aggregate accuracy hides segment failures.** 97% overall can be 99% on typed invoices and 70% on handwritten forms. Report accuracy per document type, source, layout and field before deciding how much review to remove.
**Stratified random sampling** of auto-accepted, high-confidence outputs, across document types, vendors and fields, measures the error rate you can't otherwise see and catches drift.
**Deterministic signals route too.** Schema or validation failures, stated vs computed total mismatches, and missing required fields should send an item to review whatever its confidence.
Prioritise the human queue by **risk and impact** (amount, customer tier, legal exposure), not just arrival order.
**Close the loop**: reviewer corrections become labelled data for recalibrating thresholds, building few-shot examples and spotting new failure segments.
Reduce review **gradually and per segment** as evidence builds; keep a sampling floor even for segments that look good.
For agent outputs (code fixes, research claims), observable evidence such as tests passing, independent corroborating sources and historical acceptance rates beats the agent's own 'I'm confident'.
traps: Setting 'auto-accept if confidence ≥ 0.8' without checking what 0.8 means on labelled data.
Dropping human review because overall accuracy is high, without a per-segment breakdown.
Reviewing only low-confidence items, so confidently wrong outputs are never seen.
Routing on a document-level average confidence that a single bad field barely moves.
Asking the model to re-rate its own confidence as the 'calibration' step.

docs.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

lessons.drill: Label 50 extracted documents by hand across at least three document types. Bucket the model's field confidences (0.5-0.7, 0.7-0.9, 0.9+) and compute the real accuracy per bucket and per document type. Write down the threshold you would pick for each field, and how many items a 5% stratified audit sample would send to review each day at your volume.

lessons.title: Information provenance
lessons.summary: When information passes through several agents and summaries, the link between a claim and its source breaks easily. The exam tests carrying claim-to-source mappings as structured data through every step, keeping dates and publication details so conflicts can be explained, and surfacing conflicting sources instead of quietly choosing one.
keyPoints: Represent findings as **structured claims**: claim text, source ID or URL, a locator (page, section, quote), publication date and source type. Every handoff (subagent → coordinator → synthesis) passes this structure, not free prose.
**Prose summaries strip provenance.** Re-attaching citations after synthesis by searching for supporting text produces misattributions. Preserve the mapping instead of rebuilding it.

**Conflicts are information.** When sources disagree, report both values with their source, date and method, and explain the likely cause (different years, definitions, samples). If you apply a rule such as 'prefer the most recent primary source', say so.
**Dates matter**: a 2021 figure and a 2025 figure may both be right. Without publication dates the synthesis can't tell an update from a contradiction.
**Ground answers in quotes**: extract verbatim supporting quotes first, then answer only from them, and retract claims that have no supporting quote.

The **Citations API** (`"citations": {"enabled": true}` on document blocks) returns text blocks carrying `citations` with `cited_text`, `document_index`, `document_title` and a location. Your app must keep and render them. Citations can't be combined with `output_config.format` (400 error).

Anthropic's research system has subagents **write outputs to storage and pass lightweight references** to limit the 'game of telephone', and uses a dedicated citation step that matches claims in the report to locations in the source documents.
Carry **source quality** metadata too (primary study, official statistics, vendor blog, content farm) so synthesis can weigh sources openly.
Treat **uncited claims as unverified** and mark them as such rather than presenting them with the same confidence.
traps: Having the coordinator 'clean up' subagent findings into fluent paragraphs before synthesis, which drops sources and dates.
Silently picking the larger, newer or more convenient number when sources conflict.
Dropping publication dates to save tokens.
Enabling citations but only concatenating `text` fields in the UI, so the citations are thrown away.
Asking the synthesis model to 'add citations at the end' from memory.

code.src:
{
  "claim": "Global grid-scale battery capacity grew ~2x in 2024",
  "source_id": "S7",
  "source": {"title": "Energy Storage Outlook", "publisher": "IEA",
             "published": "2025-03", "type": "official_statistics"},
  "locator": "p. 14, Table 2.1",
  "quote": "installed capacity roughly doubled over 2024",
  "conflicts_with": ["S11"]
}

docs.title: How we built our multi-agent research system

lessons.drill: Give Claude two short documents that disagree on one number and differ in publication year. Ask once for 'a summary' and once with the structured-claim schema above plus the instruction to report conflicts with dates. Compare: does the first version silently pick one value? Then enable citations on the documents and render each cited_text beside its sentence.

questions.stem: On the internal developer platform, an engineer wrote an MCP server that runs as a local stdio process and reads files from her laptop. Which TWO Claude surfaces can launch and use this server directly on her machine? (Select TWO.)
options: claude.ai in the browser, by adding the server's file path as a custom connector
Claude Code, configured with the server as a stdio MCP server
The Messages API MCP connector, pointing at `stdio://localhost`
The Claude Desktop app, which can start local MCP servers on the machine
A claude.ai Project, by uploading the server's source code as project knowledge
explanations: A web page cannot spawn local processes; claude.ai custom connectors reach remote MCP servers over HTTP.
Correct. Claude Code runs locally and supports stdio MCP servers that it launches as child processes.
The API's MCP connector calls remote servers reachable over the internet, not local stdio processes.
Correct. Claude Desktop runs on the user's machine and can start local stdio MCP servers (configured directly or installed as a desktop extension).
Uploading code as knowledge lets Claude read it, not run it as a tool server.

questions.stem: The developer-platform team wants every employee using claude.ai in the browser to look up internal ticket status through Claude. The ticket system has a REST API on the corporate network. What is the BEST approach?
options: Ask each employee to run a stdio MCP server for the ticket API on their laptop and point the browser tab at it
Paste an export of all tickets into a shared Project once a day
Expose the ticket API through an authenticated remote MCP server and add it as a claude.ai connector
Give employees an API key so they can call the Messages API with a ticket tool
explanations: The browser app cannot launch or reach a local stdio process.
A daily paste is stale, bloats context, and exposes every ticket to every user.
Correct. claude.ai integrates external systems through connectors to remote MCP servers, which can enforce per-user auth.
That bypasses claude.ai entirely and spreads API keys to employees.

questions.stem: In the team's Claude Code feature workflow, a developer just finished and committed a bug fix. Their next task, an unrelated UI feature, is in a different part of the repo. The current session is full of stack traces and test logs from the bug hunt. What should they do FIRST?
options: Run `/clear` to start the new task with a fresh context
Run `/compact` so the bug-fix history is summarized and kept
Keep going in the same session; more context always helps Claude
Add the stack traces to CLAUDE.md so they are not lost
explanations: Correct. For an unrelated task, clearing removes irrelevant tokens that cost money and can distract the model; CLAUDE.md is still loaded.
Compaction is for continuing the same task with less context; here nothing from the bug hunt is needed.
Irrelevant context adds cost and can degrade focus; it does not help.
CLAUDE.md is loaded into every session; one-off logs would pollute every future task.

questions.stem: On the developer platform, halfway through a large refactor of a big codebase in Claude Code, the context window is nearly full. The developer wants to keep working on the same refactor without losing the decisions made so far (naming scheme, files already migrated). What is the BEST action?
options: Run `/clear` and re-explain the refactor from memory
Run `/compact` with instructions to keep the naming scheme and the list of migrated files
Start a second terminal and run a parallel session on the same files
Switch to a model with a larger context window mid-session
explanations: Clearing throws away the decisions the developer explicitly wants to keep.
Correct. Compaction summarizes the conversation to free space; focus instructions tell it what must survive.
A parallel session has none of the current decisions and risks conflicting edits.
This does not address the accumulated noise and may not be available; summarizing is the intended tool.

questions.stem: A developer on the team building features with Claude Code closed their terminal yesterday in the middle of a Claude Code session and wants to pick up exactly where they left off in the same project. Which command should they use?
options: `claude -p "continue"`
`/compact` in a new session
`claude --continue` (or `claude --resume` to choose a specific session)
`claude --plugin-dir .` to reload the project
explanations: `-p` runs a one-shot headless prompt in a new session; it does not restore the old conversation.
Compacting a new, empty session has nothing to summarize.
Correct. `--continue` reopens the most recent conversation in the directory; `--resume` lets you pick one.
`--plugin-dir` loads a plugin for one session; it does not restore conversations.

questions.stem: On the team's feature-development workflow, a developer has corrected Claude Code four times on the same failing approach to a migration. Each correction leads to another variation of the same wrong fix, and the transcript now contains all the failed attempts. What is the MOST effective next step?
options: Run `/clear` and restart with a sharper prompt that states why the approach fails
Run `/compact` so the failed attempts become a shorter summary
Raise the effort level to the maximum and ask Claude to reconsider the approach in the same session
Keep correcting with stronger wording such as "IMPORTANT: do not do this again"
explanations: Correct. When a session is cluttered with failed attempts, a clean session with a better initial prompt usually beats more corrections.
A summary still carries the failed approach forward as context.
More reasoning on top of the same anchored context often reproduces the same pattern.
Repeated stronger wording in a polluted context rarely breaks the loop; the failed attempts keep anchoring the model.

questions.stem: For engineers using Claude Code on a large internal codebase, which TWO practices reflect good session hygiene? (Select TWO.)
options: Keep one long-lived session for the whole week so Claude remembers every decision and file it has seen
Put durable conventions such as build commands and style rules in CLAUDE.md
Paste entire log files into the chat so Claude never has to ask for more
Disable all CLAUDE.md files to save tokens
Delegate broad codebase searches to a subagent so the file dumps stay out of the main context
explanations: Long-lived sessions accumulate irrelevant context and eventually require compaction; scope sessions to tasks.
Correct. CLAUDE.md is loaded at session start, so stable conventions survive `/clear` and new sessions.
Large raw pastes consume context; share the relevant excerpt or let Claude read the file with tools.
A concise CLAUDE.md is worth its tokens; removing it means re-explaining conventions every session.
Correct. A subagent works in its own context and returns only its conclusion, keeping the main thread lean.

questions.stem: A custom scheduling tool that the platform exposes to Claude receives inputs such as "next Tuesday afternoon" and "3/4" (ambiguous between March 4 and April 3), which break the backend. The tool schema currently has `"start": {"type": "string"}`. What is the BEST schema change?
options: Specify `"format": "date-time"` and a description requiring ISO 8601 with a timezone offset
Add a server-side regex post-processor that detects the date format and normalizes it
Rename the field to `start_time_please_use_iso`
Split the field into separate integer fields for day, month, year, and hour so no string parsing is needed
explanations: Correct. Claude relies on the schema and descriptions; an explicit format and description remove the ambiguity at the source.
Guessing after the fact keeps the ambiguity; fix the contract instead.
A field name alone is a weak signal compared with a type, format, and description.
Separate integers still leave the timezone unspecified and give Claude no guidance on resolving relative dates; a precise format and description fix the actual ambiguity.

questions.stem: A support-resolution agent's ticket-triage tool has a `priority` parameter typed as a free string. The backend accepts only `low`, `medium`, `high`, `urgent`, but Claude sometimes sends `P1` or `critical`. What is the simplest effective fix?
options: Add a few-shot example in the system prompt that shows one ticket with a valid priority value
Constrain `priority` with an `enum` of the four accepted values, each described
Map unknown values to `medium` silently in the backend
Change the type to `integer` from 1 to 4
explanations: A single example helps a little but does not constrain the value.
Correct. `enum` is the standard way to constrain a parameter to a fixed set, and descriptions help Claude choose between levels.
Silent remapping hides errors and mis-prioritizes urgent tickets.
An unexplained integer scale is more ambiguous than named levels.

questions.stem: The support-agent team adds `strict: true` to the tool below so Claude's inputs always match the schema, but the schema is not accepted for strict use. Which change is REQUIRED?
options: Add `"additionalProperties": false` to the nested `address` object as well
Give every property a `default` value
Set `"additionalProperties": true` on the top-level object
Add `"minProperties": 1` to the `address` object
explanations: Correct. Strict tool use and structured outputs require `additionalProperties: false` on every object, including nested ones.
Defaults are not required; required-ness is expressed with `required`.
Strict mode does not support `additionalProperties` set to anything other than `false`.
`minProperties` is not a strict-mode requirement.

questions.stem: An invoice-extraction pipeline uses a JSON schema where `po_number`, `due_date`, and `vat_id` are all required strings. On invoices that lack a PO number, Claude returns plausible-looking but invented PO numbers. Which schema change BEST addresses the root cause?
options: Add "Never invent values; double-check every field against the invoice" to the system prompt
Raise the effort level so Claude checks more carefully
Make the field nullable and describe null as "not present on the invoice"
Keep the field required but add `"minLength": 6` so short placeholder values are rejected
explanations: A generic instruction does not remove the schema pressure to produce a string.
More reasoning does not help when the contract has no valid way to say "missing".
Correct. If the schema forces a value, the model must output something; giving it a legitimate "not present" value removes the incentive to fabricate.
A length constraint pushes even harder toward producing a fake value, and length constraints are not supported in strict structured outputs anyway.

questions.stem: A support-resolution agent has two tools, `search_customers` ("Searches customers") and `find_customer` ("Finds a customer"). Logs show Claude picks between them almost at random, and the wrong one returns empty results. What should the developer do FIRST?
options: Add a third tool, `lookup_customer`, that calls both and returns whichever result is non-empty
Merge the two tools, or rewrite each description to state what it searches and when to use it
Lower the temperature to 0 so the model's tool choice becomes deterministic across requests
Force `find_customer` with `tool_choice` on every request
explanations: Adding another overlapping tool increases confusion.
Correct. Claude chooses tools from their names and descriptions; overlapping, vague tools should be consolidated or clearly differentiated.
Sampling settings do not fix ambiguous tool contracts.
Forcing one tool removes the agent's ability to choose and still uses the wrong one for some queries.

questions.stem: A document-extraction backend parses Claude's output with `json.loads()` and fails about 2% of the time because of a leading sentence or a trailing comment. The output must always match a known schema. Which approach is MOST reliable?

code.src:
resp = client.messages.create(
    model=MODEL,
    max_tokens=1024,
    system="Extract the order. Respond only with JSON.",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": email_body}],
)
data = json.loads(resp.content[0].text)  # fails ~2% of the time

options: Use structured outputs: `output_config.format` with the JSON schema
Add "Respond ONLY with JSON" in capital letters to the prompt
Strip everything before the first `{` and after the last `}`
Wrap `json.loads()` in a retry loop that resends the request until parsing succeeds
explanations: Correct. Structured outputs constrain generation to the schema, removing the parsing failures (you should still check `stop_reason` for `refusal` or `max_tokens`).
Prompting reduces but does not eliminate format drift.
Brittle string slicing breaks on nested or multiple JSON objects.
Retries add cost and latency and still give no guarantee.

questions.stem: You are designing the input schema for the support agent's `create_refund` tool. Which THREE practices will MOST improve how reliably Claude fills it in? (Select THREE.)
options: Accept a single free-text `details` string and parse it on the server with your own validation rules
Give every property a description that states units and format (for example "amount in cents, integer")
Name properties with short codes such as `a1`, `r2` to save tokens
Use `enum` for fields with a fixed set of values such as `reason`
Nest every field three levels deep to group them logically
Mark truly required fields in `required` and leave genuinely optional ones out
explanations: Free text pushes the parsing problem to the server and loses validation.
Correct. Descriptions with units and formats are how Claude knows what to put in each field.
Cryptic names remove meaning Claude uses to fill fields; the token saving is negligible.
Correct. Enums constrain values the backend can accept.
Unnecessary nesting makes the schema harder to fill correctly with no benefit.
Correct. Accurate `required` lists prevent Claude from inventing values for optional fields or skipping needed ones.

questions.stem: A platform team with a Java backend wants to run Claude Code non-interactively in CI for a nightly code-maintenance job, using its agent loop and built-in tools. The Agent SDK libraries are Python and TypeScript. Which approach BEST fits without adding a new runtime language to the service?
options: Port the Agent SDK's TypeScript source to Java by hand and keep it in sync with each upstream release
Run the Claude Code CLI headless (`claude -p --output-format json`) as a subprocess
Run the Claude Desktop app on a build server and trigger it nightly with an OS-level scheduler
Call claude.ai's web endpoints from Java
explanations: Porting the SDK is large, unsupported work.
Correct. The docs point other languages to running the CLI headless as a subprocess, which drives the same agent loop.
Desktop is interactive and not designed for unattended jobs.
Consumer web endpoints are not an integration surface for automation.

questions.stem: In the support agent's manual tool loop, a response comes back with `stop_reason: "max_tokens"` and its last content block is a `tool_use` block for `write_file` whose `input.content` looks shorter than expected. What should the loop do?
options: Execute the tool, since the JSON parsed successfully
Return a `tool_result` with `is_error: true` saying the file was written
Send a user message saying "continue" and append Claude's next output to the file
Do not run the tool; retry the turn with a higher `max_tokens`
explanations: A truncated input can still parse as a valid but partial object; running it writes a corrupt file.
Reporting a fabricated result corrupts the conversation state.
Stitching continuations into a tool input is fragile and still risks executing a partial call.
Correct. `max_tokens` with a `tool_use` block means the tool input may be cut off, so retry with more output budget rather than execute.

questions.stem: In the support agent's tool loop, a response has `stop_reason: "tool_use"` with two `tool_use` blocks. What must the next request contain for the loop to continue correctly?
options: Only a user message with the two results as plain text
The full assistant `content` as-is, then one user message with a `tool_result` per `tool_use_id`
The assistant message with its `tool_use` blocks removed to save tokens, followed by both results
Two separate user messages, one per tool result, each referencing its `tool_use_id`
explanations: Results must be `tool_result` blocks tied to their `tool_use_id`, following the assistant turn that requested them.
Correct. Append the whole assistant turn (including any thinking and both `tool_use` blocks), then return all results in a single user turn.
Every `tool_result` must match a `tool_use` in the preceding assistant turn; removing them produces an invalid request.
All results for one assistant turn belong in one user message; consecutive user messages for parallel results are incorrect.

questions.stem: A document-processing platform must process 60,000 new records through the extraction pipeline every night. Results are needed by 9 a.m.; nobody waits on individual items, and cost is the main concern. Which approach BEST fits?
options: Fan out 60,000 streaming requests in parallel from a worker pool sized to the rate limit
Submit the work through the Message Batches API
Use the most capable model with fast mode
Send all products in a single request with a very large `max_tokens`
explanations: Real-time calls cost full price and fight rate limits for work nobody is waiting on.
Correct. Non-urgent bulk work is the Batches API's use case: 50% of standard prices, most batches finish within an hour, and the maximum is 24 hours.
Fast mode targets latency at premium pricing, the opposite of this requirement.
One request cannot produce 60,000 descriptions reliably within output limits.

questions.stem: In the extraction pipeline, a batch job writes results back to a database by iterating results and assigning them to `requests[i]` in the order they were submitted. QA finds descriptions attached to the wrong products. What is the fix?
options: Match each result to its request using `custom_id`, since result order is not guaranteed
Sort the results by `created_at` before assigning
Use streaming instead of batches
Submit smaller batches so ordering is preserved
explanations: Correct. Batch results may come back in any order; each request's `custom_id` is how you match them.
Results do not carry a per-request ordering you can rely on.
This abandons the cost benefit instead of fixing the matching.
Ordering is not guaranteed at any batch size.

questions.stem: An extraction-pipeline batch has ended. `request_counts` shows 59,200 succeeded, 500 errored, and 300 expired. The errored results include a mix of `invalid_request` errors and server errors. Which TWO actions are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: Resubmit the entire batch so all results come from one run
Resubmit the expired and server-error requests in a new batch; requests that did not succeed are not billed
Wait; expired requests are retried automatically and will finish within another 24-hour window
Switch the failed requests to `stream: true` inside the next batch
Fix the `invalid_request` requests before resubmitting them, since resending unchanged will fail again
explanations: Re-running succeeded requests doubles cost for no benefit.
Correct. Expired and errored requests were never completed and are not billed; retrying them is safe.
Expired requests are final; they must be resubmitted.
Streaming is not supported inside batch requests.
Correct. Validation errors are deterministic; the request itself must be corrected.

questions.stem: For the extraction platform, which TWO workloads are good fits for the Message Batches API rather than real-time Messages calls? (Select TWO.)
options: A customer-support chat where the user is waiting for each reply
Running a 5,000-case evaluation suite after each prompt change
An IDE autocomplete feature
Re-classifying last year's support tickets with a new taxonomy
A multi-step agent that must call tools and react to results within a single session
explanations: A waiting user needs low latency; batches can take up to 24 hours.
Correct. Evals are bulk, latency-insensitive work that benefits from half-price processing.
Autocomplete is latency-critical.
Correct. Backfills over historical data are classic batch work.
Each batch request is single-shot; an interactive tool loop needs real-time calls.

questions.stem: An invoice-extraction service asks Claude to 'return JSON only'. About 3% of responses fail `JSON.parse` because they're wrapped in Markdown code fences or followed by a short explanation. The downstream system needs a fixed schema. Which approach BEST meets the requirement?
options: Add 'IMPORTANT: output ONLY raw JSON, no prose' in capitals at the start and end of the system prompt.
Set temperature to 0 so the model produces the same well-formed JSON on every request.
Strip code fences with a regex and cut the text at the last closing brace before calling `JSON.parse`.
Use structured outputs with a JSON schema in `output_config`, then validate the parsed object with Zod before using it.
explanations: Stronger wording may lower the failure rate, but it guarantees nothing. Constraining the output is the reliable fix.
Lower randomness doesn't guarantee format compliance, and some newer models reject non-default sampling parameters.
This fixes today's failure pattern but breaks on nested braces or new formats, and it still doesn't guarantee the schema.
Correct. Structured outputs constrain the response to valid JSON matching your schema, and validation catches business-rule problems the schema can't express.

questions.stem: A document-processing pipeline categorizes 200,000 customer-submitted product reviews every night. Results only need to be ready within 24 hours, and the team has been asked to cut LLM spend. Which approach BEST meets the requirements?
options: Send each review with `AsyncAnthropic` at high concurrency and stream the responses into the database.
Submit the reviews through the Message Batches API and collect the results when the batch ends.
Put all 200,000 reviews into one large prompt so a single request categorizes them together.
Run a synchronous loop on a cheap model, processing one review at a time overnight.
explanations: This works, but you pay full price and compete with interactive traffic for rate limits. Streaming doesn't help here.
Correct. Batches handle large asynchronous jobs at 50% of the standard price and normally finish within 24 hours.
That would exceed the context window, makes per-item results unreliable, and makes failures hard to isolate.
Sequential processing at 200k scale may not finish, and it misses the batch discount.

questions.stem: In the team's CI pipeline, Claude Code GitHub Action jobs have sometimes run for over an hour and consumed far more tokens than expected. Which TWO changes MOST directly cap runaway cost? (Select TWO.)
options: Use `fetch-depth: 0` so Claude has full git history and needs fewer turns to understand changes.
Set a job-level `timeout-minutes` and a `concurrency` group so jobs can't run indefinitely or pile up.
Pin the action to `@beta`, which has lower default turn limits than v1.
Delete the repository's CLAUDE.md so Claude reads less context on each run.
Add `--max-turns` to `claude_args` to limit how many iterations Claude can take per run.
explanations: Full history makes checkout bigger and doesn't limit iterations or runtime.
Correct. Workflow timeouts and concurrency controls are documented guardrails against runaway jobs.
The beta version is outdated, and moving back to it isn't a cost control.
Keeping CLAUDE.md short is good advice, but deleting it removes the team's standards and doesn't cap a runaway loop.
Correct. This is the documented way to cap the agent loop in the action.

questions.stem: In the team's CI pipeline, Claude-assisted PR reviews are meant to catch security problems (injection, missing authz checks) consistently across 30 repos. Today, developers paste diffs and ask 'review this', and the results vary a lot. Which approach BEST improves consistency while keeping appropriate control?
options: Replace the unit test suite with Claude review, since Claude can reason about behavior the tests miss.
Put explicit review criteria in the committed CLAUDE.md or review prompt, run review on every PR, and keep human approval and tests required.
Let Claude approve and auto-merge any PR where it reports no issues, so human reviewers can spend their time only on the PRs Claude flagged.
Ask developers to add 'be thorough and check security' to their ad-hoc review requests.
explanations: Review doesn't execute code. Tests are needed to verify behavior, including behavior Claude claims is correct.
Correct. Specific, shared criteria make reviews consistent. Automation makes them happen every time. Humans and CI stay as the gate.
This removes human control and treats a confident-sounding review as proof. AI review should add to required approvals, not replace them.
Vague instructions produce vague, inconsistent reviews, and this still depends on each person remembering.

questions.stem: A team using Claude Code wants to refactor a 3,000-line billing module that has no automated tests and is business-critical. What should they do FIRST?
options: Have Claude explain the module and document its design, then let a senior engineer refactor by hand.
Have Claude refactor first, then generate tests against the new code to confirm it works.
Have Claude write characterization tests that capture current behavior, get them passing in CI, then refactor in small commits on a branch.
Ask Claude to rewrite the whole module into clean, smaller files in one pass, then review the full diff carefully.
explanations: Documentation helps, but this skips the step that makes any refactor safe: tests that pin current behavior.
Tests written after the refactor describe the new behavior, so they can't catch regressions from the old behavior.
Correct. Characterization tests lock in existing behavior so each small refactor step can be checked automatically.
With no tests, a large diff can't be checked for behavior changes, and one big change is hard to review or revert.

questions.stem: In the team's CI pipeline, the Claude Code GitHub Action's PRs keep using `npm install` and default exports, although the team uses pnpm and named exports only. A developer has these rules in `CLAUDE.local.md` in the repo root, and they work fine on his laptop. What is the BEST fix?
options: Move the rules into the committed project `CLAUDE.md` at the repository root.
Copy the rules into `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on the developer's laptop so they apply in every project.
Add the rules to the PR description template so Claude reads them when it opens a PR.
Store the rules in a repository secret and pass them to the action through an environment variable.
explanations: Correct. The action checks out the repo, and Claude reads the committed CLAUDE.md. `CLAUDE.local.md` is personal and kept out of git, so it never reaches the runner.
User-level memory lives only on that machine. The CI runner never sees it.
A PR template is read after the work is done, and it isn't loaded as standing instructions.
Secrets are for credentials. Conventions belong in version-controlled CLAUDE.md where people can review them.

questions.stem: An engineer on the internal Claude-powered developer platform wants Claude Code to know their personal sandbox URL and preferred test accounts when working in one specific repository. Teammates shouldn't see these instructions. Where should they go?
options: `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, since user memory is private to the developer.
`./CLAUDE.md` in the project root, under a 'Personal notes' heading.
`./CLAUDE.local.md` in the project root, kept out of version control.
The `env` block of the committed `.claude/settings.json`.
explanations: It's private, but it applies to every project, and these notes belong to just one repo.
The project CLAUDE.md is committed and shared, so every teammate would get these notes.
Correct. CLAUDE.local.md is for personal instructions in one project and loads alongside the project CLAUDE.md.
That file is shared with the team, and settings aren't the place for instructions to Claude.

questions.stem: A team uses Claude Code to build features in their codebase. The project CLAUDE.md says: 'Never modify files under `db/migrations/` - generate a new migration instead.' Claude still occasionally edits existing migrations during large refactors. The team needs a guarantee. What should they do?
options: Add a permission deny rule such as `Edit(./db/migrations/**)`, or a PreToolUse hook that blocks edits to that path.
Rewrite the instruction in capitals with 'CRITICAL' and repeat it at the top and bottom of CLAUDE.md.
Move the instruction into `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` so it loads before the project file.
Put a copy of the rule in a `db/migrations/CLAUDE.md` file as well as the root CLAUDE.md.
explanations: Correct. Permissions and hooks are enforced by the harness no matter what the model decides.
CLAUDE.md is context, not enforcement. Stronger wording may help, but it can't guarantee anything.
Load order doesn't make an instruction binding, and it would no longer be shared with the team.
Nested files help with relevance but are still guidance only. There's no hard guarantee.

questions.stem: A team using Claude Code on their codebase has a root CLAUDE.md that has grown to 900 lines, and Claude follows it less reliably. Someone proposes splitting it into ten files pulled in with `@docs/claude/*.md` imports 'to cut context usage'. What is the MOST accurate assessment?
options: It organizes but doesn't save context: imports load with the parent file. Use path-scoped `.claude/rules/` and skills instead.
Good plan, but use `CLAUDE.local.md` files instead of imports, since local files don't count toward context.
Good plan. Imported files are read only when Claude decides they're relevant to the current task, so context usage drops sharply across sessions.
Bad plan, because Claude Code ignores `@` imports in project CLAUDE.md files for security reasons.
explanations: Correct. The docs say imports don't reduce context cost. Path-scoped rules load only for matching files, and skills load on demand.
Local files load into context just like CLAUDE.md, and they aren't shared with the team.
That describes skills, not `@imports`. Imports are expanded at load time.
Project imports work. Only imports pointing outside the project need a one-time approval.

questions.stem: An engineer on the developer-platform team is writing `@` imports in a project's `.claude/CLAUDE.md`. Which TWO statements about how imports resolve are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: A relative import path resolves from the file that contains the import, not from the session's working directory.
Relative import paths always resolve from the directory where the developer launched `claude`.
Imported files can't contain imports of their own, which keeps loading predictable.
An import pointing outside the repo (for example into the home directory) loads silently with no prompt.
Text such as `` `@README` `` inside a Markdown code span isn't treated as an import.
explanations: Correct. Relative imports are resolved against the importing file's location.
They resolve from the importing file. Launching from a subdirectory doesn't change that.
Recursive imports are supported, up to a limited depth.
The first time a project uses imports from outside the working directory, Claude Code shows an approval dialog.
Correct. Import parsing skips code spans and fenced code blocks, so you can mention a path without importing it.

questions.stem: On the developer platform, a monorepo team wants Claude to follow API-specific conventions (validation, error format) only when it works on files under `src/api/`, without adding those lines to every session's context. What is the BEST mechanism?
options: A `.claude/rules/api.md` file with `paths: ["src/api/**/*.ts"]` frontmatter.
An `env` variable `API_RULES` in `.claude/settings.json` holding the conventions.
An `## API` section near the top of the root CLAUDE.md.
A user-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on each API developer's machine.
explanations: Correct. Path-scoped rules load only when Claude reads or edits matching files.
Environment variables don't put instructions into Claude's context.
The root CLAUDE.md loads in every session, which is the context cost the team wants to avoid.
This loads for every project on those machines, isn't shared, and doesn't depend on which files Claude touches.

questions.stem: The developer platform team wants every engineer's Claude Code to connect to the same internal Postgres MCP server. The connection string includes a password that must not be committed. What is the BEST setup?
options: Commit `.mcp.json` with the full connection string, since the repository is private.
Add the connection string to the project CLAUDE.md so Claude can connect when it needs to.
Have each developer run `claude mcp add` with the default local scope and paste the connection string.
Commit a project `.mcp.json` that uses `${PG_URL}`; each developer sets `PG_URL` locally.
explanations: A private repo is still the wrong place for a credential. Anyone with access, and every clone, gets the password.
CLAUDE.md is model context. A secret there leaks into prompts, and it doesn't configure MCP.
This works per person but isn't shared, so the definitions drift between developers.
Correct. Project scope shares the server definition through git, and `${VAR}` expansion keeps the secret out of the repo.

questions.stem: On the developer platform, an engineer added an MCP server named `tickets` with local scope (pointing at a staging URL). The repo's committed `.mcp.json` also defines `tickets`, pointing at production with an extra auth header. Which configuration does Claude Code use for `tickets` in that repo?
options: A merge of the two: the staging URL from local scope plus the auth header from the project entry.
Both servers, connected separately, with tool names automatically prefixed by scope.
The local-scope entry, in full: the staging URL without the project's auth header.
The project entry, because a committed team configuration takes priority over personal settings.
explanations: Fields aren't merged across scopes. The winning entry is used as a whole.
When the same name appears in several scopes, Claude Code connects only once.
Correct. Precedence is local > project > user, and the whole entry from the winning scope is used.
For MCP servers, local scope ranks above project scope.

questions.stem: A bank's extraction pipeline must run a quarterly compliance review over 1.2 million archived documents. The same 6,000-token review instructions are sent with every document. Results are due two weeks after the quarter closes, and the budget is tight. Which TWO choices BEST fit the requirements? (Select TWO.)
options: Run the job through the Message Batches API instead of real-time requests.
Use the most capable model tier for every document so no review needs to be redone.
Put the shared instructions first in the prompt and mark them for prompt caching.
Raise `max_tokens` to the model maximum on each request to avoid truncated reviews.
Stream every response so reviewers can watch results arrive.
explanations: Correct. No user is waiting, and batches cost 50% less while staying off real-time rate limits.
Without an eval showing a smaller tier falls short, this ignores the budget requirement.
Correct. A long, identical prefix repeated across many requests is exactly what prompt caching is for.
Set `max_tokens` to what the task needs. The maximum adds no value and makes runaway outputs more costly.
Nobody is watching in real time, and streaming doesn't cut cost.

questions.stem: A lender's regulators require every loan application to go through the same five documented checks in a fixed order (identity, income, debt ratio, sanctions, policy exceptions), with an audit record of each step's input and output. The team wants Claude to help with the checks. Which architecture BEST fits?
options: An autonomous agent with tools for all five checks that decides which checks to run and in what order.
A single large prompt containing all five check procedures that returns one combined verdict.
A deterministic workflow (prompt chain) that runs the five checks in code-defined order, with programmatic gates and logs for each step.
A multi-agent swarm in which specialist agents negotiate a consensus verdict.
explanations: Agent autonomy adds unpredictability where the process has to be fixed and auditable.
This hides each step's output, making per-check auditing and debugging difficult.
Correct. When the steps are known and fixed, a workflow gives predictability and auditability. Use agents for open-ended problems.
This over-engineers a fixed sequence and makes audit trails harder to produce.

questions.stem: In an invoice-extraction pipeline, a zero-shot extraction prompt returns correct fields, but the formatting varies: date formats differ, and null fields are sometimes omitted and sometimes written as "N/A". What is the most direct prompt-level fix?
options: Ask the model to 'be consistent'
Raise effort to `max`
Move the formatting instructions out of the system prompt and into the user message, closer to the input
Add a few `<example>`-tagged input/output pairs showing the exact format, including missing fields
explanations: A vague instruction does not show the model what 'consistent' means. Examples do.
Effort governs how thoroughly the model works, not consistency of format.
Placement alone does not define the format you want.

Correct. Few-shot (multishot) examples are one of the most reliable ways to pin down format and edge-case handling. Include edge cases such as missing values. Structured outputs can enforce the schema as well.

questions.stem: The support resolution agent summarises each ticket for its case notes using five few-shot examples. All five are short billing tickets written by the same agent. On long technical tickets, the outputs are oddly short and copy phrases from the examples. Which TWO changes BEST address this? (Select TWO.)
options: Diversify the examples across ticket types, lengths and edge cases so the model stops copying surface patterns
Remove the examples entirely and go zero-shot, since examples always constrain the model's output length
Duplicate the strongest example several times so that it carries more weight than the others during generation
State explicitly that the examples illustrate format and that length should match the input ticket's complexity
Move the examples after the ticket to be summarised so they are the last thing the model reads before writing
explanations: Correct. Models generalise from examples, including unintended features such as length or phrasing. Diversity reduces that overfitting.
This throws away format control. The problem is the examples' coverage, not the use of examples, and examples do not inherently constrain length.
Duplicating an example strengthens exactly the surface pattern that is causing the problem.
Correct. Saying what the examples are meant to demonstrate helps the model separate the format from incidental details.
Moving the examples does not fix their lack of diversity. Long reference material usually goes before the question, not after it.

questions.stem: A multi-agent research system must read about 300 sources per question, extract findings, and write a synthesised report that needs deep judgment. The team wants high quality at a sustainable cost. Which coordinator/subagent architecture BEST fits, before any eval tuning?
options: The cheapest tier for everything, retrying the synthesis until a reviewer approves it
Use the most capable tier for every call, including per-source extraction, so quality is maximised at every step of the pipeline
A top-tier orchestrator for planning and synthesis, with per-source extraction delegated to cheaper, faster workers
A different model for each turn of a single conversation, chosen by a router per message
explanations: Synthesis needs the judgment of a stronger model, and retry loops on a weak synthesiser add cost and latency.
This pays frontier prices for mechanical extraction that a cheaper tier probably handles well.

Correct. When there is a lot of independent work to hand off, matching the tier to each sub-task is effective: frontier judgment where it matters, cheap fast workers for the high-volume extraction. Validate it on evals.
Switching models within one conversation breaks the prompt cache (caches are model-scoped) and can drop prior reasoning. Choose the model per route or conversation.

questions.stem: A document-extraction pipeline built for an older model forces JSON by ending `messages` with a prefilled assistant turn containing `{`. After moving to a recent model generation, every call returns a 400. What is the recommended replacement?
options: Put the `{` at the end of the user message instead
Keep the prefill, but add an `anthropic-beta` header to re-enable it
Keep asking for JSON in the prompt, then use a regex to pull the first `{...}` span out of the text and parse that
Use structured outputs (`output_config.format` with a JSON schema) so the response is guaranteed to match the schema
explanations: A stray brace in the user turn does not constrain the output, and it may confuse the model.
No beta header restores last-turn prefill on these models.
Regex extraction is fragile defensive parsing. Structured outputs remove the need for it.

Correct. Recent models reject a prefilled final assistant turn. Structured outputs replace the most common use of prefill (forcing JSON) with schema-guaranteed output. Assistant messages elsewhere in the history, for example in few-shot examples, are still fine.

questions.stem: A CI pipeline runs an Agent SDK code-auditing job that must be read-only, and the developer writes the configuration below. In testing, the agent edits a file and runs a shell command without any prompt. What is the MOST likely reason?

code.src:
options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    allowed_tools=["Read", "Grep", "Glob"],
    permission_mode="bypassPermissions",
)
async for msg in query(prompt="Audit src/ for SQL injection", options=options):
    print(msg)

options: `allowed_tools` is ignored unless `setting_sources` includes "project"
Grep is implemented on top of Bash internally, so allowing Grep implicitly allows Bash and, through it, file writes
`allowed_tools` only pre-approves listed tools, and `bypassPermissions` approves unlisted tools as well
The prompt mentioned SQL injection, which makes the agent switch to `acceptEdits` mode automatically
explanations: `allowed_tools` is a programmatic option that applies regardless of setting sources.
Grep is a separate built-in tool; allowing it does not grant Bash.
Correct. To make the agent read-only, use `disallowed_tools` for write/exec tools, a non-bypass mode such as `dontAsk`, or a `PreToolUse` hook.
Prompt content does not change the permission mode; the configured `bypassPermissions` mode is the cause.

questions.stem: In the team's CI pipeline, an Agent SDK agent runs headlessly to summarize pull requests. Nobody is available to approve tool calls. The agent must be able to use Read, Glob and Grep, and any other call that would need approval must be refused immediately rather than waiting. Which configuration BEST meets this?
options: `permissionMode: "dontAsk"`, so listed tools run and anything that would otherwise prompt is denied
`permissionMode: "acceptEdits"`, which approves only read operations in the working directory
`permissionMode: "bypassPermissions"`, because the allow list already restricts the agent to three tools
`permissionMode: "plan"`, since plan mode never executes any tool
explanations: Correct. `dontAsk` converts every would-be prompt into a denial, which is the documented locked-down headless setup when paired with `allowedTools`.
`acceptEdits` auto-approves file edits and filesystem commands, the opposite of what a read-only summarizer needs.
`allowedTools` does not constrain `bypassPermissions`; Bash, Write and Edit would be approved too.
Plan mode is for exploring and planning; edits route to the approval callback and some calls still run, so it is not a hard deny policy for headless CI.

questions.stem: In the CI pipeline, an Agent SDK agent runs in `bypassPermissions` mode inside a disposable container. Security asks for a guarantee that the agent never writes to files under `/etc`, with the reason shown to the model so it can choose another approach. Where should the developer implement this check?
options: In a `PostToolUse` hook that reverts the file if the path starts with `/etc`
In a `PreToolUse` hook that returns `permissionDecision: "deny"` plus a `permissionDecisionReason` for the model
In the `canUseTool` callback, returning a denial message that explains the `/etc` restriction to the model
In the system prompt, with a firm instruction never to modify `/etc`
explanations: `PostToolUse` fires after the tool ran; the write has already happened.
Correct. Hooks run before the permission mode is applied, a hook deny holds even in `bypassPermissions`, and the reason is passed back to Claude.
In `bypassPermissions` most calls are approved before `canUseTool` is consulted, so the check would be silently skipped.
Instructions steer behaviour but are not an enforcement guarantee; security requirements need a deterministic control.

questions.stem: An engineering-productivity team's Agent SDK coding assistant registers the hook below to protect `.env` files. During a red-team exercise the agent still created `.env` by running `echo "KEY=1" > .env`. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: `permissionDecision: "deny"` is only honoured when `permissionMode` is `default`
The `Write|Edit` matcher is tested against the tool name, so the hook never ran for the Bash call
The hook must be registered under `PostToolUse` instead, because only then does it see the final, resolved file path that the tool wrote
Returning `{}` for other files caused the SDK to disable the hook after the first call
explanations: A hook deny applies in every mode, including `bypassPermissions`.
Correct. Matchers match tool names only; a shell redirect goes through the Bash tool, which `Write|Edit` does not match.
`PostToolUse` runs after execution and cannot prevent the write; the problem is the matcher scope.
Returning `{}` simply allows that call; it does not unregister the hook.

questions.stem: A support-resolution agent built on the Agent SDK is getting hooks for auditing and safety. Which TWO statements about SDK hooks are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: A `PreToolUse` hook that returns a deny decision blocks the call even when the session is in `bypassPermissions` mode
A hook that returns an async output can still block the tool call once its background work finishes
A hook `matcher` such as `"*.env"` filters calls by the file path in the tool input
Hook callbacks run in the application's own process and do not consume the agent's context window
A `PostToolUse` hook can prevent a dangerous tool from executing by returning a deny decision
explanations: Correct. Hooks are evaluated before the permission mode, and a hook deny holds in every mode.
Async outputs let the agent proceed immediately, so they cannot block, modify or inject context.
Matchers match the tool name (or event-specific field), not arguments; check `tool_input.file_path` inside the callback.
Correct. Hooks are callbacks in your process; they only affect context if they deliberately add context.
`PostToolUse` fires after the tool has run; blocking must happen in `PreToolUse`.

questions.stem: A support-resolution agent built on the Agent SDK runs in short-lived serverless containers. Each user message is handled by whichever container is free, and the code passes the stored `session_id` as `resume`. Users report that follow-ups often behave as if the agent has no memory of earlier turns. What should the team do FIRST?
options: Increase `max_turns` so that the full conversation fits in a single session
Set `fork_session: true` on every request so each container gets its own copy of the session
Persist transcripts to shared storage, such as a `SessionStore` adapter, because session files are written to each container's local disk
Switch to `continue: true`, which locates the right session by user rather than by ID and therefore works across containers
explanations: The turn limit is unrelated; the session exists, but its transcript is not on the container handling the request.
Forking still needs the original transcript to exist on that host; it does not solve missing files.
Correct. Session transcripts are written to local disk by default; another host can only resume them if they are mirrored to shared storage (or the app passes needed state into a fresh session).
`continue` resumes the most recent session in the current directory on that machine; it has the same local-disk problem.

questions.stem: In the team's code-generation workflow, an Agent SDK session has analyzed an authentication module, and a developer wants to try an OAuth2 redesign in a separate conversation while keeping the original JWT-focused conversation untouched for later. Which option should they use?
options: Call `query()` with `continue_conversation=True`, which automatically creates a branch
Resume the original session ID with `fork_session=True`
Resume the original session ID with no extra options; the SDK automatically copies the history whenever the prompt changes topic
Start a new `query()` and paste the original prompt, because sessions cannot be branched
explanations: `continue` appends to the most recent session; it does not branch.
Correct. Forking branches the conversation history and leaves the original session unchanged. Note it does not branch file changes on disk.
Plain resume adds to the original session, modifying its history.
The SDK supports forking directly; a new query would also lose the analysis already performed.

questions.stem: A nightly developer-productivity agent built with the TypeScript Agent SDK sometimes logs `undefined` as its final output. The relevant code is below. What is the BEST fix?
options: Wrap `saveReport` in a retry loop because the result is populated asynchronously after the message arrives
Read the final answer from the last `system` message in the stream instead, since system messages always carry the completed output text
Remove `maxTurns` so the agent can never stop early
Branch on `m.subtype`: only `success` has `result`; handle `error_max_turns` and similar subtypes
explanations: The field is absent on error subtypes, not delayed; retrying will not populate it.
System messages carry lifecycle events such as `init` and `compact_boundary`, not the final answer.
Unbounded runs are risky in production; the correct move is to handle the limit, not delete it.
Correct. Error result subtypes carry cost, usage and `session_id` but no `result` field, so the code must branch on `subtype`.

questions.stem: In the team's Agent SDK code-generation assistant, the main agent discusses a failing test (`tests/test_billing.py::test_tax`) with the user for several turns, then delegates the fix to a custom `test-fixer` subagent. The subagent spends many turns searching for "the failing test" and fixes the wrong one. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: Subagents cannot read files outside the directory in which they are defined
The parent's `max_turns` limit was reached during the discussion, so the subagent received only a truncated copy of the parent transcript
Non-fork subagents start fresh: they see only their own prompt and the Agent tool's prompt string
The subagent's `model` defaulted to a smaller model that cannot read pytest output
explanations: Subagents use the session's working directory and whatever tools they are granted; there is no per-definition directory restriction.
Subagents never receive the parent transcript at all, truncated or otherwise.
Correct. Anything the subagent needs, such as the test ID and error, must be included in the delegation prompt (and the parent's instructions can require that).
Model choice affects quality, but the symptom (not knowing which test) points to missing context, not capability.

questions.stem: A support-resolution agent's hand-written loop fails on the second iteration with a 400 error saying a `tool_result` block has no corresponding `tool_use` block. Based on the code below, what is the fix?

code.src:
resp = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=16000,
                              tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)
while resp.stop_reason == "tool_use":
    text = "".join(b.text for b in resp.content if b.type == "text")
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": text})
    results = [run_tool(b) for b in resp.content if b.type == "tool_use"]
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})
    resp = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=16000,
                                  tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)

options: Send the tool results as a `system` message instead of a `user` message
Set `tool_choice` to `none` on follow-up requests so the API stops validating tool blocks
Strip the `tool_use_id` field from each result so the API falls back to matching tool results to tool calls by their position
Append `resp.content` (the full block list, including `tool_use` blocks) as the assistant turn
explanations: Tool results belong in a user message; changing the role does not restore the missing `tool_use` blocks.
That prevents further tool calls and does not fix the malformed history.
`tool_use_id` is required to pair results with calls; removing it makes things worse.
Correct. Each `tool_result` must answer a `tool_use` block in the preceding assistant turn; keeping only the text drops those blocks.

questions.stem: A support-resolution agent used to call three independent lookup tools in one turn, but after a harness refactor it now calls them one per turn, tripling latency. The new result-handling code is below. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: Parallel tool use must be re-enabled explicitly with a beta header whenever the harness changes how it builds messages
`await` inside the loop disables parallel tool use on the API side
The tool results are missing `is_error: false`, so Claude assumes the tools are unreliable
Each result goes in its own user message instead of one message for the turn
explanations: Parallel tool use is on by default; no header is needed.
Sequential execution in your code is slower but does not change what the API allows; the message structure is the problem.
`is_error` defaults to false and only needs to be set for failures.
Correct. Splitting parallel results across messages trains Claude away from making parallel calls; return them all in one message (and run them concurrently).

questions.stem: A support-resolution agent's `get_invoice` tool sometimes times out when calling a billing service. The team wants Claude to recover gracefully, for example by retrying or asking the user. Which TWO practices should the harness follow? (Select TWO.)
options: Raise an exception that ends the loop, so the user can retry the whole conversation
Keep the `tool_use_id` of the failed call on the error result, in the same user message as the other results for that turn
Return a `tool_result` for that call with `is_error: true` and a short, actionable error message
Omit the failed call from the results so Claude does not see confusing error text
Send the error later as a plain text user message after the other tool results
explanations: Crashing the loop throws away progress when Claude could have recovered.
Correct. Every `tool_use` must get a matching result, including failures, in the single results message.
Correct. An error result lets Claude reason about the failure and choose a recovery path.
A missing result makes the next request invalid and hides the failure from Claude.
Errors should be structured `tool_result` blocks tied to the call, not free text in a separate message.

questions.stem: The support agent's loop treats every response whose `stop_reason` is not `tool_use` as finished. Users occasionally receive answers that end mid-sentence, and the logs show nothing abnormal. Which change BEST addresses the root cause?
options: Switch to streaming so the client receives the rest of the answer as it is generated
Retry the identical request whenever the final text does not end with sentence punctuation, up to three times, and return the longest version
Add "Always finish your sentences" to the system prompt
Branch on every stop reason; treat `max_tokens` as truncation, and cap iterations
explanations: Streaming changes delivery, not the `max_tokens` cap that truncates the output.
Retrying the same request with the same cap usually truncates again, and text heuristics are unreliable.
The model cannot exceed `max_tokens`; this does not address the cap.
Correct. Only `end_turn` means a complete answer; `max_tokens` with a low limit explains mid-sentence endings.

questions.stem: In a multi-agent research system, a due-diligence task requires reviewing 40 contracts and producing a risk memo. Running everything in one loop, the agent's context fills with full contract text and tool output, and by contract 25 its analysis gets noticeably worse. Which design change BEST addresses this?
options: Raise `max_tokens` so the model has more room to reason over the contracts
Delegate contracts to subagents that return short structured risk summaries
Ask the agent in the prompt to "forget" contracts once it has finished them
Move all 40 contracts into a cached system prompt so they are cheaper to resend on each turn and always available to the agent
explanations: `max_tokens` limits output length; it does not relieve input context pressure.
Correct. Subagents isolate the reading-heavy work so the coordinator's context grows by summaries, not transcripts.
The model cannot remove content from its own context; the harness must manage what is sent.
Caching reduces cost, not context load; the window still fills with all the text.

questions.stem: In the team's Claude Code workflow, to speed up a small refactor (renaming a function and updating its four call sites in two files), a developer configures the main agent to spawn five subagents, one per edit. The job now takes longer, uses several times more tokens, and two subagents made conflicting edits to the same file. What is the BEST recommendation?
options: Keep the five subagents but also give each one Bash access so they can take file locks before editing shared files
Do this coupled task in the main agent; save subagents for independent, context-heavy work
Raise the concurrency limit so all subagents finish sooner
Pass the parent's full conversation transcript to each subagent so they coordinate
explanations: This adds more machinery to a task that does not benefit from delegation.
Correct. Subagents add tokens and coordination cost and do not share state; small, interdependent edits are better done in one context.
More concurrency increases the risk of conflicting edits and does nothing for cost.
This erases the context-isolation benefit and still does not prevent concurrent conflicting writes.

questions.stem: A support-resolution agent currently performs every action through a general `bash` tool, including sending customer emails with `curl` to the mail API. The team now needs to require human approval before any email is sent and to log the recipient and subject. What is the BEST design change?
options: Promote email sending to a dedicated `send_email` tool with typed recipient, subject and body arguments the harness can gate and log
Add a system prompt rule telling Claude to ask for approval before sending email
Keep the bash tool and match `curl` commands to the mail API with a regular expression that triggers an approval prompt
Remove network access from the bash tool so emails cannot be sent at all
explanations: Correct. A dedicated tool gives the harness an action-specific hook with structured arguments; an opaque bash command string is hard to gate reliably.
Instructions are not an enforced approval gate.
Fragile: the same action can be expressed many ways in shell, and recipient/subject are buried in an opaque string.
That blocks the required capability rather than gating it.

questions.stem: A developer-productivity agent built on the Agent SDK runs long sessions that trigger automatic compaction. After compaction, the agent sometimes forgets a rule stated in the initial prompt ("never touch the migrations folder"), and auditors want the complete pre-compaction transcript retained. Which TWO actions address these needs? (Select TWO.)
options: Have subagents return their full transcripts to the parent so nothing is ever summarized
Register a `PreCompact` hook that archives the full transcript before it is summarized
Add more MCP servers so the agent can look the rule up when needed
Set `max_turns` low enough that compaction never happens
Move persistent rules into CLAUDE.md, which is re-injected on every request, instead of relying on the initial prompt
explanations: Subagents return only their final message, and pulling transcripts in would accelerate compaction.
Correct. `PreCompact` runs before compaction and is the documented place to archive transcripts.
Extra tool definitions consume more context and do not preserve the rule.
This caps the agent's work instead of managing context, and long tasks would fail.
Correct. Compaction summarizes older history, so early instructions may be lost; CLAUDE.md content is loaded each request.

questions.stem: A report-generation pipeline asks Claude to write a report outline, runs a code check that the outline covers five required sections, and only then asks Claude to write the full report from the approved outline. Which pattern from "Building effective agents" is this?
options: Prompt chaining, with a programmatic gate that checks the outline before the drafting step runs
Orchestrator-workers, because one call produces the plan the next call executes
Evaluator-optimizer, because the outline is checked before drafting
Routing, because the outline decides which prompt runs next
explanations: Correct. Sequential LLM calls where each consumes the previous output, with a code check as the gate.
An orchestrator decides subtasks dynamically and delegates them to workers; this flow is fixed in code.
Evaluator-optimizer loops an LLM critic and generator; this is a single deterministic check on the way through.
