questions.stem: An engineer on the internal platform has corrected Claude Code twice about how the team's auth middleware works, and the third attempt is still wrong. The session is long and contains both failed attempts. What does Anthropic's guidance recommend?
options: Correct it a third time with more emphasis, in capitals, on the parts it keeps missing
Run `/compact` so the failed attempts are summarized and keep correcting
Fork the session so the failed attempts are preserved for later reference
`/clear` and start again with one better prompt that includes what was learned
explanations: A third correction mostly adds to a context that already contains two failed attempts for Claude to keep re-reading.
Compaction carries a summary of the failed attempts forward.
A fork keeps exactly the context that is causing the problem.
Correct. A fresh context plus a prompt that folds in the lessons usually works better than continuing to correct.

questions.stem: In CI, a first step runs the analysis below and saves the session ID. A later step resumes the session to apply the fix, but Claude reports it has no access to the issue-tracker tools it used before. What is the MOST likely cause?

code.src:
# step 1
out=$(claude -p "Diagnose the failing build; check linked tickets" \
  --mcp-config ci/tracker-mcp.json --output-format json)
echo "$out" | jq -r .session_id > sid.txt

# step 2 (same runner)
claude -p "Apply the fix you proposed and update the ticket" \
  --resume "$(cat sid.txt)"

options: The session expired between the two pipeline steps
`--resume` restores the conversation but not launch flags like `--mcp-config`; pass it again on the resumed run
Resumed sessions run with tools disabled until `--continue` is also passed
Each `-p` run loses MCP servers unless the server is defined in `~/.claude.json`
explanations: Sessions persist as local transcripts; a later step in the same job can resume them.

Correct. Configuration passed on the command line, such as `--mcp-config`, `--settings`, `--plugin-dir` and `--add-dir`, has to be passed again when resuming. Settings files are re-read automatically.
There is no such rule; `--continue` and `--resume` are alternative ways to choose the session.
MCP config passed with `--mcp-config` works in `-p` runs; it just isn't remembered by the session.

questions.stem: The extraction pipeline runs Agent SDK workers in short-lived containers. When validation fails, the pipeline sends a correction request ("`total` doesn't match the line items; recheck page 3") to whatever worker is free, using `resume` with the original session ID. These retries usually fail with a session-not-found error. Which design is the MOST robust and simplest?
options: Use `continue_conversation=True` on the retry so whichever worker is free picks up the latest session
Raise `max_turns` on the first run so corrections never need a second request
Resume with `fork_session=True` so the retry gets its own copy of the session
Skip resume: send a fresh request with the document, the extracted JSON and the validation errors
explanations: A new container has no sessions on disk, so there is nothing to continue.
The first run doesn't know about the validation failure that happens afterwards in pipeline code.
Forking still needs the original session file on that machine.
Correct. Session files are local to the host that wrote them. Passing the captured results into a fresh request avoids shipping transcripts around; the docs note this is often more robust.

questions.stem: The research system's lead agent runs multi-hour jobs and its context regularly approaches the limit, after which it loses track of its own plan and redoes finished work. Which THREE practices BEST address this? (Select THREE.)
options: Have the lead save its research plan and progress to external memory so it can reload them after its context is truncated
Move the lead to a model with a larger context window and keep all worker output in context
Have subagents write full findings to storage and return only condensed results with references
Disable compaction so that nothing in the lead's context is ever summarized away
When a phase completes, hand off to a fresh agent with a clean context, passing state through stored notes
Ask subagents to return their full transcripts so the lead never loses any detail
explanations: Correct. Anthropic's research lead saves its plan to memory because context can be truncated; reloading it restores direction.
A larger window delays the problem and worsens attention dilution.
Correct. Condensed returns plus references keep the lead's context small without losing detail.
Without compaction the lead simply runs out of context.
Correct. Fresh contexts with a stored-state handoff are how long-running agents continue past context limits.
Full transcripts accelerate the context overflow they are meant to prevent.

questions.stem: In the multi-agent research system, the search subagent has two tools: `search` ("Searches documents.") backed by the firm's internal index of peer-reviewed papers, updated quarterly, and `web_search` ("Searches the web."). For questions about events from the last few weeks, the subagent keeps querying `search`, finds nothing recent, and the final report says the topic has no coverage. Which change BEST addresses the root cause?
options: Merge both into a single `search` tool that sends every query to both backends and returns the union of the raw results
Add a rule to the coordinator's system prompt listing phrases such as "this month", "latest" or "recent" that should make every subagent use web search instead of the internal index
Rename the internal tool `papers_search` and rewrite both descriptions to say what each one covers and when to prefer it
Force `tool_choice` to `web_search` whenever the user's question mentions the current year
explanations: Sending every query to both backends doubles result volume and mixes sources with different trust levels, which hurts provenance, without making the choice clearer.
A keyword list in another agent's prompt is brittle and sits at the wrong layer; the subagent still sees two indistinguishable tools.
Correct. The descriptions are the main signal Claude uses to choose between tools; stating coverage, recency and when to use each removes the ambiguity at the source.
Forcing a tool on a keyword heuristic removes judgment entirely and misfires on questions that mention a year but need peer-reviewed sources.

questions.stem: In the invoice extraction pipeline, the extractor agent first calls `list_vendors` (which pages through all 4,000 vendors) to find a match, then calls `lookup_vendor(vendor_id)`, which returns the full vendor record of about 180 fields. Each invoice now uses tens of thousands of tokens and matching accuracy falls on long invoices. The extractor only needs the canonical vendor ID, legal name, tax ID and default currency to fill the schema. Which THREE changes are MOST appropriate? (Select THREE.)
options: Move the pipeline to a model tier with a larger context window so that the full 180-field vendor records fit without trimming
Return only the fields the extraction step uses (vendor ID, legal name, tax ID, default currency) by default
Replace `list_vendors` with a search tool that takes a name or tax ID and returns the top few candidate vendors
Remove the vendor ID from results, because opaque IDs are where the model makes mistakes
Add a `response_format` option so the agent can request the detailed record only when it actually needs more fields
Base64-encode each vendor record to reduce the number of tokens it occupies
explanations: A bigger window treats the symptom; the irrelevant fields still dilute attention and cost tokens on every call.
Correct. Returning only high-signal fields keeps context small and focused on what the next step needs.
Correct. Search beats list: the agent should never page through every vendor to find one match.
The canonical vendor ID is required to write the extracted record; removing it breaks the downstream step. The fix for confusing IDs is to pair them with readable names, not to drop them.
Correct. A concise/detailed switch keeps the default lean while still allowing the full record when a case needs it.
Base64 does not reduce tokens for the model and makes the content unreadable to it.

questions.stem: In the CI pipeline, `claude -p` reviews pull requests and posts findings through a custom tool `post_review_comment(path, line, body)`. About a fifth of the calls are rejected by the code host because `path` arrives as `./src/app.ts` or an absolute runner path, and `line` sometimes refers to the old version of the file. The tool schema currently declares both parameters with type only. What is the BEST fix?
options: Add a paragraph to the repository's CLAUDE.md explaining the code host's comment API so Claude formats calls correctly
Post-process failed calls on the server by fuzzy-matching each comment body against the diff hunks to work out the intended file and line, then re-post the comment there automatically
Describe each parameter precisely (`path` repo-relative like `src/app.ts`; `line` on the new side of the diff) and reject other values with an error stating the expected format
Switch the review job to a more capable model tier, which is better at inferring API conventions
explanations: CLAUDE.md can help, but the tool's own parameter descriptions travel with the tool and are what Claude reads when filling the call; this is the wrong layer.
Guessing on the server hides the input problem and will sometimes attach comments to the wrong line.
Correct. Precise parameter descriptions with an example fix most calls up front, and an actionable validation error lets Claude correct the rest itself.
A bigger model cannot infer a convention the interface never states; the schema is underspecified.

questions.stem: Every MCP tool behind the support-resolution agent returns `{"error": "Request failed"}` with `isError: true` on any failure. Logs show two patterns: the agent retries `issue_refund` several times when the refund was blocked by policy, and it escalates to a human whenever `get_order` times out, even though the same call usually succeeds seconds later. Which TWO changes BEST address this? (Select TWO.)
options: Add an `error_category` (transient, validation, business_rule, permission) and a `retryable` flag to every error result
Add a system-prompt rule: "Always retry a failed tool up to three times before escalating."
Make each error message state the next step, e.g. "retry in a few seconds", "fix field X" or "do not retry; escalate"
Return HTTP 500 for every failure so that the MCP client's transport layer retries the request automatically before the model ever sees it
Move the agent to a larger model tier so that it can infer the real cause of each failure from the surrounding conversation
explanations: Correct. Category and retryability tell the agent whether another attempt can possibly help, which separates the timeout case from the policy case.
A blanket retry rule makes the policy case worse (three identical refused refunds) and still treats all failures the same.
Correct. Actionable messages give the agent the next step for each case instead of leaving it to guess.
Transport-level errors hide the tool-level detail from the model and would retry the policy refusal too.
The model cannot infer what the tool never reported; the error result is uninformative regardless of model size.

questions.stem: The support agent's `issue_refund` MCP tool enforces a $500 per-refund limit for automated refunds; larger refunds need a human approver. When a customer asks for $640, the tool returns `isError: true` with the text "Refund failed." The agent retries the same call twice, then tells the customer there is a system problem. What should the tool return instead?
options: A successful result `{"refunded": false}` so the agent's loop continues without an error branch
Automatically refund the $500 maximum, report success, and let the customer contact support again if they want the remaining $140 refunded
`isError: true`, category `business_rule`, `retryable: false`, stating the $500 limit and that the agent should escalate to a human approver
A JSON-RPC `-32602 Invalid params` error, since the amount is outside the accepted range
explanations: A bare `refunded: false` success carries no reason, so the agent still cannot explain the outcome or choose the escalation path.
Silently changing the business outcome without the customer's or a human's agreement is a policy violation dressed up as success.
Correct. A business-rule error marked non-retryable, with the limit and the escalation path, stops the retries and tells the agent exactly what to do.

The MCP spec reports out-of-range values and business-rule failures as tool execution errors (`isError: true`); protocol errors are for unknown tools and malformed requests, and clients may not pass them to the model at all.

questions.stem: After a credential rotation, the service account used by the support agent's `update_shipping_address` tool lost its write scope, so every call now gets a 403 from the address service. The fix will take the platform team a day. Meanwhile the team wants the agent to handle these conversations correctly. Which tool result is BEST?
options: `isError: true`, category `permission`, `retryable: false`, saying the agent cannot change addresses and should hand off to a human
`isError: true` with the full 403 response body, the request headers and the token's current scopes, so the agent has every detail it might need
Retry the call inside the tool using an administrator credential, and return success if that works
`isError: true`, category `transient`, `retryable: true`, message "Address service unavailable, try again later"
explanations: Correct. A permission error marked non-retryable, with a concrete handoff path, lets the agent resolve the conversation correctly while the scope is fixed.
Headers and token details waste context, may leak secrets into the transcript, and still do not tell the agent what to do.
Silently escalating privilege bypasses the access control that failed; it is a security problem, not error handling.
Calling it transient invites repeated retries that cannot succeed today and tells the customer to wait for nothing.

questions.stem: In the research system, a subagent's `fetch_journal_articles` tool hits a publisher API that returned 401 for most of last week after a licence lapsed. The tool caught the 401 and returned an empty article list as a normal result. The synthesis step then wrote that "no peer-reviewed evidence was found" in that journal. What is the BEST fix?
options: Tell the coordinator in its system prompt to treat any empty result from that journal as suspicious and to mention possible gaps in the report
On auth failures return `isError: true` with an access-failure message; return an empty list only when a search truly found nothing
Retry the 401 inside the tool until the publisher starts accepting the credentials again
Drop the journal from the subagent's sources until the licence is renewed
explanations: A prompt heuristic cannot tell a real empty search from a failed one; the tool must report the difference.
Correct. "Could not check" and "checked, found nothing" must be distinguishable so the coordinator can report the gap or try another source.
A 401 from an expired licence will not fix itself on retry; this burns time and budget.
Removing the source hides the coverage gap instead of reporting it, and the report still overstates what was checked.

questions.stem: During a parallel fan-out, the research system's search subagents often get HTTP 429 responses with a `Retry-After` of 2 to 5 seconds from the search provider's MCP server. Today each 429 becomes an `isError` result, and subagents spend whole turns re-issuing the call, sometimes giving up early. How should the architect handle these errors?
options: Add an instruction to every subagent prompt to wait 30 seconds after any tool error before trying again
Keep returning `isError: true` on every 429 so the model decides on each retry with full information
Retry inside the tool until the call eventually succeeds, however long that takes, so that subagents never have to see or reason about a rate-limit error at all
Retry the 429 inside the tool a bounded number of times, honouring `Retry-After`; if it still fails, return a transient, retryable `isError` result
explanations: A model cannot actually wait between turns because of a prompt instruction; this is a prompt fix for a control problem.
Each model-driven retry costs a full turn and tokens for a decision that code can make better.
Unbounded retries can hang a subagent indefinitely and blow the run's time and cost budget.
Correct. Cheap, deterministic recovery belongs in code; the model sees the error only when retries are exhausted, and then with enough structure to choose its next move.

questions.stem: A research subagent calls `search_papers` with `published_after: "last year"`. The backend rejects anything that is not an ISO date, and the tool returns `isError: true` with the text "Error". The subagent then drops the date filter and returns papers from the 1990s. What is the BEST change to the tool's error result?
options: Name the field, the accepted format and the value received, e.g. "`published_after` must be YYYY-MM-DD; got 'last year'. Example: 2025-01-01"
Ignore the invalid `published_after` value and return the unfiltered results as a normal success, so the subagent still gets papers to work with
Substitute today's date minus 365 days and continue without telling the agent
Return a JSON-RPC protocol error so that the MCP client rejects the malformed call before it ever reaches the search backend
explanations: Correct. An actionable validation message lets the subagent fix its input and call again, which is exactly the recovery you want.
Silently ignoring the filter produces wrong results that look valid.
Guessing the meaning on the agent's behalf may be wrong and hides the problem; the agent should supply the date it means.
A protocol error is typically shown generically and gives the model less to work with than a clear error result.

questions.stem: In the extraction pipeline, `lookup_vendor` returns `{"vendor": null}` both when no vendor matches and when the vendor database is unreachable. Pipeline code sends every invoice with a null vendor to the new-vendor onboarding queue. During a 40-minute database outage, 900 invoices from existing vendors were misrouted. Which TWO changes BEST prevent this? (Select TWO.)
options: Return a transient, retryable `isError` result when the database is unreachable, and keep a successful `{"vendor": null}` for a real no-match
Add a prompt instruction telling the extractor to look more carefully and double-check its reasoning whenever the vendor lookup comes back null
Return `isError: true` for both the no-match and the unreachable case, so that no invoice is ever routed to onboarding automatically again
During outages, serve the vendor list from a cache without marking the data as possibly stale, so the pipeline keeps running at full speed
Have pipeline code park invoices whose lookup failed with a retryable error for re-processing, instead of routing them as no-match
explanations: Correct. Separating "could not check" from "checked, no match" is the core fix.
The extractor cannot distinguish the two cases from identical output, so double-checking adds cost without information.
A real no-match is a valid answer; treating it as an error stalls legitimate onboarding and conflates the two cases again.
Unflagged stale data swaps one silent failure for another.
Correct. Once errors are classified, deterministic routing in code can hold retryable failures rather than misrouting them.

questions.stem: In the contract extraction pipeline, the `validate_iban` MCP tool returns the full 40-line Java stack trace as its error text whenever validation fails. Reviewers notice internal hostnames copied into extraction notes, and error turns use far more tokens than successful ones. What should the tool do instead?
options: Return a normal success with an empty result whenever validation fails, so no error text reaches the model
Raise `MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS` so the full trace always fits
Keep returning the trace, but add a rule to the extractor's prompt that internal hostnames and stack frames must never be copied into extraction notes
Log the trace server-side and return `isError: true` with a short cause, e.g. "IBAN checksum invalid for `payee_iban`"
explanations: An empty success hides the failure, so invalid IBANs would flow through as if valid.
More room for noise is the opposite of the fix and leaves the leak in place.
A prompt rule does not remove the sensitive data from context and leaves the token waste.
Correct. The model needs the actionable cause; diagnostic detail belongs in server logs.

questions.stem: The developer-productivity platform runs 12 internal MCP servers built by different teams, each reporting failures differently. The platform team is writing one error contract that every server must follow so agents and hooks can react consistently. Which THREE elements should the contract require? (Select THREE.)
options: The complete upstream response, including status line and headers, in every error so that agents always have maximum context
Tool execution failures reported in the tool result with `isError: true`
JSON-RPC error codes for business-rule failures so every client handles them the same way
A `retryable` boolean, plus a suggested wait when it is known
One fixed message, "Operation failed", across all servers so no internal details leak
An `error_category` drawn from a small fixed set such as transient, validation, business_rule and permission
explanations: Raw upstream responses waste context and can leak credentials or internal details.
Correct. In-band `isError` results reach the model so it can adapt; this is the MCP mechanism for execution failures.
Protocol errors are for unknown tools and malformed requests; business-rule failures belong in the tool result where the model can read them.
Correct. Retryability is what lets an agent or hook decide between retrying and changing course.
A uniform generic message removes exactly the information the agent needs to recover.
Correct. A shared, small category set lets prompts, hooks and coordinators handle every server's errors the same way.

questions.stem: A CI job runs `claude -p` to check database migrations through an MCP tool `check_migration`, then gates the merge on Claude's verdict. The tool's handler catches connection failures and returns "No issues found." During a database maintenance window, a destructive migration passed review and shipped. What is the MOST important fix?
options: Lower `--max-turns` so the job finishes before connection problems can affect it
Add "be extra careful with destructive migrations" to the CI prompt
Run the review job twice in parallel against the same database and allow the merge only when both runs independently report that the migration has no issues
Return `isError: true` saying the check could not run, and gate the merge on a structured field that records whether the check ran
explanations: Turn limits do not change what the tool reports; the false "no issues" would still be returned.
The model was told there were no issues; a more careful prompt cannot detect a failure the tool disguised as success.
Two runs against the same unreachable database will both receive the same false success.
Correct. The tool must never report success on failure, and the pipeline should gate on an explicit "check ran" signal so an unverifiable run fails.

questions.stem: The support-resolution agent was given every tool the company's MCP servers expose: 48 tools across billing, shipping, CRM administration, marketing campaigns and internal analytics. It regularly picks the wrong tool (for example a marketing contact lookup instead of the CRM customer lookup), and tool definitions consume a large share of each request. What is the BEST change?
options: Scope the agent to the tools support resolution needs, split by role into specialists with a few tools each, and drop admin and marketing tools
Move the agent to the largest available model tier, which is better at choosing correctly among many similar-looking tools from different servers
Add a long section to the system prompt that explains, tool by tool, when each of the 48 tools should and should not be used
Set `tool_choice` to `any` so the agent always commits to a tool rather than hesitating between them
explanations: Correct. A scoped tool set per role improves selection, cuts context and removes tools the agent should never use.
Selection accuracy degrades with large tool sets regardless of tier, and the definitions still cost context on every request.
More prompt text adds context and leaves 48 overlapping tools in place; it treats the symptom.
Forcing a call does nothing to help the agent pick the right tool, and current models reject forced `tool_choice` with a 400.

questions.stem: The support agent is built with the Agent SDK. A security review finds that the refund subagent has requested `mcp__crm__delete_contact` during testing, although refunds only need two billing tools. What is the MOST likely cause, and the fix?
options: No `tools` field means the subagent inherits every tool, and `allowed_tools` only pre-approves calls; set `tools` to the two billing tools
Add a sentence to the subagent's prompt forbidding any CRM tool and explaining that refunds never require changes to customer contact records
`allowed_tools` is applied in order, so put the billing tools first in the list to give them priority
Switch to `permission_mode="bypassPermissions"` so that only the tools in `allowed_tools` can execute
explanations: Correct. An omitted `tools` field means the subagent inherits the parent's tools, and allow rules auto-approve listed tools without removing others. Listing `tools` scopes the subagent.
A prompt rule is a request, not a restriction; the tool remains available.
Order in the allow list has no effect on which tools exist; the CRM tools are still offered to the subagent.
`bypassPermissions` approves calls to unlisted tools too; `allowed_tools` does not constrain it, so this widens access.

questions.stem: After the support agent has created an escalation ticket, the harness makes one final request to produce the customer-facing message. In a few percent of cases Claude calls `lookup_order` again on that request, delaying the reply. The team wants no tool calls on this request but wants to keep the `tools` array byte-identical so the cached prefix is reused. Which configuration BEST fits?
options: `tool_choice: {"type": "none"}` on the final request, with the same `tools` array as earlier turns
`tool_choice: {"type": "auto", "disable_parallel_tool_use": true}` on the final request
Set a very low `max_tokens` on the final request so there is no room for a tool call
Omit the `tools` array on the final request so tools cannot be called
explanations: Correct. `none` prevents tool use while the definitions stay in the request, and changing `tool_choice` does not invalidate the cached tools and system prefix.
This still allows one tool call per response; it limits parallelism, not whether a tool is called.
A tight token limit risks truncating the customer message and does not reliably prevent a short tool call.
Removing the tools changes the request prefix, which loses the cache the team wants to keep.

questions.stem: In the multi-agent research system, the coordinator was given `web_search`, `web_fetch` and the tool for delegating to subagents. Transcripts show it often runs searches and fetches pages itself instead of delegating, so its context fills with raw pages and synthesis quality drops on long questions. What is the BEST change?
options: Tell the coordinator in its prompt to delegate all searching and to avoid fetching pages itself
Remove search and fetch from the coordinator and give them only to the search subagents
Raise the coordinator's context budget so the raw pages it fetches and its working synthesis both fit comfortably in one window
Force `tool_choice` to the delegation tool on every coordinator turn
explanations: A prompt instruction may help, but the tools remain available and the coordinator will still reach for them.
Correct. Scoping tools by role keeps the coordinator on decomposition and synthesis and keeps raw content in subagent contexts.
More context postpones the problem and keeps irrelevant raw content in the coordinator's window.
Forcing delegation every turn stops the coordinator from ever writing its synthesis, and current models reject forced `tool_choice` modes.

questions.stem: The research system's synthesis subagent was given web search and fetch "just in case" it finds a gap. Reviewers find that final reports now cite sources the analysis subagents never vetted, and some claims have no traceable citation. What should the architect do?
options: Keep the tools but add a prompt rule that the synthesis subagent may only search when a claim is unsupported
Remove search and fetch from the synthesis subagent; it works from the vetted findings it is given and reports gaps back to the coordinator
Add a second synthesis subagent that independently re-checks every citation the first one added from its own searches before the report is published
Move synthesis into the coordinator so a single agent both searches and writes the report
explanations: The permission remains and so does the behaviour; a prompt rule does not scope the tool set.
Correct. Least-privilege tool sets keep each stage in its role, and returning gaps keeps the coordinator in charge of further research.
Adding a checker treats the symptom and adds cost while unvetted sources keep entering.
Merging roles gives one agent even more tools and context, which is the opposite of scoping.

questions.stem: The research system's own harness calls the Messages API with tools from seven MCP-backed services, 160 tools in total. Tool definitions alone take about 50k tokens per request, and subagents often choose a near-duplicate tool from the wrong service. Which TWO changes BEST address this? (Select TWO.)
options: Add the tool search tool and mark most tools `defer_loading: true`, keeping the few most-used tools loaded
Mark every tool, including the tool search tool, `defer_loading: true` so nothing loads up front
Give each subagent only the services and tools its role needs instead of the full catalog
Raise `max_tokens` so subagents have more room to reason about which tool to choose
Move all 160 tool descriptions into the system prompt and keep only short tool names and schemas in the `tools` array
explanations: Correct. Tool search loads only the definitions Claude needs, which cuts context and keeps selection accurate with large catalogs.
At least one tool, normally the search tool itself, must stay non-deferred; deferring everything is rejected with a 400.
Correct. Role-scoped tool sets shrink each agent's choice to what it actually uses.
Output budget does not change how many definitions crowd the context or how similar they are.
The descriptions would still occupy the context, and separating them from the tool definitions makes selection harder.

questions.stem: A search subagent in the research system needs to run about a dozen independent queries per sub-question. Transcripts show exactly one search per turn and 12 sequential turns. Its request configuration was copied from another service:
options: Lower `max_tokens` so each turn finishes faster
Split the work into twelve subagents, one per query, so that the coordinator can run all of the queries concurrently
Remove `disable_parallel_tool_use` so Claude can request several independent searches in a single turn
Change `tool_choice` to `{"type": "any"}` so the subagent must call a tool on every turn
explanations: Shorter turns do not reduce the number of sequential turns.
Twelve subagents add coordination overhead to work a single agent can parallelise with tool calls.
Correct. `disable_parallel_tool_use: true` caps Claude at one tool call per response; removing it lets independent searches go out together.
Forcing a call does not let the agent issue more than one per turn while parallel use is disabled.

questions.stem: The extraction pipeline guarantees JSON by forcing a tool: `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "record_invoice"}` with `strict: true`. After moving to a newer model version, every request returns a 400 saying `tool` and `any` tool_choice types are not supported for this model. The tool exists only to obtain schema-valid JSON. What is the BEST change?
options: Switch to `tool_choice: {"type": "any"}`, which still forces a call but lets the model pick the tool
Use structured outputs (`output_config.format`) with the invoice JSON schema instead of a forced tool call
Drop the tools, ask for JSON in the prompt, and extract it from the reply text with a regular expression
Pin the pipeline to the previous model version indefinitely so the forced tool call keeps working without any code changes
explanations: `any` is also a forced mode and is rejected by the same models.
Correct. When a forced call only existed to get JSON, structured outputs give schema-constrained output directly and work on models that reject forced `tool_choice`.
Prompt-only JSON loses the schema guarantee and regex parsing is fragile.
Pinning is a stopgap that blocks future upgrades; the design should not depend on a model-specific feature it does not need.

questions.stem: The document pipeline has three extraction tools: `record_invoice`, `record_contract` and `record_form`. Documents arrive unlabelled, and each response must call exactly one of the three. The pipeline runs on a current model that rejects forced `tool_choice` modes. Which configuration BEST meets the requirement?
options: `tool_choice: {"type": "any", "disable_parallel_tool_use": true}`, which guarantees exactly one call to one of the three tools
`tool_choice: {"type": "auto"}` alone, trusting the prompt to produce one call per document
`tool_choice: {"type": "none"}`, with the extracted fields returned as JSON text that the pipeline parses
`tool_choice: {"type": "auto", "disable_parallel_tool_use": true}`, `strict: true` on the tools, a prompt requiring one record call, and code that retries if no record tool was called
explanations: `any` is a forced mode; current models reject it with a 400, so this request fails outright.
Without a verification step nothing catches a response with no call, and without `disable_parallel_tool_use` Claude may call more than one tool.
`none` prevents tool calls and gives up the schema guarantees the tools provide.
Correct. `auto` lets Claude pick the right extractor, disabling parallel use caps it at one call, `strict` keeps arguments schema-valid, and the code check covers the turns where no call was made.

questions.stem: To "let it finish the job", the extraction agent was also given `update_erp` and `email_vendor` tools. Occasionally it posts a record to the ERP before the pipeline's validation and human-review steps have run, and a few vendors received emails about invoices that were later rejected. What is the BEST fix?
options: Remove `update_erp` and `email_vendor` from the extractor; pipeline code posts and notifies only after validation and review pass
Add a prompt rule that the agent must complete every validation step and wait for human review before it calls `update_erp` or `email_vendor`
Add a hook that logs every `update_erp` and `email_vendor` call so the audit trail is complete
Lower the model's temperature so it follows the intended order more consistently
explanations: Correct. An extraction step should only extract; side-effecting actions belong in deterministic code after the checks.
A prompt rule is probabilistic; the premature posts are exactly the failures it would not prevent.
Logging records the problem but does not stop it.
Sampling settings do not enforce ordering or remove the capability.

questions.stem: A CI review job must never modify the checkout. The shared wrapper script that launches every CI job adds `--permission-mode acceptEdits`, which the auto-fix jobs need. In one review run, Claude edited a file while "fixing" a typo it found. The review job is invoked as:

code.src:
claude -p "Review the diff in pr.diff. Do not change any files." \
  --allowedTools "Read,Grep,Glob" \
  --permission-mode acceptEdits \
  --output-format json

options: `--allowedTools` only pre-approves; restrict availability with `--tools "Read,Grep,Glob"` or bare-name `--disallowedTools "Edit,Write,Bash"`
Add `--max-turns 1` so Claude has no turns left in which to make edits
Switch to `--permission-mode bypassPermissions` so that only the tools named in `--allowedTools` are allowed to run during the review
Repeat "Do not change any files" at both the start and the end of the prompt, and add it to CLAUDE.md, so the instruction carries more weight
explanations: Correct. Allow rules auto-approve but do not remove other tools. `--tools` restricts the built-in tool set, and bare-name deny rules remove tools from context.
One turn breaks the review itself and does not remove the capability.
`bypassPermissions` approves unlisted tools as well; it would make edits easier, not impossible.
Prompt emphasis is still a request; the edit tools stay available and auto-approved by `acceptEdits`.

questions.stem: A CI auto-fix job should have exactly these tools: the built-ins Read, Edit and Bash, plus the tools of one MCP server, `tickets`. The repository's committed `.mcp.json` declares five other servers that developers use. Which TWO settings together achieve this? (Select TWO.)
options: `--allowedTools "Read,Edit,Bash,mcp__tickets__*"` on its own
`--tools "Read,Edit,Bash"` to restrict the built-in tool set
Rely on `--tools "Read,Edit,Bash"` alone, since it also removes tools from every MCP server not listed
`--mcp-config ci-mcp.json --strict-mcp-config`, where `ci-mcp.json` declares only the `tickets` server
A CLAUDE.md section listing which tools the CI job is allowed to use
explanations: Allow rules pre-approve listed tools; every other built-in and every MCP server's tools remain available.
Correct. `--tools` restricts which built-in tools exist in the session.
`--tools` does not affect MCP tools; the five other servers would still load.
Correct. `--strict-mcp-config` ignores all other MCP configuration, so only the servers in the CI file load.
CLAUDE.md is context, not enforcement; it does not change the tool set.

questions.stem: The team adds a project subagent so Claude Code can run the test suite during reviews without ever modifying files. Its frontmatter is shown below. Which tools does the subagent get?

code.src:
---
name: test-reviewer
description: Runs the test suite and reviews failures. Use after code changes.
tools: Read, Edit, Write, Bash
disallowedTools: Edit, Write
---
Run the tests, read failing files, and report root causes. Never modify files.

options: Read and Bash
Read, Edit, Write and Bash, because an explicit `tools` list takes precedence over `disallowedTools`
Every tool the main session has, except Edit and Write
None; the subagent fails to load because the two fields conflict
explanations: Correct. The subagent gets the `tools` list minus anything in `disallowedTools`.
When both fields are set, `disallowedTools` wins; a tool listed in both is removed.
Inheriting everything except the denied tools is the behaviour when only `disallowedTools` is set.
Setting both fields is valid; Claude Code resolves them rather than failing.

questions.stem: The team connected an internal `docs` MCP server to Claude Code through the project `.mcp.json`. The server exposes API specification files as resources and a `release_notes` prompt that takes a version argument. A developer asks how these show up in a Claude Code session. Which TWO statements are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: A resource can be attached to a prompt by typing `@docs:` and choosing it, e.g. `@docs:file://api/orders.yaml`
Resources are model-controlled: Claude decides on its own to call them, exactly like tools
The prompt runs as a slash command, e.g. `/mcp__docs__release_notes 2.3`
The `release_notes` prompt becomes a tool that Claude may call autonomously whenever it thinks release notes would help
Resources only become usable after their content has been copied into the project's CLAUDE.md file
explanations: Correct. MCP resources appear in the `@` autocomplete and are referenced as `@server:protocol://path`.
Resources are application-controlled context that the user or client attaches; tools are the model-controlled primitive.
Correct. MCP prompts are user-controlled templates and appear as slash commands in the `/mcp__server__prompt` form.
Prompts are user-invoked templates, not tools; Claude does not call them on its own.
Resources are read from the server on demand; copying them into CLAUDE.md would load them every session for no reason.

questions.stem: The team wants Claude Code to read GitHub issues and pull-request review threads while it implements features. A developer proposes writing a custom stdio MCP server that wraps the dozen GitHub REST endpoints the team uses. What should the tech lead recommend?
options: Build the custom server as proposed, since a server tailored to the team's dozen endpoints will be smaller and easier to reason about
Paste the GitHub REST API reference into CLAUDE.md so Claude can construct `curl` calls through Bash when it needs issue data
Add a maintained, existing GitHub MCP server to the project `.mcp.json`, with the token supplied through `${GITHUB_TOKEN}`
Have each developer run `claude mcp add` at local scope with their own token pasted into the command
explanations: A custom wrapper duplicates a maintained integration and becomes the team's code to secure and keep current.
A large API reference in CLAUDE.md costs context every session and replaces a typed integration with ad hoc shell calls.
Correct. Adopting an existing server for a common system is the default; project scope shares the configuration and env-var expansion keeps the token out of git.
Local scope works for one person but is not shared, so every developer has to configure it by hand and setups drift.

questions.stem: The repository's committed `.mcp.json` declares five MCP servers developers use locally, including two stdio servers that need a local database. In CI, `claude -p` jobs are slow to start and log connection failures for those servers. The CI jobs only need the `tickets` server. What is the BEST configuration?
options: Pass `--tools "Read,Edit,Bash"`, which stops MCP servers that are not needed from loading
Run with `--mcp-config ci-mcp.json --strict-mcp-config`, where `ci-mcp.json` declares only `tickets`
Add a CI step that deletes `.mcp.json` from the checkout before Claude Code starts
Pass `--disallowedTools "mcp__*"` so that none of the developers' MCP servers are used by the job
explanations: `--tools` restricts built-in tools only; it does not affect MCP servers.
Correct. `--strict-mcp-config` makes the job use only the servers in the given file, ignoring all other MCP configuration.
Mutating the checkout is fragile and easy to break when the file moves or other configuration sources exist.
This removes every MCP tool, including the `tickets` tools the job needs.

questions.stem: The research system, built on the Agent SDK, connects a vendor's scholarly-database MCP server named `scholar`, which exposes a tool named `search`. The literature subagent is defined as below, yet in testing it never calls the database and reports that no search tool is available. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: Subagents cannot use MCP tools; only the main agent can, so searches must be routed through the coordinator
The server must use the stdio transport for its tools to be visible to subagents
MCP tools are named `mcp__<server>__<tool>`, so the list must say `mcp__scholar__search`; the bare name `search` matches no tool
The tool also has to be added to `allowed_tools`, because a subagent's `tools` list only applies to built-in tools
explanations: Subagents can be given MCP tools in their tool list; the coordinator does not have to proxy them.
Transport does not affect tool visibility; remote HTTP servers expose tools the same way.
Correct. MCP tools are exposed with the server-prefixed name, and that full name is what tool lists, permission rules and hook matchers use.
`allowed_tools` pre-approves calls; it does not make a tool exist, and `tools` lists accept MCP tool names.

questions.stem: While changing a timeout in `client.ts`, Claude Code's Edit call fails because `old_string` (`timeout: 3000,`) appears three times in the file. Only the occurrence inside `retryPolicy()` should change. What should happen next?
options: Retry the Edit with an `old_string` that includes enough surrounding lines from `retryPolicy()` to match exactly once
Retry the Edit with `replace_all: true` so the call succeeds
Switch to a regular-expression `old_string` that targets the line inside `retryPolicy()`
Rewrite the whole file from memory with the Write tool, changing only the one value inside `retryPolicy()` and keeping the rest as it was
explanations: Correct. Edit needs `old_string` to match exactly once; adding surrounding context pins down the intended occurrence.
`replace_all` changes all three occurrences, two of which must stay as they are.
Edit does exact string replacement; it does not support regex or fuzzy matching.
Rewriting from memory risks silently changing other lines; Write is for new files or deliberate full rewrites, ideally after a fresh Read.

questions.stem: A developer asked Claude Code to "add an entry for the new export feature to CHANGELOG.md". After the change, the file contains only the new entry; three years of history are gone. The transcript shows a single Write call containing the new entry. What explains this, and what should Claude have done?
options: Write was given a relative path, so it created a second CHANGELOG.md in another directory; Claude should have passed an absolute path
The file was not read first, so Write fell back to truncating it; Claude should have called Read immediately before the same Write call
Write needs `append: true` to keep existing content; Claude should have set that flag on the call
Write replaces the whole file with the given content; Claude should have used Edit anchored on a unique line such as the top heading
explanations: The stem shows the original file itself lost its history; this is not a path problem.
Reading first would not change what Write does with content that contains only the new entry; it still overwrites the file.
Write has no append mode; it creates or fully overwrites a file.
Correct. Write never appends or merges. A partial change belongs in Edit (or a Read followed by a Write of the complete new content).

questions.stem: In a Go service, a developer asks Claude Code to find every function that takes an empty-interface parameter. Claude's Grep call with pattern `interface{}` does not return those files, although the developer knows several committed, non-ignored files contain that text. What is the MOST likely reason?
options: Grep uses ripgrep regex syntax, where `{` and `}` are metacharacters; the pattern should be `interface\{\}`
Grep only searches file names, so Claude should have used a Glob pattern that matches the text instead
The files are probably listed in `.gitignore`, which Grep respects, so the search skipped them without reporting it
Grep skips files with a `.go` extension unless a `type` filter is set explicitly
explanations: Correct. Grep is built on ripgrep, so regex metacharacters in the pattern must be escaped; unescaped, ripgrep rejects `interface{}` as an invalid repetition instead of matching the literal text.
This reverses the tools: Grep searches contents and Glob matches paths.
Grep does skip gitignored files, but the stem says the files are committed and not ignored.
Grep searches all non-ignored files by default; `type` and `glob` are optional filters.

questions.stem: Claude Code runs `export DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost/test` in one Bash call and `npm run migrate` in the next. The migration fails because `DATABASE_URL` is not set. The team wants migrations to work reliably in every session. What should they do?
options: Add a CLAUDE.md rule telling Claude to run `export` once at the start of each session, since the Bash tool's shell keeps variables after the first export
Run `cd` into the project directory first, because the working directory resets between calls and that clears the environment
Env vars don't persist between Bash calls: chain them in one command, or set them session-wide via `CLAUDE_ENV_FILE` or a SessionStart hook
Switch the migration to run through the Write tool, which shares the environment of the main session
explanations: Each Bash command runs in a separate process; an earlier `export` is gone by the next call.
The working directory does carry over inside the project; it is environment variables that do not persist.
Correct. Variables must be set within the same command, or provided session-wide through `CLAUDE_ENV_FILE` or a SessionStart hook.
Write creates or overwrites files; it does not run commands or carry an environment.

questions.stem: During iterative refinement, a developer asks Claude Code to check the response from the dev server it just started. Claude calls WebFetch on `http://localhost:3000/health` and the call is refused before any request is made. What should Claude use instead?
options: WebSearch with the query `localhost:3000 health` to locate the endpoint
`curl` through the Bash tool, because WebFetch refuses `localhost` and other hostnames without a dot
WebFetch again with `https://localhost:3000/health`, since the HTTP scheme is what was refused
A `WebFetch(domain:localhost)` allow rule added to project settings
explanations: WebSearch queries a public search backend and cannot reach a local server.
Correct. WebFetch refuses local and dotless hostnames by design; local servers are reached with `curl` via Bash.
WebFetch upgrades HTTP to HTTPS on its own; the refusal is about the host, not the scheme.
The refusal happens before permission rules matter; an allow rule does not make WebFetch reach localhost.

questions.stem: A CI job asks `claude -p` to diagnose a failed integration test from a 3 MB `test-output.log`. Claude's first Read call on the whole file returns an error telling it to read a portion or search instead. What is the BEST next step?
options: Read the log sequentially in pages with `offset` and `limit`, from the first line to the last, so that no part of the output is missed
Grep the log for failure markers like `FAIL` or `Error:`, then Read only the surrounding line ranges with `offset` and `limit`
Raise the job's model tier to one with a larger context window and Read the whole file again
Ask Claude to `cat` the whole log through Bash, which has no size limit on its output
explanations: Paging through 3 MB fills the context with passing-test noise before the failure is even found.
Correct. Search first, then targeted reads: the failure lines are found cheaply and only the relevant context enters the window.
The limit is on the Read call, not just the window; and loading the whole log would still bury the signal.
Bash output is also capped, and dumping the whole log is the same context problem in a different tool.

questions.stem: The CI auto-fix job must never change Terraform under `infra/`. The team added the deny rule below to the project's `.claude/settings.json`, yet a run still modified `infra/main.tf` with the Edit tool. What is the BEST correction?
options: Use `Write(//infra/**)`, because a double slash is required for a path relative to the project root
Add a CLAUDE.md rule telling Claude never to modify files under `infra/`, alongside the existing deny rule
Replace it with `Edit(/infra/**)`; path rules for file changes are written as `Edit(...)`, which covers Edit, Write and NotebookEdit
Move the rule from `deny` into `ask`, since an ask rule also blocks unattended runs
explanations: A `Write(...)` path rule matches no call in either form, and `//` denotes an absolute filesystem path, not a project-relative one.
CLAUDE.md is context, not enforcement; the deny rule itself is what needs fixing.
Correct. `Edit(path)` rules govern every built-in tool that writes files; a rule written as `Write(path)` matches nothing.
An ask rule is weaker than a deny, and it would still use the same ineffective `Write(...)` path form.

questions.stem: On the developer-productivity platform, a new engineer asks Claude Code: "Where is the rate limiter configured in this monorepo, and which services call it?" The repository has about 9,000 files. Which TWO tool uses are the BEST way to start? (Select TWO.)
options: Glob for paths such as `**/*rate*limit*` to find candidate configuration files by name
Read every file under `services/` first, so that the full picture is already in context before Claude answers
Grep for the limiter's constructor (e.g. `RateLimiter(`) across the repo, then Read only the matching files
WebSearch for the rate-limiting library's documentation
Write a summary of every top-level directory to a notes file before searching anything
explanations: Correct. Glob finds files by name pattern, which is the fast way to locate likely config files.
Reading thousands of files floods the context; search first, then read selectively.
Correct. Grep finds usages by content, and targeted Reads follow only the hits.
Library docs do not say where this repo configures or calls the limiter.
Summarising every directory up front is slow and mostly irrelevant to the question.

questions.stem: The platform team wants Claude Code's web lookups to go through the company's licensed enterprise search provider instead of the built-in WebSearch tool, for compliance logging. Which approach BEST meets this?
options: Set an environment variable that points the built-in WebSearch tool at the enterprise provider's API endpoint
Write a skill that tells Claude to send each query to the provider's search URL with WebFetch and parse the results
Connect an MCP server exposing the provider's search as a tool, and deny `WebSearch` in managed or project settings
Add a CLAUDE.md instruction asking Claude to prefer the enterprise provider whenever it searches
explanations: The WebSearch backend is not configurable; there is no setting that redirects it.
WebFetch runs an extraction prompt over a single page; it is not a search integration, and nothing stops the built-in search from being used.
Correct. A different search backend comes in through an MCP tool, and a deny rule on `WebSearch` keeps lookups on the compliant path.
A preference in CLAUDE.md neither provides the integration nor guarantees the built-in tool is not used.

questions.stem: An engineer on the platform asked Claude Code to summarise a vendor's API changelog with WebFetch. Claude replied that "the page does not mention any deprecations", but the page has listed a deprecation near the bottom for months. What is the MOST likely explanation and fix?
options: WebFetch served a stale copy from its cache; wait for the cache to expire and fetch the page again
The changelog domain is not on the preapproved list, so WebFetch only returned the page title and first paragraph
WebFetch returns an extraction prompt's answer, not the raw page; refetch with a prompt about deprecations, or get the raw page with `curl`
WebSearch should have been used instead, because WebFetch cannot read pages that are longer than one screen of content and stops early
explanations: The cache window is short and the deprecation has been on the page for months, so staleness does not explain it.
The preapproved list affects whether a permission prompt appears, not how much of the page is processed.
Correct. WebFetch runs the given prompt over the fetched content in a separate model call; what reaches Claude depends on what the prompt asked for.
WebSearch returns titles and URLs without page content, and WebFetch handles long pages.

questions.stem: A source-gathering subagent in the research system has only the WebSearch tool. Reviewers find that its quoted passages often do not appear in the cited pages, and some citations point to low-quality content farms. Which TWO changes BEST address this? (Select TWO.)
options: Add WebFetch so the subagent reads each page before quoting it, since WebSearch returns titles and URLs, not page content
Raise the per-session web search limit so the subagent can run more searches per question
Use `allowed_domains` on WebSearch to restrict results to vetted publishers when a question needs authoritative sources
Replace WebSearch with the Read tool pointed at each result URL to get the exact text
Pass both `allowed_domains` and `blocked_domains` in the same WebSearch call for the most precise filtering of results
explanations: Correct. Without fetching the page, the subagent is quoting from titles and its own memory; WebFetch retrieves the content.
More searches return more titles and URLs, not page text, and do nothing about source quality.
Correct. Domain allow-listing on WebSearch keeps low-quality sources out of the candidate set.
Read reads local files; it does not fetch URLs.
The two lists cannot be combined in a single WebSearch call.

questions.stem: The support agent uses the Agent tool to hand order investigations to a subagent that calls several order and shipping tools. The parent agent then tells customers "your refund amount has been confirmed" without quoting the amount, because it never sees the order records the subagent looked up. What is the BEST change?
options: Give the parent the same order and shipping tools so it can repeat the lookups itself after the subagent finishes
Define the subagent's output so its final message includes the facts the parent needs (order ID, amount, dates, status) in a fixed structure
Run the subagent directly inside the parent's context so that all of its intermediate tool calls and outputs are visible to the parent agent
Increase the parent's context window so the subagent's tool outputs fit alongside the conversation
explanations: Duplicating every lookup wastes calls and undoes the reason for delegating.
Correct. The parent sees only the subagent's final result, so that result must carry the specific facts in a predictable shape.
Sharing the whole intermediate transcript defeats the context isolation a subagent provides; the parent needs the facts, not the raw calls.
The subagent's intermediate outputs never reach the parent, whatever the parent's window size.

questions.stem: While prototyping the extraction pipeline in Claude Code, an engineer asks Claude to pull vendor rows from `vendors_q3.xlsx`. Claude's Read call on the file is refused. What is the BEST way forward?
options: Fetch the spreadsheet with WebFetch using a `file://` URL, which converts documents to Markdown before returning them
Read the file again with `offset` and `limit` so only part of it is loaded
Rename the file to `vendors_q3.csv` so the Read tool will accept it
Use a spreadsheet skill, or a script run through Bash that converts the sheet to CSV, then Read the result
explanations: WebFetch is for web URLs, not local files.
Paging does not help; Read refuses binary formats such as `.xlsx` regardless of range.
Renaming does not change the binary content; the result would be unreadable.
Correct. Read refuses binary formats; a skill for the file type or a conversion script gets the data into a readable form.

questions.stem: To make CI runs start faster and behave the same on every runner, the platform team added `--bare` to the pipeline's `claude -p` invocation. Since then, Claude's automated fixes ignore the conventions in the repository's committed root `CLAUDE.md` (pnpm only, named exports), although the same prompt run locally without the flag follows them. What is the BEST fix?

code.src:
claude --bare -p "Fix the failing lint errors in src/" \
  --allowedTools "Read,Edit,Bash(pnpm lint *)" \
  --permission-mode dontAsk

options: Move the file to `.claude/CLAUDE.md`, which is the location Claude Code reads in non-interactive runs.
Pass the conventions explicitly with `--append-system-prompt-file CLAUDE.md`, or drop `--bare`.
Duplicate the conventions into `CLAUDE.local.md`, because local instructions are appended last and therefore win.
Add `--setting-sources project` so the project scope is loaded in addition to the bare defaults.
explanations: Both `./CLAUDE.md` and `./.claude/CLAUDE.md` are project locations; neither is read when `--bare` skips CLAUDE.md discovery.

Correct. `--bare` skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, MCP servers, auto memory and CLAUDE.md. The documented pattern is to pass what the run needs with flags such as `--append-system-prompt-file`, or not to use bare mode.
`CLAUDE.local.md` is personal and normally gitignored, so it isn't on the runner, and bare mode would skip it anyway.
`--setting-sources` selects which settings files load; it doesn't undo bare mode's skipping of CLAUDE.md discovery.

questions.stem: A monorepo's CI review job runs `git diff origin/main... | claude -p "Review this diff"` from the repository root. Payment-specific review rules live in `services/billing/CLAUDE.md`, and the root `CLAUDE.md` holds general rules. Reviews of billing PRs never apply the billing rules. Jobs for other services must not receive the billing rules. What is the BEST change?
options: Import `@services/billing/CLAUDE.md` from the root `CLAUDE.md` so it always loads.
For billing PRs, run the job with `services/billing/` as the working directory so that file is loaded at launch.
Rename the file to `services/billing/CLAUDE.local.md` so it loads with higher priority.
Pass `--add-dir services/billing` so Claude Code loads that directory's CLAUDE.md.
explanations: This would load the billing rules in every job, including other services' reviews, which the requirement forbids.

Correct. CLAUDE.md files in the working directory and its ancestors load at launch, so billing's file and the root file both load. Subdirectory files otherwise load only when Claude reads or edits a file there, and a piped diff isn't a file read.
`CLAUDE.local.md` is personal and normally gitignored; it is also loaded under the same on-demand rule as a subdirectory CLAUDE.md.
`--add-dir` grants file access; CLAUDE.md files from added directories aren't loaded by default.

questions.stem: The team's committed `CLAUDE.md` says "Never modify files under `db/migrations/` - migrations are append-only." A nightly `claude -p` auto-fix job nevertheless edited an existing migration to make a failing test pass. The team needs this to be impossible for the CI job and for developers' sessions. What is the BEST fix?
options: Rewrite the line in capitals under a `## CRITICAL` heading at the very top of `CLAUDE.md`.
Move the instruction into the organization's managed-policy CLAUDE.md so individual users can't exclude it.
Repeat the instruction in the CI prompt as well as in CLAUDE.md, so it appears in two places.
Add a deny rule such as `Edit(/db/migrations/**)` to the committed `.claude/settings.json`.
explanations: Emphasis may improve adherence, but CLAUDE.md is context, not enforcement; it can't make the edit impossible.
A managed CLAUDE.md can't be excluded, but it is still guidance. The docs say to enforce with settings such as `permissions.deny`.
Repetition is still a prompt-level request. It doesn't block the tool call.
Correct. Permission deny rules are enforced by the client whatever Claude decides, and the committed project settings apply both on the runner and in teammates' sessions.

questions.stem: The internal developer platform team must roll out two things to every engineer's Claude Code across all repositories: (1) secure-coding guidance (e.g. "use the shared crypto helpers") that individual engineers can't switch off with `claudeMdExcludes`, and (2) a hard block on reading `.env` files. Engineers own their repos and home directories. Which TWO mechanisms BEST meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
options: A managed-policy CLAUDE.md deployed to the OS-level managed location via MDM or similar tooling.
A `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` written to each engineer's home directory by an onboarding script.
A `permissions.deny` rule for `.env` reads in managed settings.
A template `CLAUDE.md` committed to every repository by a platform bot.
A `claudeMdExcludes` entry in managed settings that excludes every project CLAUDE.md so only the org guidance loads.
explanations: Correct. A managed CLAUDE.md applies to all users on the machine in any repository and can't be excluded with `claudeMdExcludes`.
Engineers can edit or delete their own user file, so it doesn't meet the 'can't switch off' requirement.
Correct. Blocking is a settings concern: managed settings rules are enforced by the client and can't be overridden by user or project files.
Repo owners can change or delete it, it doesn't cover new repos automatically, and it would still be guidance rather than a block.
This removes legitimate team guidance and still doesn't enforce anything; the org guidance already can't be excluded.

questions.stem: An engineer on the platform team starts Claude Code in `monorepo/tools/cli/`. The ancestor file `monorepo/CLAUDE.md` is owned by another team and full of instructions irrelevant to the CLI, which crowd the engineer's context. The other team still needs that file. What should the engineer do?
options: Delete the root `CLAUDE.md` in a local commit and avoid pushing it.
Add the root file's path to `claudeMdExcludes` in their `.claude/settings.local.json`.
Write "Ignore the instructions in the monorepo root CLAUDE.md" in `tools/cli/CLAUDE.md`.
Start Claude Code with `--add-dir ..` so the root is treated as an additional directory instead.
explanations: This is fragile and risks the deletion leaking into a push; the file would also reappear on every pull.
Correct. `claudeMdExcludes` skips specific CLAUDE.md files by path or glob, and putting it in local settings keeps the exclusion to this engineer's machine.
Both files still load; contradictory instructions make Claude pick one arbitrarily rather than reliably ignoring the other.
Ancestors of the working directory load at launch regardless; `--add-dir` only grants access to extra directories.

questions.stem: Early in a long Claude Code session, a developer told Claude "use the new `Result<T>` error helper, never throw." After the session auto-compacted, Claude started throwing exceptions again, while it still follows the rules in the project-root `CLAUDE.md`. What is the MOST likely explanation and fix?
options: Compaction removed every CLAUDE.md file from context; run `/init` after each compaction so the file is regenerated and re-injected into the session.
Auto memory overrode the instruction; disable auto memory with `/memory`.
The session exceeded the model's context window; switch to a model with a larger window so compaction never happens.
The instruction lived only in conversation and didn't survive the summary; add it to `CLAUDE.md` so it is re-read from disk after compaction.
explanations: The symptom contradicts this: CLAUDE.md rules are still followed, because the project-root CLAUDE.md is re-read from disk after compaction.
Nothing indicates auto memory is involved; it is a separate notes system and doesn't override instructions.
Larger windows postpone compaction but don't fix where the instruction lives; long sessions still compact.
Correct. Conversation-only instructions survive only as far as the summary keeps them. Durable conventions belong in CLAUDE.md.

questions.stem: The team has a committed project skill, `.claude/skills/release-notes/SKILL.md`, that developers run as `/release-notes v2.3` interactively. They now want the release pipeline to produce the same notes with `claude -p`. A developer claims slash commands only work in the interactive terminal, so the skill's instructions must be copied into a CI prompt file. What should the architect do?
options: Agree, and keep a copy of the skill body in `ci/release-prompt.txt` that the pipeline passes as the prompt.
Rewrite the skill as an MCP prompt, since MCP prompts are the only reusable prompts available in print mode.
Run the job with `--bare` so the skill directory is loaded without the interactive UI.
Run `claude -p "/release-notes v2.3"`; user-invoked skills are expanded in print mode.
explanations: Duplicating the skill creates two copies that drift apart, and it isn't necessary.
MCP prompts are a different mechanism; there's no need to re-host the skill on a server.
The opposite: `--bare` skips skill auto-discovery, so the project skill wouldn't be found.
Correct. In `-p` mode, user-invoked skills and custom commands work: include `/skill-name` in the prompt and Claude Code expands it. Only terminal-only built-ins such as `/login` are unavailable.

questions.stem: A `pr-summary` skill used by the CI pipeline tells Claude to "fetch the PR diff and comments with gh, then summarize." Logs show Claude spends several turns working out the right `gh` invocations before it starts summarizing, and some runs hit `--max-turns`. The team wants the diff and comments in front of Claude from the start. Which change BEST achieves this?

code.src:
---
name: pr-summary
description: Summarize a pull request. Use when asked to summarize or describe a PR.
allowed-tools: Bash(gh *)
---
Fetch the PR diff and comments with gh, then summarize the changes and risks.

options: Raise `--max-turns` so Claude has enough turns to discover the commands.
Add a SessionStart hook that runs `gh pr diff` and appends the output to CLAUDE.md before each CI run starts.
Add a CLAUDE.md section listing the exact `gh` commands to use for pull requests.
Inject the data with `` !`gh pr diff` `` and `` !`gh pr view --comments` `` lines in the skill body.
explanations: This treats the symptom and adds cost; Claude still spends turns fetching data that could be supplied up front.
Rewriting a committed instruction file with run data is fragile and loads the diff into every session, not just this skill.
Claude would still have to call the commands itself, turn by turn; it only shortens the discovery.
Correct. Dynamic context injection runs each `` !`command` `` before the skill content is sent and replaces the placeholder with its output, so Claude starts with the actual data.

questions.stem: To keep the CI job's main context small, an engineer adds `context: fork` to the team's `api-conventions` skill. The skill body is a list of guidelines (error envelope, pagination style, naming) with no task. Since the change, when Claude loads the skill during an automated endpoint change, the generated handlers ignore the conventions and the skill's result is empty. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: Forked skills can't run in print mode, so the skill is skipped silently in CI.
The fork gets the guidelines as its prompt but no task, so it returns little, and the conventions never reach the context writing the code.
`context: fork` requires an `agent` field; without it the skill fails to load.
The forked subagent inherits the CI job's `--max-turns` budget and exhausts it before reaching the guidelines, so it returns an empty result.
explanations: Forked skills do run in print mode; with `-p`, Claude Code waits for the forked result.

Correct. With `context: fork`, the skill body becomes a subagent's prompt. The docs warn that a guidelines-only skill gives the subagent no task, so it returns without meaningful output. Reference skills should load inline.
`agent` is optional; if it is omitted, the general-purpose subagent is used.
Nothing suggests a turn limit; the problem is that the fork has no task and its output doesn't carry the conventions back.

questions.stem: The developer-platform team has built a set of Claude Code skills, two hooks and an MCP server for the internal deploy system. Forty product repositories should use them, teams should be able to pin a version and upgrade deliberately, and the skills must not collide with skills a repo already defines. What is the BEST distribution mechanism?
options: Have a bot copy the files into every repository's `.claude/` directory and open a PR in each repo whenever the platform team changes them.
Publish the skill text in a shared wiki and link it from each repo's CLAUDE.md.
Install everything into each engineer's `~/.claude/` with an onboarding script.
Package them as a plugin in an internal marketplace; repos enable it in committed settings, and its skills are namespaced.
explanations: This works, but it multiplies copies and PR churn, gives no versioned unit, and same-named skills would collide with existing repo skills.
A link isn't a skill. Claude wouldn't get progressive loading, and hooks and the MCP server wouldn't be installed.
Personal installs don't reach CI or new teammates, and they can't be versioned per repository.
Correct. Plugins bundle skills, hooks and MCP servers into one versioned, installable unit from a marketplace, and plugin skills are namespaced so they don't clash with project skills.

questions.stem: On the internal platform, an engineer has a personal `~/.claude/skills/review/SKILL.md`. The repository they work in also commits `.claude/skills/review/SKILL.md` and an older `.claude/commands/review.md`, and a platform plugin ships a skill named `review`. Which TWO statements about what happens are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: When the engineer types `/review`, the personal skill is used, because personal skills take precedence over project skills.
The project skill wins over the personal one, because repository configuration overrides user configuration.
Between the project skill and `.claude/commands/review.md`, the skill takes precedence.
The plugin's `review` skill replaces both, because plugins are installed last.
Claude Code refuses to start until the duplicate names are resolved.
explanations: Correct. For skills sharing a name, enterprise beats personal and personal beats project.
For skills it is the other way round: personal skills beat project skills (unlike settings precedence, where project beats user).
Correct. When a skill and a `.claude/commands/` file share a name, the skill wins.
Plugin skills are namespaced as `/plugin-name:review`, so they load alongside rather than replacing anything.
Name clashes are resolved by precedence; they don't block startup.

questions.stem: The team wrote a project skill that walks Claude through adding a feature flag (config entry, typed accessor, default, cleanup ticket). When developers say "add a feature flag for the new checkout", Claude never loads it and improvises instead; typing `/feature-flag` works fine. What should they change FIRST?

code.src:
---
name: feature-flag
description: Helper utilities for the config package.
---
1. Add the flag to config/flags.yaml ...

options: Add `user-invocable: true` so Claude is allowed to invoke the skill on its own.
Rewrite `description` to say what the skill does and when to use it, e.g. "Add or remove a feature flag. Use when asked to create, add, gate or clean up a feature flag."
Move the procedure into the root `CLAUDE.md` so it is always in context.
Add `context: fork` so the skill runs in a subagent with its own context window.
explanations: `user-invocable` controls whether the user can run it from the `/` menu, and it is `true` by default; it doesn't affect Claude's matching.
Correct. Claude decides whether to load a skill from its description. A vague description that doesn't mention feature flags gives it nothing to match against.
This would load a multi-step procedure into every session; procedures belong in skills.
Forking changes where the skill runs once invoked; it doesn't help Claude decide to invoke it.

questions.stem: A developer created a `migration-check` skill in `~/.claude/skills/migration-check/SKILL.md` and it works well for them. Teammates on the same repository report that Claude never uses it and `/migration-check` doesn't exist for them. What should the developer do?
options: Ask each teammate to copy the folder into their own `~/.claude/skills/`.
Move the skill to `.claude/skills/migration-check/SKILL.md` in the repository and commit it.
Add `disable-model-invocation: false` to the skill so it is shared.
Reference the skill's path from the root `CLAUDE.md` with an `@` import.
explanations: This works but creates unversioned copies that drift and never reach CI.
Correct. Personal skills apply only to that user. Project skills in `.claude/skills/` are shared through version control.
That field only controls whether Claude may auto-load the skill, and `false` is already the default; it has nothing to do with sharing.
Importing loads the skill text into every session as CLAUDE.md content; it doesn't create a skill, and the file isn't on teammates' machines anyway.

questions.stem: The team wants its testing conventions (factory helpers, no network in unit tests) to load only when Claude Code works on test files such as `src/cart/cart.test.ts`. They create `.claude/rules/testing.md`. Which frontmatter achieves this?
options: `paths: ["**/*.test.ts"]`
`globs: "**/*.test.ts"`
`applyTo: "**/*.test.ts"`
`when: "editing test files"`
explanations: Correct. `paths` is the only rule frontmatter field Claude Code reads; it accepts glob patterns, and the rule loads when Claude works with a matching file.
`globs` isn't a field Claude Code reads from rules; it is ignored and the rule loads in every session.
`applyTo` is another tool's convention; Claude Code ignores it.
Rules aren't triggered by natural-language conditions. Description-based loading is how skills work, not rules.

questions.stem: A developer ported the team's frontend conventions from another AI tool into `.claude/rules/react.md`, shown below. `/context all` shows the rule loaded in every session, including backend-only sessions that never touch a `.tsx` file. What is the cause?

code.src:
---
globs: "src/components/**/*.tsx"
description: React component conventions
---
# React rules
- Function components only
- Co-locate styles in *.module.css

options: Rules in `.claude/rules/` always load at launch; for conditional loading the team needs a CLAUDE.md file inside `src/components/` instead.
The `description` field makes Claude treat the rule as globally relevant to every session.
The glob must be written relative to the `.claude/rules/` directory, so it matched every file.
Claude Code reads only `paths` from rule frontmatter. The unknown fields are ignored, so the rule has no path scope and loads at launch.
explanations: Rules can be conditional; that is what `paths` frontmatter does.
`description` is also ignored for rules; it neither scopes nor broadens them.
Project rule patterns are relative to the directory containing the `.claude` folder, and this pattern was never read anyway.
Correct. Any field other than `paths` is ignored without an error, and rules without `paths` load at launch with the same priority as `.claude/CLAUDE.md`. Rename `globs` to `paths`.
