questions.stem: The team's test conventions apply to `*.spec.ts` files that sit next to the source in about 30 feature directories. Someone proposes adding the same `CLAUDE.md` to each of those 30 directories. What is the BEST alternative?
options: Keep the 30 files but have each `@import` a single shared `docs/testing.md`, so the text lives in one place.
One root `CLAUDE.md` section titled "Testing", so the rules load once instead of 30 times.
One `.claude/rules/testing.md` with `paths: ["**/*.spec.ts"]`.
A `testing` skill with `disable-model-invocation: true` that developers run before writing tests.
explanations: This de-duplicates the text but keeps 30 files to maintain, and each file still loads whenever Claude touches any file in its directory, not only test files.
This loads the test conventions into every session, including sessions that never touch tests.
Correct. A single path-scoped rule matches test files anywhere in the tree and loads only when Claude touches one, with no duplicated files.
This depends on developers remembering to run it, and Claude can never apply it on its own.

questions.stem: A developer is checking when the rule `.claude/rules/sql.md` (frontmatter `paths: ["db/**/*.sql"]`) enters Claude Code's context during a session. Which TWO events cause it to load? (Select TWO.)
options: Claude uses the Read, Write or Edit tool on `db/queries/orders.sql`.
The session starts in a repository that contains at least one matching `.sql` file.
Claude runs `cat db/queries/orders.sql` through Bash to view that single file.
The developer mentions "the orders SQL" in a prompt without Claude opening any file.
The developer opens `/memory` and selects the rule.
explanations: Correct. A path-scoped rule loads when Claude uses Read, Write or Edit on a matching file.
Path-scoped rules don't load at launch just because matching files exist; only rules without `paths` do.
Correct. A Bash command that counts as a read of a single file, such as `cat` or `head`, also triggers the rule.
Mentions don't trigger rules; loading follows file access, not prompt wording.
`/memory` opens the file in an editor; it doesn't inject the rule into the conversation.

questions.stem: In the platform monorepo, the web team added `packages/web/.claude/rules/components.md` with the frontmatter below. Engineers start Claude Code at the monorepo root. When Claude edits `packages/web/src/Button.tsx`, the rule never loads. What is the MOST likely reason?

code.src:
---
paths:
  - "packages/web/src/**/*.tsx"
---
# Component rules ...

options: Patterns are relative to `packages/web/` (where this rule's `.claude` folder is), so use `src/**/*.tsx`.
Rules are only read from the `.claude/rules/` directory at the root where Claude Code was started, never from nested packages.
Path-scoped rules don't work with `.tsx` files unless braces like `*.{ts,tsx}` are used.
Nested rules load only after the engineer runs `/cd packages/web` and restarts the session.
explanations: Correct. For project rules, each pattern is relative to the directory that contains the rule's `.claude` folder. The pattern looks for `packages/web/packages/web/src/...`, which doesn't exist.
Rules in a subdirectory's `.claude/rules/` are supported and load on demand.
`**/*.tsx` patterns match `.tsx` files directly; brace expansion is optional.
No restart or directory change is needed for nested rules; the problem is the pattern.

questions.stem: An engineer on the developer-platform team keeps `~/.claude/rules/style.md` saying "indent with tabs". A service repository commits `.claude/rules/style.md` saying "indent with 2 spaces". Neither file has `paths`. What happens in a session in that repository?
options: Both load, user rules first; neither overrides the other, so Claude may follow either.
The user rule wins because it is personal and loads last.
Claude Code reports a conflict at startup and loads neither rule.
The project rule replaces the user rule because project scope has higher precedence.
explanations: Correct. User-level rules load before project rules, and neither set overrides the other. With conflicting rules Claude may follow either, so they should be kept consistent.
User-level rules load before project rules, not last, and loading order still doesn't make one override the other.
There is no conflict detection that blocks loading.
Rules don't override each other by scope; both are concatenated into context.

questions.stem: The CI review job runs `git diff origin/main...HEAD | claude -p "Review this diff for problems"` with built-in tools turned off (`--tools ""`), since it only needs the piped diff. The repository has `.claude/rules/sql.md` scoped with `paths: ["**/*.sql"]` containing the team's SQL review checklist. Reviews of PRs that change `.sql` files never apply the checklist. What is the BEST fix?
options: Rename the rule to `.claude/rules/sql.local.md` so CI treats it as unconditional.
Add `--append-system-prompt "Apply the rules in .claude/rules"` so Claude knows it should consult the rules directory during review.
Change the pattern to `**/*` so the rule matches whatever the diff contains.
Move the checklist into the review prompt or a skill the job invokes; a piped diff never triggers a path-scoped rule.
explanations: There is no `.local.md` convention for rules; the file would still be a path-scoped rule that never triggers.
With no file tools the job can't open the rules directory, and the sentence alone doesn't load a path-scoped rule.
Path rules still need a file access to trigger, and `**/*` would make the checklist load for any file in interactive sessions too.

Correct. Path-scoped rules load when Claude reads or edits a matching file. The job only sees a diff on stdin, so nothing ever matches. Put the review criteria where this job always sees them, or let it read the changed files.

questions.stem: To stop untrusted repository hooks from running in CI, an engineer changed the pipeline to `claude -p ... --setting-sources user`. Afterwards, automated fixes stop following the conventions in `.claude/rules/` (both the unconditional and the path-scoped rules), even when Claude edits matching files. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: Path-scoped rules don't load in `-p` mode, and unconditional rules need an interactive session to be approved.
Rules are stored in the user scope, so restricting to `user` should have loaded them; the runner's home directory is misconfigured.
`--setting-sources user` switches the run into bare mode, which skips every instruction file.
Excluding `project` from `--setting-sources` also skips the project's `.claude/rules/` files.
explanations: Rules load in print mode; unconditional rules load at launch and path-scoped rules on matching file access.
Project rules live in the repository's `.claude/rules/`, which is project scope, not user scope.
`--setting-sources` selects which settings sources load; it doesn't turn on bare mode, and the symptom is limited to project rules.

Correct. The docs state project rules are skipped if you exclude `project` from `--setting-sources`. Keep `project` and control hooks another way, for example `--bare` with the needed context passed explicitly.

questions.stem: A CI job sometimes generates database migrations, and developers do the same locally. The team wants its migration conventions (reversible, no data backfills in schema migrations) to apply in both places, but only when Claude works on files under `db/migrations/`. Where should the conventions go?
options: In the CI job's `--append-system-prompt`, and in each developer's `CLAUDE.local.md`.
In the root `CLAUDE.md`, so every session and every CI run has them.
In a committed `.claude/rules/migrations.md` with `paths: ["db/migrations/**"]`.
In each developer's `~/.claude/rules/migrations.md`.
explanations: This keeps two copies in different places, and local files aren't shared or committed.
This loads the conventions into every session, not only migration work.
Correct. A committed path-scoped rule reaches both the runner and teammates, and loads only when Claude works on matching files.
User-level rules don't reach CI or teammates.

questions.stem: Company-wide coding rules live in a separate `shared-standards` repository. The CI job checks it out next to the service and runs `CLAUDE_CODE_ADDITIONAL_DIRECTORIES_CLAUDE_MD=1 claude -p ... --add-dir ../shared-standards`. The shared repo's unconditional rules apply, but its path-scoped rules (for example `paths: ["**/*.proto"]`) never do, even when Claude edits `.proto` files. What is the BEST fix?
options: Copy the shared rule files into the service repository's `.claude/rules/` (for example in a CI step) before running Claude.
Rewrite the shared rules without `paths` frontmatter so that they load unconditionally from the added directory on every run.
Symlink `../shared-standards/.claude/rules` into the service repo's `.claude/rules/`.
Pass `--add-dir` twice, once for the repo root and once for `.claude/rules/`, so path matching uses the right base.
explanations: Correct. With the environment variable set, an added directory's rules load except those with `paths`. Rules in the project's own `.claude/rules/` keep their path scoping.
This makes them load, but every protobuf, SQL and frontend rule would then sit in context for every run, which defeats path scoping.
A symlink pointing outside the working directory is treated like an external import: it needs a one-time approval, and even then only rules without `paths` load.
`--add-dir` grants file access to directories; adding more doesn't change which rules from them load.

questions.stem: Before relying on `.claude/rules/` in `claude -p` runs, the CI team writes down how rules behave (no `--bare`, default setting sources). Which THREE statements are correct? (Select THREE.)
options: A rule without `paths` frontmatter loads at launch with the same priority as `.claude/CLAUDE.md`.
A rule with `paths` loads when Claude reads, writes or edits a file that matches one of its patterns.
Claude Code reads only the `paths` field from rule frontmatter; other fields are ignored.
Only files directly in `.claude/rules/` are loaded; subdirectories such as `.claude/rules/backend/` are ignored.
In print mode all path-scoped rules load at launch, because there is no interactive session to trigger them.
A path-scoped rule overrides conflicting text in CLAUDE.md for the files it matches.
explanations: Correct. Unconditional rules load at launch like `.claude/CLAUDE.md`.
Correct. Path-scoped rules load on matching file access through Read, Write or Edit.
Correct. `paths` is the only field read; anything else is ignored without an error.
`.md` files are discovered recursively, so subfolders like `frontend/` and `backend/` are supported.
Print mode doesn't change the trigger; path-scoped rules still load on matching file access.
Instructions are concatenated context, not an override hierarchy; conflicting instructions make Claude pick one arbitrarily.

questions.stem: A developer on the Claude Code team has a failing unit test whose stack trace points at an off-by-one error in `paginate()` in `src/lib/paging.ts`. The fix is likely a single line and the test already reproduces the bug. How should they run Claude Code?
options: Ask Claude directly to fix `paginate()` and rerun the failing test until it passes.
Enter plan mode, have Claude survey the codebase, and approve a written plan before any edit.
Delegate the investigation to an Explore subagent first, then decide on an approach.
Ask Claude to interview them about pagination requirements and write a spec first.
explanations: Correct. A small, well-located fix with a reproducing test is a direct-execution task; the test is the feedback loop.
Plan mode adds a review round with no benefit when the location and the fix are already clear.
There is nothing to discover; the stack trace already pinpoints the code.
Requirements aren't in question; the expected behaviour is captured by the failing test.

questions.stem: The team wants Claude Code to move the app from server-side sessions to short-lived JWTs. The change touches middleware, about 40 route handlers, the mobile client and tests, and the team hasn't decided how refresh tokens should work. Nothing should be edited until the approach is agreed. What is the BEST way to start?
options: Start in `acceptEdits` mode and let Claude work through the handlers, relying on git to revert anything wrong.
Start in plan mode, review and correct the proposed approach (including refresh tokens), then approve it.
Ask Claude in default mode to "write a plan first and wait for my OK", then reply "go".
Have Claude convert one handler at a time directly, settling the refresh-token design as it goes.
explanations: Fast, but it commits to an undecided design across dozens of files before anyone has reviewed the approach.
Correct. Large, ambiguous, multi-file changes are what plan mode is for: Claude explores and proposes, and edits stay blocked until the plan is approved.

Default mode does prompt before each edit, but 'wait for my OK' is only a request: the developer ends up approving or rejecting edits one by one instead of reviewing one agreed approach. Plan mode blocks edits until a plan is approved.
Settling the core design piecemeal is how inconsistent implementations and rework happen in cross-cutting changes.

questions.stem: A tech lead is explaining plan mode to the team before a large refactor. Which TWO statements are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: Claude can read files and run shell commands to explore, but it doesn't edit source files until the plan is approved.
Plan mode commits a `PLAN.md` file to the repository so the plan is versioned.
Approving the plan exits plan mode and switches to the permission mode of the option chosen, and Claude starts editing.
Plan mode automatically switches the session to a smaller model to make exploration cheaper.
Once a plan is approved the session can't return to plan mode; a new session is required.
explanations: Correct. Plan mode lets Claude research and propose; source edits stay blocked until approval.
Plan mode presents the plan for approval; it doesn't commit files.
Correct. Each approve option names the mode the session switches to, for example auto or manually approved edits.
Plan mode is a permission mode, not a model setting.
You can cycle back with `Shift+Tab` or prefix the next prompt with `/plan`.

questions.stem: In plan mode, Claude proposes a plan for a caching layer. Step 3 uses a deprecated in-house cache client instead of the new `cachekit` library; everything else looks right. What should the developer do?
options: Approve the plan and correct the client choice once Claude reaches step 3.
Choose "No, keep planning" and say to use `cachekit`, or edit the plan with `Ctrl+G` before approving.
Approve the plan, then add a CLAUDE.md line about `cachekit` for future sessions.
Reject the plan, run `/clear`, and re-describe the whole task from scratch.
explanations: By step 3, the earlier steps may already be built around the old client; fixing the plan is cheaper than fixing code.
Correct. Plan review is the cheap moment to correct course: keep planning with feedback, or open the plan in your editor with `Ctrl+G` and fix it directly.
A CLAUDE.md note may help later sessions, but this plan would still be implemented with the deprecated client.
Throwing away a mostly good plan and its exploration is wasteful; a targeted correction is enough.

questions.stem: A developer spent a long Claude Code session exploring a payments module and refining a migration plan with Claude. The session has compacted three times, and Claude has started contradicting decisions agreed early on. The plan is now final, and implementation will take many more hours. What is the BEST next step?
options: Have Claude write the final plan and key decisions to a file, then start implementation in a fresh session from that file.
Continue in the same session, since all the exploration context it has gathered is valuable for implementation and would be lost.
Run `/compact` once more with no instructions, then start implementing in this session.
Switch to a model with a larger context window and continue, so there are no more compactions.
explanations: Correct. A written plan is a durable definition of done. A fresh session starts with a clean context instead of a thrice-summarized history that has already lost decisions.
Continuing is normally fine, but here the context has already degraded: decisions are being lost across compactions.
Another unfocused compaction loses more detail; the agreed decisions need to be written down.
A bigger window delays compaction but leaves the noisy, partly summarized history in place.

questions.stem: A team lead is triaging this week's Claude Code tasks. Which TWO most clearly warrant starting in plan mode? (Select TWO.)
options: Renaming a local variable inside one function.
Adding a caching layer to the order service when nobody knows yet where invalidation must happen.
Fixing a typo in a user-facing error message.
Upgrading the ORM by a major version, which changes query APIs used across many modules.
Bumping a dev-only dependency's patch version.
explanations: Small and fully specified; direct execution is faster.
Correct. An unclear design with cross-cutting effects benefits from exploring and agreeing on an approach before edits.
A trivial, well-located change; planning adds nothing.
Correct. A multi-module change with migration risk is where reviewing a plan first pays off.
Routine and low-risk; run it directly and let tests confirm.

questions.stem: An engineer new to a 4,000-file legacy service asks Claude Code to explain how invoice numbers are generated before changing anything. In a previous attempt, Claude read dozens of files into the conversation, and its later answers on the actual change got noticeably worse. What should the engineer do this time?
options: Reference the whole `src/` directory with `@src` so Claude has everything up front.
Ask Claude to use a subagent (such as the built-in Explore agent) to investigate and report back a summary.
Run `/compact` after every few file reads to keep the context small.
Raise the effort level so Claude reads each file more carefully and keeps more of the important details in mind for the change.
explanations: A directory reference shows a file listing, not contents, and loading the service wholesale would make the context problem worse.
Correct. A subagent reads files in its own context window and returns only the findings, so the main conversation stays focused for the change.
Frequent compaction is costly and lossy; it treats the symptom rather than keeping exploration out of the main context.
Effort affects how carefully Claude reasons, not how much exploration output piles up in the main context.

questions.stem: The platform's monorepo `CLAUDE.md` says "always report file paths relative to the repo root and skip anything under `vendor/`." Engineers notice that when Claude delegates codebase searches to the built-in Explore subagent, its findings include `vendor/` files and absolute paths, while the main conversation follows the rule. What is the MOST likely explanation and fix?
options: Explore starts without CLAUDE.md; state those constraints in the delegation prompt or use a custom subagent.
Explore runs a smaller model that can't follow instructions; set `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL` to a larger model.
Explore inherits only user-scope CLAUDE.md; move the rule to `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` for each engineer.
Subagents can't read the repository root, so they fall back to absolute paths; add the root with `--add-dir`.
explanations: Correct. Explore and Plan start without CLAUDE.md files and the git status snapshot to keep research fast. Other built-in and custom subagents load the CLAUDE.md hierarchy.
Explore uses the main conversation's model by default, and the symptom is missing instructions, not capability.
Explore doesn't load user-scope CLAUDE.md either, and moving a team rule to personal files would break it for CI and teammates.
Subagents work in the same working directory; path style comes from instructions, not access.

questions.stem: The team that maintains the multi-agent research system wants Claude Code to change how the coordinator decomposes questions: subagent prompts, the routing table and the synthesizer's citation merging are all affected, and nobody is sure which tests cover the routing logic. Which approach BEST fits?
options: Start in plan mode so Claude maps the affected modules and tests, then review and approve the plan before edits.
Use `acceptEdits` so Claude can move quickly, and review the full diff at the end.
Give Claude file-by-file instructions directly, starting with the coordinator.
Ask Claude to rewrite the coordinator from scratch in a new module, so the existing code and its untested routing paths stay untouched.
explanations: Correct. The change is cross-module with unclear test coverage. Exploring and agreeing on a plan first avoids building on a wrong assumption.
A large end-of-run diff is the most expensive place to discover that the approach was wrong.
Directing edits file by file assumes the engineer already knows the blast radius, which they don't.
A rewrite ignores the existing behaviour and tests and greatly expands the risk.

questions.stem: When an issue is labelled `needs-design`, the CI pipeline should have Claude Code propose an implementation plan and post it as an issue comment. The job must not modify the checked-out code. Which invocation BEST meets this?
options: `claude -p "Propose a plan; do not edit any files" --permission-mode acceptEdits`
`claude -p "Propose a plan for issue #412" --max-turns 1`
`claude -p "Propose a plan for issue #412" --permission-mode plan --output-format json`
`claude -p "Propose a plan" --permission-mode bypassPermissions`, followed by `git checkout .`
explanations: `acceptEdits` auto-approves file edits; the prompt asks Claude not to edit but nothing blocks it.
One turn may not be enough to explore the code, and a turn limit doesn't block edits.
Correct. Plan mode keeps its blocks in non-interactive runs, so Claude can read and propose but not edit; JSON output gives the script the plan text in `result`.
This lets anything run, including commands with side effects that `git checkout` can't undo.

questions.stem: The team wants a CI workflow where Claude Code designs and then implements medium-sized features from issues. Past fully automatic runs sometimes built the wrong thing across many files before anyone looked. What is the BEST pipeline design?
options: One `claude -p` job in `acceptEdits` mode that is prompted to write a plan first and then implement it, with the PR as the review point.
One job in plan mode with a high `--max-turns`, so Claude can plan and then implement within the same run.
Two parallel jobs, one planning and one implementing, compared at the end.
A plan-mode job posts the plan; after a human approves it, a separate job with scoped edit permissions implements it and opens a PR.
explanations: Planning inside an edit-capable run gives no checkpoint: the wrong design is fully built before anyone reviews it.
Plan mode blocks edits in `-p` runs, so this job could never implement; more turns don't change that.
The implementer can't benefit from a plan it never sees; this doubles cost without a checkpoint.
Correct. It separates proposing from applying, puts the cheap human check on the plan before code exists, and keeps the PR review for the result.

questions.stem: A nightly CI job asks Claude Code to fix the auto-fixable lint errors that accumulated during the day; each fix is small and mechanical, and the lint command verifies the result. An engineer suggests running the job in plan mode "to be safe". What is the BEST response?
options: Run it directly with edits and only the lint command allowed; in a `-p` run, plan mode would block every fix.
Agree, but add `--max-turns 50` so the plan has room to be executed.
Use plan mode, then run a second unattended job in `bypassPermissions` mode that applies whatever plan the first job produced.
Agree; plan mode in print mode shows the plan and then applies it once the turn ends.
explanations: Correct. Small, well-scoped mechanical fixes with a verifying command are direct-execution work. Scope the permissions instead of planning.
Turn limits don't lift plan mode's edit block.
This adds a pointless stage and the riskiest permission mode for a mechanical task.
Plan mode doesn't auto-apply in print mode; its blocks stay in place, so nothing would be fixed.

questions.stem: A developer asked Claude Code to "make the duration formatting in the dashboard more readable." Two attempts produced formats the product team rejected ("1.02 hours", "61 min 1 s"). What is the MOST effective next prompt?
options: Repeat the request with "IMPORTANT: make it much more human-readable this time."
Ask Claude to propose ten alternative formats and pick the best one itself.
Give exact input→output pairs, e.g. `59 → "59s"`, `3600 → "1h"`, `3661 → "1h 1m 1s"`, `0 → "0s"`, and ask for them as test cases.
Switch to a larger model, since formatting taste is a capability problem.
explanations: Emphasis doesn't tell Claude what 'readable' means; the ambiguity remains.
Claude still lacks the product team's criterion, so its choice is another guess.
Correct. Concrete examples remove the ambiguity, cover edge cases like zero, and turned into tests they give Claude a check it can run.
The problem is an unspecified target, not model capability.

questions.stem: A product engineer wants Claude Code to add rate limiting to the public API but hasn't settled limits per tier, burst behaviour, headers, or how internal callers are exempted. Previous vague requests produced an implementation that had to be redone. What is the BEST way to start?
options: Ask Claude to implement a reasonable default now and refine it over several follow-up prompts.
Write a long prompt that guesses every decision up front so Claude never needs to ask.
Ask Claude to interview them until it could write the spec, write it to `SPEC.md`, then build from it in a fresh session.
Start in plan mode and approve whatever plan Claude proposes for the unspecified parts, since plan mode exists to settle open questions.
explanations: This repeats the pattern that already caused rework: Claude fills undecided requirements with guesses.
Guessed decisions written confidently are still guesses; the engineer hasn't actually decided them.
Correct. An interview surfaces the open decisions. The spec becomes a written definition of done, and a fresh session builds from it with a clean context.
Plan mode reviews how to implement; it doesn't resolve product decisions nobody has made. Approving guesses just moves them into the plan.

questions.stem: QA reports three checkout bugs: tax is rounded per line instead of per order, a percentage discount and a coupon stack in the wrong order, and currency conversion happens before discounts instead of after. All three affect the same `computeTotal()` path. How should the developer give these to Claude Code?
options: One bug per prompt, verifying each fix before describing the next, so Claude focuses on one thing at a time.
All three in one message, with the intended order of operations and a worked example total.
Only the tax bug first, since the other two may disappear once rounding is fixed.
Three parallel sessions in separate worktrees, one per bug, then merge the three branches once each one's tests pass.
explanations: Sequential prompts suit independent issues. Here each fix changes the same calculation, so a fix designed in isolation can break or mask the next.
Correct. Interacting issues should be given together so Claude can design one consistent order of operations, and a worked example gives it a concrete target.
The bugs are about ordering in a shared path; fixing one won't make the others disappear, and a partial view invites a partial design.
Parallel branches would produce three conflicting edits to the same function.

questions.stem: The team wants Claude Code to build a new pricing rules engine test-first. In earlier attempts, when an implementation failed, Claude sometimes "fixed" it by loosening assertions. Which TWO practices BEST keep Claude iterating on the implementation rather than the tests? (Select TWO.)
options: Write the tests first, confirm they fail, commit them, and tell Claude to make them pass without modifying them.
Ask Claude to report a confidence score with each change and reject low-confidence ones.
Add a deny rule such as `Edit(/tests/pricing/**)` to the project settings while the implementation is being written.
Raise the effort level so Claude is less tempted to take shortcuts.
Have Claude write tests and implementation together in one step so they stay consistent.
explanations: Correct. Committed, failing tests become a fixed target, and any change to them shows up in the diff.
Self-reported confidence isn't a control and doesn't protect the tests.
Correct. A permission deny rule makes edits to the test files impossible, a deterministic version of 'don't touch the tests'.
Effort affects reasoning depth; it doesn't stop test edits.
Writing both together lets the tests be shaped to fit the implementation, which is the failure mode being fixed.

questions.stem: In long local Claude Code sessions, Claude sometimes ends its turn with "all done" while `pnpm typecheck` still fails. The project CLAUDE.md already says "Run `pnpm typecheck` and fix all errors before finishing." The team wants Claude Code itself to stop Claude from finishing while the typecheck fails. What should they add?
options: A PostToolUse hook that runs the typecheck after every edit and prints the result.
A `Stop` hook that runs the typecheck and exits with code 2 when it fails, sending Claude back to work.
A `/goal` condition that a separate model evaluates against the conversation after every turn until it judges the goal met.
A second, more emphatic CLAUDE.md line at the top of the file.
explanations: Feedback after edits helps, but it doesn't stop Claude from ending the turn while errors remain.
Correct. A Stop hook runs whenever Claude tries to end its turn; exit code 2 sends Claude back to work. It is enforced by the harness, up to the hook's block limit.
Useful for long runs, but it is a model's judgement of the conversation, not the harness running the check.
CLAUDE.md is guidance; the existing instruction already shows that guidance isn't enough here.

questions.stem: A nightly `claude -p` job is asked to "fix the failing tests" and opens a PR when it finishes. Reviewers found that in two PRs Claude had changed expected values in the tests instead of fixing the bug in the source. Which change BEST prevents this from reaching review?
options: Deny edits to test paths for this job, pass the failing test output in the prompt, and have the pipeline rerun the suite itself before opening the PR.
Add "never modify tests" to the prompt and to CLAUDE.md, and keep the rest of the job unchanged.
Increase `--max-turns` so Claude has time to find the real bug instead of taking a shortcut.
Have the same session review its diff with `--continue` before the PR is opened.
explanations: Correct. A deny rule makes test edits impossible, the specific failure output points Claude at the real problem, and an independent rerun in the pipeline doesn't depend on Claude's own claim of success.
A prompt instruction helps but is probabilistic; nothing stops the edit or catches it before review.
More turns don't change which path Claude takes, and they cost more.
The generating session is primed by its own reasoning and tends to approve its own shortcut.

questions.stem: A CI job runs `claude -p` on each merged PR to draft a changelog entry. Output varies from run to run: sometimes past tense, sometimes imperative, sometimes with the PR number, sometimes not. What is the MOST effective first change?
options: Include two or three real PR → changelog-entry examples in the prompt that show the exact format.
Switch to the largest available model.
Run the job three times and keep the most common phrasing.
Add "be consistent" to the prompt.
explanations: Correct. Concrete input/output examples pin down tense, structure and whether to include the PR number.
A bigger model still has to guess the house style.
Voting over unspecified outputs triples cost and still doesn't define the format.
'Consistent' doesn't say which format to be consistent with.

questions.stem: A CI auto-fix step runs `claude -p "Fix the build"` with edit permissions only, and the pipeline then runs the tests. If they fail, a wrapper script reruns the same command, up to five times. Most retries fail the same way. What is the BEST redesign?
options: Allow the test command (e.g. `Bash(pnpm test *)`) so Claude can run it and iterate to green within one run, include the failure output in the prompt, and cap the run with `--max-turns`.
Run five copies in parallel and keep the first one whose tests pass.
Increase the retry count to ten, since some runs do eventually pass.
Switch the retries to a larger model while keeping the same prompt.
explanations: Correct. Claude needs a check it can run: with the test command allowed and the specific failure in hand, it can fix, rerun and adjust inside one run, while the turn cap bounds cost.
Parallel blind attempts multiply cost and still give Claude no feedback to learn from.
Each retry starts blind with the same prompt, so it repeats the same mistake; more retries only add cost.
The missing ingredient is feedback, not model size.

questions.stem: A scheduled CI job asks Claude Code to "clean up the feature flags". Results vary: one run deleted flags still referenced by mobile clients, another changed nothing and asked which flags were meant. No one watches the job. What should the prompt include?
options: An instruction to ask the on-call engineer whenever anything is ambiguous.
Explicit criteria: which flags qualify (e.g. fully rolled out for 30+ days), what to leave untouched, and what to report when unsure.
A request to be careful and conservative.
Nothing more; turning on `bypassPermissions` so Claude is never blocked will make it decisive and avoid runs that change nothing at all.
explanations: Nobody is watching the job, so questions go unanswered.
Correct. Unattended runs can't ask clarifying questions, so the prompt must define what done looks like, what is out of bounds, and what to do with ambiguous cases.
Vague caution doesn't define which flags qualify.
Removing permission checks makes the destructive outcome more likely and doesn't resolve the ambiguity.

questions.stem: Before letting an overnight `claude -p` job refactor a logging module unattended, the team lists what must be in place so the run converges and stays safe. Which THREE belong on the list? (Select THREE.)
options: A test or lint command Claude is allowed to run, with the instruction to make it pass.
A cap such as `--max-turns` or `--max-budget-usd`.
The result delivered as a PR that a person approves, not a direct push to main.
`--permission-mode bypassPermissions` so the job never stalls overnight.
An instruction to interview the developer before starting.
A larger context window so the job never needs to compact.
explanations: Correct. A pass/fail check tells Claude when it is actually done.
Correct. Something must stop a run that isn't converging.
Correct. A human sign-off covers what you can't take back.
Bypass removes the limits on what the run can touch; scoped `--allowedTools` with `dontAsk` keeps it from stalling without that risk.
Nobody is available to answer overnight.
Context size isn't the convergence problem; done criteria, checks and caps are.

questions.stem: The research system's synthesis agent formats citations with a helper that the team is reworking in Claude Code. After several rounds, Claude's version still mishandles sources with no publication date and sources with more than three authors, and each correction breaks a case that used to work. What should the developer do?
options: Describe the desired style again in more detail, emphasizing the two failing cases.
Keep correcting in the same session, since by now Claude holds the most context about the problem and the earlier failed attempts.
Ask Claude to review its own output after each change and say whether it looks right.
Turn concrete source → expected-citation pairs, including the no-date and four-author cases, into tests and iterate to green.
explanations: More description is how the loop started; regressions show Claude can't check all cases at once.
Repeated corrections pile failed attempts into the context; a runnable check is what's missing.
Self-review without a fixed reference can't detect regressions reliably.
Correct. Example pairs pin down the expected output for the edge cases, and as tests they catch regressions on every iteration.

questions.stem: In the CI pipeline, a `claude -p` job implements a fix and captures its `session_id`. A second step then asks for a security review of the resulting diff. Reviews almost never find problems, yet humans later catch issues in about one PR in five. How should the review step be run?

code.src:
sid=$(claude -p "$TASK" --output-format json | jq -r .session_id)
# review step: which form?

options: `claude -p "Review your changes for security issues" --resume "$sid"`
`claude -p "Review your changes for security issues" --resume "$sid" --fork-session`
A new, non-resumed `claude -p` session given only the diff and explicit review criteria.
Resume the same session with a higher effort level so that it scrutinizes its own work harder before the PR is posted.
explanations: The resumed session has its own reasoning in context and tends to confirm it.
`--fork-session` only gives the resumed conversation a new ID; it still carries the generator's full context, so the review isn't independent.
Correct. A separate session that only sees the diff and the criteria isn't anchored to how the code was written, which is what an independent review needs.
More effort doesn't remove the bias of reviewing your own reasoning.

questions.stem: The PR review job runs `claude -p` on every push. On long-lived PRs it re-reviews the whole change each time, re-posts comments developers have already addressed, and costs keep growing. Which TWO changes BEST address this? (Select TWO.)
options: Give the job only the changes since the last reviewed commit (e.g. `git diff $LAST_REVIEWED_SHA..HEAD`) when that commit is still in the branch.
Add `--max-turns 1` so each review is cheap.
Pass the previous review's findings into the prompt and ask it to report only new or still-unresolved issues.
Switch the reviewer to the largest model so it remembers what it said before.
Remove the repository's CLAUDE.md from the runner to reduce input tokens.
explanations: Correct. Reviewing only the new commits avoids paying for, and commenting on, unchanged code again.
A one-turn cap cripples the review without fixing duplicate comments.
Correct. Each `-p` run starts fresh; giving it the earlier findings lets it skip what was already raised and fixed.
Model size doesn't give a fresh run memory of earlier runs.
CLAUDE.md carries the review criteria; removing it makes reviews worse, not deduplicated.

questions.stem: The team's CI pipeline runs `claude -p` on every pull request with the prompt "Review this PR thoroughly and flag any issues." Each PR now gets 20–30 comments, most of them about naming, formatting and code the PR did not touch. Developers have started ignoring the bot entirely, including its rare real bug reports. Which change BEST fixes the root cause?
options: Append "Only flag important issues and avoid nitpicks" to the existing prompt
Ask Claude to attach a confidence score between 0 and 1 to each finding, and have the CI job post only the findings scored at 0.8 or higher while discarding the rest
Rewrite the prompt to define what counts as a finding (correctness, security, data loss in changed lines), what to skip (style, naming, unchanged code) and each severity
Cap the number of posted comments at five per PR, keeping the first five the model reports
explanations: "Important" and "nitpick" are still undefined, so the threshold stays with the model and the noise continues.
Self-reported confidence is not calibrated against what the team considers a finding; it filters on the wrong signal.
Correct. The cause is an undefined reporting threshold. Explicit include/exclude criteria and severity definitions are the main lever for cutting false positives in review prompts.
A cap hides the symptom and may drop the real bug if it is reported sixth.

questions.stem: In the CI review job, findings labelled `critical` block the merge. The prompt asks Claude to label each finding `critical`, `major` or `minor`, without further detail. About 60% of findings come back `critical`, including a missing docstring and an unused import, so merges stall. The team wants the label itself to be trustworthy. What should the architect change?
options: Define each severity with a concrete condition and an example (critical = exploitable or data-corrupting on a reachable path) and say critical blocks merges
Change the merge gate to block only when three or more critical findings are reported on the same PR
Add "Use the critical label sparingly and only when truly necessary" to the severity instructions
Run the reviewer twice in parallel on the same diff and keep a critical label only when both independent runs assign it to the same finding
explanations: Correct. Undefined labels collapse toward the top. Concrete definitions with an example each, plus the reason (critical blocks merges), give the model a threshold it can apply consistently.
This changes the gate rather than the labels; one real critical bug would no longer block the merge.
"Sparingly" and "truly necessary" are vague qualifiers that leave the threshold undefined.
Two runs with the same undefined scale will often agree on the same inflated labels; it doubles cost without defining what critical means.

questions.stem: A security-review step in the CI pipeline (`claude -p` with a review prompt) reports hard-coded credentials in `tests/fixtures/`, where the values are deliberately fake, and reports old vulnerabilities in files the pull request did not modify. Security engineers say both kinds of finding are noise for this gate. Which TWO prompt changes BEST reduce these false positives? (Select TWO.)
options: Add "Be conservative and avoid false positives" at the top of the review prompt
State that values under `tests/fixtures/` are synthetic test data and are not to be reported as secrets, giving that reason
Add "CRITICAL: You MUST NEVER report a false positive" to the system prompt
Raise the reasoning effort to the maximum so the reviewer thinks harder about each finding
Limit the scope explicitly: report only issues introduced by lines changed in this diff, and state that pre-existing issues are out of scope for this gate
explanations: A vague qualifier: it does not tell the reviewer which findings to drop.
Correct. An explicit exclusion with its reason lets the model skip fixture data and generalise to similar synthetic values.
Shouted absolutes do not define what a false positive is and can over-trigger on current models.
More effort does not supply the missing criteria; the reviewer would still consider fixtures and unchanged code in scope.
Correct. Defining scope (changed lines only, pre-existing issues excluded) removes the second class of noise at its cause.

questions.stem: The support-resolution agent's system prompt says "Be conservative with refunds." QA finds the agent refuses some clearly eligible refunds (a defective item returned within a week) while approving others that policy excludes (used items past 60 days). The refund tool itself works correctly. Which prompt change BEST improves the consistency of the agent's refund decisions?
options: Replace the line with "Use your judgment as an experienced support agent when deciding refunds"
Replace the line with the actual eligibility criteria (time window, item condition, defect vs change of mind) and the path for out-of-policy cases
Move the agent to a more capable model tier so it reasons about refunds more carefully
Add two few-shot examples of correctly approved refunds to the system prompt so the agent can see what a good, policy-compliant refund decision looks like
explanations: Still leaves the threshold undefined; judgment without criteria is what produced the inconsistency.
Correct. Concrete, checkable conditions replace a vague adjective, and an explicit path for out-of-policy cases removes the remaining guesswork.
A larger model cannot apply a policy it was never given; "conservative" remains ambiguous.
Two approvals only show the positive side and no boundary; the agent may lean toward approving more.

questions.stem: After the team rewrote the support agent's prompt with explicit refund criteria, including "refunds above $200 require a human", decisions became far more consistent. However, in roughly 1 of 500 conversations a persistent customer still talks the agent into calling `issue_refund` for more than $200. Compliance says this must never happen. What should the architect do NEXT?
options: Add "CRITICAL: NEVER issue a refund above $200 under any circumstances" to the system prompt
Enforce the limit in code (a PreToolUse hook or tool-side check that blocks `issue_refund` above $200 and escalates), keeping the criteria in the prompt
Add few-shot examples in which the agent politely declines customers who push for larger refunds
Lower the sampling temperature for the support agent so that it follows the written refund rule more deterministically, even when customers push back repeatedly
explanations: Emphasis makes violations rarer at best; it is still probabilistic and does not meet a "never" requirement.
Correct. Explicit criteria improve judgment, but a hard business limit needs a deterministic control. A hook or tool-side check guarantees the ceiling; the prompt still guides normal decisions.
Examples may reduce the rate further but cannot guarantee the limit is never exceeded.
Lower temperature does not make behaviour deterministic and does not enforce a rule; some recent models also reject sampling parameters.

questions.stem: In the multi-agent research system, the coordinator briefs each search subagent with "Find high-quality sources on the sub-question." Final reports increasingly cite SEO blog posts, undated vendor pages and marketing whitepapers. The search tools themselves return a good mix of results. Which change BEST addresses this?
options: Give each search subagent additional search tools so it can reach more academic databases
Change the brief to "Be rigorous and use only the most reliable sources you can find"
Spell out source criteria in the brief: acceptable types (peer-reviewed, official statistics, primary documents), a recency window, and explicit exclusions
Let the synthesis subagent decide at the end which of the collected sources look trustworthy enough to cite, since it is the only agent that sees every source side by side
explanations: The tools already return good sources; the problem is the selection criterion, not reach.
"Rigorous" and "reliable" are as vague as "high-quality"; the subagent still decides what qualifies.
Correct. Concrete include/exclude criteria at the point of selection, plus a stated reason, turn "high-quality" into something the subagent can apply and you can audit.
Right idea at the wrong layer: synthesis would still face the same undefined standard, after tokens were spent collecting weak sources.

questions.stem: The research system's synthesis subagent is instructed: "Write a balanced, comprehensive report from the findings." Reports vary from 400 to 4,000 words, sometimes drop evidence that contradicts the majority view, and sometimes include claims that appear in no finding. Which THREE changes make the instructions explicit enough to fix this? (Select THREE.)
options: Specify the report structure and a length target per section
Add "Be thorough, objective and balanced in every report you write"
Require every factual claim to cite a finding ID from the input, and state that claims with no supporting finding are left out
Prefix the instructions with "IMPORTANT: ALWAYS present a balanced view"
Move the synthesis step to the most capable model tier available
When findings disagree, require both positions to be presented with their sources and dates instead of choosing one
explanations: Correct. A defined structure and length target removes the length variance that "comprehensive" invites.
Restates the same vague goals; it defines no behaviour that can be checked.
Correct. A concrete grounding rule (cite an ID or omit) addresses unsupported claims and makes outputs checkable.
Emphasis is not a definition; "balanced" remains open to interpretation and capitals can over-trigger.
A stronger model still has to guess what "balanced" and "comprehensive" mean here.
Correct. This turns "balanced" into an explicit rule for handling conflicting evidence.

questions.stem: Besides extracting fields, the invoice pipeline asks Claude to set `needs_review: true` for "invoices that look unusual." About 40% of invoices are now flagged and the review team cannot keep up; most flagged invoices turn out to be fine. Which change BEST reduces the flag rate without losing the cases reviewers care about?
options: Replace the instruction with "Only flag invoices that are truly unusual"
Ask Claude for a 1–10 suspicion score and set `needs_review` only for scores of 8 or higher
Add three examples of unusual invoices that were correctly flagged by the review team last quarter, so that the model can learn from them what the reviewers actually care about
List the conditions that warrant review (remit-to name differs from letterhead, amount in words disagrees with figures, handwritten edits to totals) and flag nothing else
explanations: Another vague qualifier; the model still decides what "unusual" means.
An uncalibrated score inherits the same undefined notion of "unusual"; the cut-off is arbitrary.
Positive-only examples show what to flag but not what to leave alone, and may increase flagging of anything that resembles them.
Correct. Concrete conditions plus an explicit "nothing else" rule define the boundary, which is what cuts false positives.

questions.stem: The contract-extraction pipeline asks Claude to "extract the key obligations" from each supplier contract into an `obligations` array. On the same contract, separate runs return between 4 and 15 items, sometimes including definitions and recitals. What is the BEST fix?
options: Set a fixed `maxItems` of 8 on the `obligations` array in the schema
Ask for "only the most important obligations" so the list stays short
Define an obligation (a named party must do, pay or deliver something, with its trigger or deadline), list what to skip (definitions, recitals) and the per-item fields
Run the extraction three times on every contract and keep only the obligations that appear in at least two of the three runs, discarding all the others as model noise
explanations: A count limit truncates arbitrarily and does not define what qualifies.
"Most important" is still undefined and would drop real obligations on long contracts.
Correct. The variance comes from an undefined term. A definition, an explicit skip list and per-item fields make the task checkable and consistent.
Voting reduces noise at three times the cost but keeps the undefined criterion; consistent misreadings survive.

questions.stem: The team's project CLAUDE.md contains "Write clean, well-tested code that follows our conventions." Claude Code's changes keep arriving without integration tests for new endpoints, and they use three different error-handling styles. Which edit to CLAUDE.md BEST fixes this?
options: Change the line to "IMPORTANT: ALWAYS write clean, well-tested code that follows ALL of our conventions"
Delete the line, since Claude Code already infers the project's conventions by reading the codebase
Replace it with checkable rules, e.g. "Every new endpoint gets an integration test in `tests/api/` using `api_client`; throw only `AppError` from `src/errors.ts`"
Add a link to the team's 40-page engineering handbook in CLAUDE.md so that Claude can go and read all of the team's coding and testing conventions itself whenever it needs them
explanations: Emphasis does not tell Claude what "well-tested" or "our conventions" mean in this repo.
The repo currently shows three styles, so inference has nothing consistent to infer from; the decision has to be stated.
Correct. Concrete rules that name the location, fixture and error type are something Claude can follow and a reviewer can check.
Pointing at a long document loads a lot of context without stating which specific rules apply to these two problems.

questions.stem: The internal developer platform offers a Claude-powered "summarise this incident channel" command. On-call engineers report that summaries mix speculation with confirmed facts, vary from three lines to two pages, and sometimes recount off-topic chat. Which revision to the command's prompt BEST addresses all three complaints?
options: "Summarise the channel concisely and accurately for an on-call engineer."
Add one example summary from last month's best-written incident review
Route the command to a larger, more capable model tier so that the summaries are more careful about separating facts from guesses and about staying on topic
"Two sections: Confirmed (each fact with its message link) and Open hypotheses; then a UTC timeline. Under 200 words. Skip off-topic chat."
explanations: "Concisely" and "accurately" are the vague goals that produced the inconsistency.
A single example helps format but will be copied closely and does not state the confirmed-vs-speculative rule or the length limit.
Model size does not define what counts as confirmed or how long the summary should be.
Correct. It states the structure, the confirmed-vs-hypothesis distinction with evidence, a length limit and an explicit skip rule.

questions.stem: The invoice pipeline assigns each line item a general-ledger category. Over months, the team has grown the category rules to two pages of prose, yet accuracy on borderline items (software subscription vs licence vs implementation services) is still poor and each new rule seems to break another case. What is the BEST next step?
options: Add another paragraph of rules that covers the specific borderline wordings found in last month's errors
Replace the borderline rules with a handful of contrastive examples near each boundary, each with a one-line reason for its category
Move categorisation to the most capable model tier and keep the existing two pages of rules as they are
Split categorisation into a separate call per category, each answering yes or no for every line item on the invoice, and keep the category with a yes
explanations: Rule accretion is what has been failing; another paragraph is likely to interact badly with the existing ones again.
Correct. When a boundary is hard to state but easy to show, a few contrastive examples with the deciding reason usually beat more prose.
A stronger model still has to reconcile two pages of overlapping rules; the ambiguity is in the instructions.
Independent yes/no calls multiply cost and can return several or zero categories for the same item, without clarifying the boundary.

questions.stem: To improve extraction, an engineer pasted three sample invoices and their expected JSON directly above the real invoice text in the user message, with no separators. Occasionally the output for the real invoice contains a vendor name or invoice number that comes from one of the sample invoices. What is the MOST likely cause and fix?
options: The model's context window is too small for four invoices; drop to a single sample invoice
The samples are too similar to real invoices; replace them with obviously synthetic data such as "ACME Corp"
Few-shot examples are unsuitable for extraction tasks like this one; remove them and rely on the JSON schema's field descriptions alone
Examples and input are not delimited; wrap each sample in `<example>` tags inside `<examples>` and the real invoice in its own tag
explanations: Four invoices are far below context limits; the issue is that the model cannot tell which text is the input.
Synthetic values may make leaks easier to spot but do not separate examples from the real input.
Examples are a reliable way to steer extraction format and edge cases; the fix is structure, not removal.
Correct. Anthropic recommends wrapping examples in `<example>`/`<examples>` tags so Claude can distinguish them from instructions and input; tagging the real document completes the separation.

questions.stem: A form-extraction pipeline processes scanned insurance claim forms. Its schema already makes optional fields nullable. The prompt has four few-shot examples, all of fully completed, clearly printed forms. On real forms with blank or illegible boxes, Claude often returns a plausible value instead of null. Which change BEST addresses this?
options: Remove the few-shot examples completely, because examples make the model too confident in its extractions
Add the instruction "Never guess" in capitals at the end of the extraction prompt
Make every field in the schema required so missing values are easier to detect downstream
Add examples where blank and illegible boxes produce null, so the examples cover that edge case and not only the happy path
explanations: The examples are useful for format; the gap is that they omit the edge case.
Shouted instructions are weaker than the four examples that implicitly demonstrate always filling every field.
Required fields force a value and make fabrication worse.
Correct. Examples teach what they show. Happy-path-only examples imply every box has a value; examples of blank and illegible boxes set the expected behaviour for those cases.

questions.stem: The contract pipeline labels each clause `high`, `medium` or `none` for risk. Its prompt includes five few-shot examples, all of them high-risk clauses (unlimited liability, automatic renewal, unilateral price change). In production, many standard clauses with similar wording, such as a mutual 30-day termination notice, are labelled `high`. Which TWO changes BEST improve precision? (Select TWO.)
options: Add contrastive examples of benign clauses that share wording with risky ones, labelled `none`
Add ten more high-risk examples so the model learns the risky patterns in more detail
Append "Only label a clause high if it is truly risky" to the classification instructions
Include in each example a one-line reason naming the feature that decides the label
Set temperature to 0 so the labels become deterministic across production runs
explanations: Correct. Examples only on one side of the boundary teach "looks like a contract clause = high". Near-boundary negatives show what does not qualify.
More one-sided examples strengthen the same bias.
A vague qualifier does not define where the boundary is.
Correct. Showing the deciding feature (e.g. "no opt-out window") teaches the decision rule rather than surface wording.
Determinism (which temperature does not guarantee anyway) would only make the wrong labels consistent.

questions.stem: The support-resolution agent first classifies each new message into an intent that decides which workflow runs. Messages such as "I was charged twice and I want to close my account" are labelled inconsistently: sometimes `billing`, sometimes `cancellation`, and the second need is dropped. The intent definitions in the prompt are already clear for single-intent messages. What is the BEST change?
options: Expand each intent definition with a longer paragraph explaining which of the intents should win whenever a single message mentions several different topics
Add a few examples of multi-intent messages showing the expected output (a primary intent plus secondary intents) with a short rationale
Replace the classifier step entirely with keyword rules that check for words like "charged" and "close"
Ask the customer to describe one issue per message before the agent will classify their message
explanations: More prose may help, but the exact output for multi-intent cases is easier to show than describe and still leaves the format undefined.
Correct. The failing case is a specific ambiguous pattern with a specific expected output shape; a few examples of it, with reasons, settle both.
Keyword rules are brittle and still need a rule for which intent wins.
This pushes the system's ambiguity onto customers and degrades the experience.

questions.stem: The research coordinator decomposes each question into sub-questions for search subagents. For comparative questions ("How do EU and US battery-recycling rules differ?"), it produces overlapping sub-questions, so subagents duplicate work while one jurisdiction's enforcement regime is never researched. The prompt already says "make sub-questions non-overlapping and complete." What is the BEST improvement?
options: Add example decompositions for several question types (comparative, causal, landscape), each with non-overlapping sub-questions covering every dimension
Increase the number of search subagents the coordinator may spawn, so that any gaps in the decomposition are more likely to be covered by one of them
Use a fixed decomposition template of exactly four sub-questions for every research question
Repeat the instruction "non-overlapping and complete" at both the start and the end of the coordinator prompt
explanations: Correct. The instruction is already present; examples show what a good split looks like for each question type, which is the part the model is getting wrong.
More subagents add cost and more duplication without changing how the question is split.
A fixed template ignores that different question types need different splits; it trades one coverage gap for another.
Repeating an instruction the model already has does not show it how to decompose a comparative question.

questions.stem: The research system's synthesis subagent must format citations in the client's house style, which has awkward cases: sources with no author, reports with both a publication and a revision date, and web pages with only an access date. A paragraph describing the style has not produced consistent results. What is the MOST effective prompt change?
options: Rewrite the style paragraph in more formal language that matches the style guide's exact wording
Ask the synthesis subagent to look up the house style on the web before it writes each report
Provide 3–5 example citations in tags, including the no-author, two-date and access-date-only cases
Move citation formatting into a separate subagent that formats citations without the rest of the report
explanations: Rewording the same description does not show the awkward cases.
The style is client-specific and not on the web; it also adds latency and tool calls.
Correct. Exact format with edge cases is easier to show than to describe; a few diverse, tagged examples covering those cases are the standard fix.
A separate subagent still needs to be shown the format; this adds orchestration without fixing the cause.

questions.stem: The CI review job already runs `claude -p --json-schema "$(cat review.json)"`, so every result is valid JSON with `file`, `line`, `severity` and `body` fields. The problem is the `body` text: some comments state the problem and a concrete fix, others are vague ("consider improving this"), and some restate the code. Reviewers want every comment to say what breaks, when, and what to change. What is the BEST fix?
options: Split `body` into many more required schema fields, such as `problem`, `trigger`, `impact`, `fix`, `alternatives` and `references`
Tighten the JSON schema with a `minLength` of 200 characters on the `body` field
Add 3–4 example findings whose `body` shows the problem → trigger → fix pattern, across different issue types
Switch the output format to `stream-json` so that the review comments can be inspected while they are being generated
explanations: Some splitting can help, but many required fields push the model to fill them even when they do not apply, and still do not show what a good value looks like.
Length is not quality and forces padding; string-length constraints are also not a reliable lever for content.
Correct. Structure is already guaranteed; what varies is the content style of a free-text field. Examples are the most reliable way to steer that style.
Streaming changes delivery, not the content of the comments.

questions.stem: The team uses Claude Code to add database migrations. CLAUDE.md describes the migration conventions in a paragraph (naming, reversible `down` step, batching large updates). Claude follows the naming but often omits the batching pattern or writes `down` steps differently from the rest of the repo. What is the BEST way to improve consistency?
options: Rewrite the paragraph in capital letters and move it to the very top of CLAUDE.md so it gets read first
Turn on plan mode for every migration task so the team can review and approve Claude's proposed approach before any migration file is written
Point Claude at two or three existing migrations that model the pattern (including a batched update) and say to follow them
Add a PostToolUse hook that rejects any migration file whose name does not match the naming pattern
explanations: Emphasis does not show what the batching or `down` pattern looks like.
Plan mode adds a review step but does not teach the pattern; the same deviations would show up in the plan.
Correct. Concrete examples in the repo act as few-shot examples for code structure, which is easier to show than to describe.
The naming is already correct; this checks the one thing that is not failing.

questions.stem: The document pipeline's schema has `"doc_type": {"enum": ["invoice", "credit_note", "receipt"]}` and uses structured outputs. A new supplier starts sending pro-forma invoices and account statements. These come back labelled `invoice` and are posted to accounts payable as real bills. Which schema change BEST prevents this class of error?
options: Add `other` to the enum plus a nullable `doc_type_detail` string, and route `other` documents to review instead of posting
Remove the enum and make `doc_type` a free-text string so the model can describe any document
Keep the enum and add a prompt line saying "if the document type is unclear, choose receipt"
Add `proforma` and `statement` to the enum so these two document types get their own labels and can be routed away from accounts payable
explanations: Correct. A closed enum with no escape hatch forces a wrong choice. `other` plus a detail field captures unexpected inputs, and routing them to review keeps them out of AP.
Free text loses the closed set downstream code relies on and makes routing unreliable.
This forces unknown documents into another wrong category instead of surfacing them.
Fixes today's two types but the next unexpected type will again be forced into the nearest label.

questions.stem: The invoice schema defines `"total": {"type": "string"}`. Downstream code receives values such as `"1.234,56"`, `"$1,234.56"` and `"1234.56 EUR"`, and its parser misreads European formats as amounts a thousand times too small. Which schema design BEST fixes this at the source?
options: Make `total` a `number` described as "grand total as printed, without currency symbol or thousands separators" and add a separate `currency` field with ISO 4217 codes
Keep `total` as a string and add a regex-based normaliser in code that strips currency symbols and infers the decimal separator from the vendor's billing country
Keep `total` as a string and add three few-shot examples that show amounts written with a dot as the decimal separator
Make `total` an object containing `raw_text`, `integer_part`, `decimal_part`, `separator` and `symbol`, all required strings
explanations: Correct. A numeric type removes formatting ambiguity at generation time, the description states the convention, and currency becomes its own typed field instead of being mixed into the value.
Guessing the separator in code reproduces the same ambiguity, now with country heuristics that fail for multinational vendors.
Examples may help but a string type still permits any format; the schema should carry the type.
Over-engineered: many required string parts push the work back into downstream parsing and invite inconsistent splitting.

questions.stem: The extraction pipeline validates each result in code (line items sum to the total, due date after issue date, vendor ID exists). On failure it sends the same request again with "Your output was invalid. Try again." appended. Only about a quarter of retries pass. What is the BEST improvement to the retry?
options: Raise the retry limit from two to five attempts so that more of the failing documents eventually pass validation without any manual intervention
Include the specific failures (e.g. "line items sum to 1,180.00 but total is 1,280.00") with the original document and the previous output
Send each retry to a more capable model tier while keeping the same generic retry message
Drop the validation step for vendors whose invoices fail most often to reduce wasted retries
explanations: More blind attempts mostly repeat the same mistake and raise cost; they also increase the chance of a value being bent to pass the check.
Correct. A retry works when the model is told exactly which rule failed and with which values, alongside the source and its previous answer, so it can re-read the relevant part.
A stronger model may help a little, but it still does not know what was wrong.
Removing validation for the worst vendors lets their errors through unnoticed.

questions.stem: A validation rule in the invoice pipeline requires `vat_id` for EU vendors. When it fails, the pipeline retries with the error fed back, up to five times. Retries usually pass on the second or third attempt, but an audit finds that many of these "fixed" VAT IDs appear nowhere on the invoice. What is the BEST change?
options: Allow `vat_id` to be null ("not printed on the document"), stop retrying in that case, and route those invoices to human review
Reduce the retry limit to two so the model has fewer chances to produce an invalid VAT ID
Add a checksum validator for VAT ID formats and keep retrying with the error fed back until the model returns an ID that passes both checks
Add "Never invent a VAT ID" to the retry message and keep the five-attempt limit for EU vendors
explanations: Correct. When the information is absent from the source, retrying cannot succeed honestly; pressure to pass validation produces fabrication. Represent absence explicitly and send it to a human.
Fewer retries reduce but do not remove fabrication, because the loop still demands a value that does not exist.
A format check makes invented IDs look even more legitimate; the problem is absence, not format.
The loop still requires a value the document does not contain; the instruction conflicts with the validation it is trying to satisfy.

questions.stem: The invoice pipeline occasionally misreads a line-item amount; the result is schema-valid and looks plausible, so nobody notices until month-end reconciliation. The team wants these errors caught at extraction time without adding a second model call per invoice. Which design BEST achieves this?
options: Add a `confidence` field to each line item and send items below 0.7 to human review
Run a second, independent extraction of every invoice with a different prompt and compare the two results field by field, flagging any disagreement
Trust the structured-output guarantee and rely on month-end reconciliation to surface any differences
Extract `stated_total` exactly as printed alongside the line items, recompute the line-item sum in code, and retry or flag the invoice on mismatch
explanations: Self-reported confidence is not calibrated; misreads are typically reported with high confidence.
Effective but it doubles extraction cost, which the requirement rules out.
Structured outputs guarantee shape, not correctness; the gap is exactly what is failing.

Correct. A self-correction field (the printed total) gives code an independent value to check the extracted parts against, at no extra call; mismatches become retries with the discrepancy or review items.

questions.stem: The extraction pipeline re-sends a document with the validation error as feedback when a check fails. Which TWO of the following failures will that retry generally NOT fix, so they should go straight to human review or a fallback path? (Select TWO.)
options: Line items sum to 1,180.00 while the extracted total is 1,280.00
`due_date` was extracted as earlier than `issue_date` on an invoice with clearly printed dates
Validation requires `po_number`, but the invoice has no PO number printed anywhere
A date came back as `03/04/2025` although the schema description asks for ISO 8601
Page 2 of the scan, which holds the line items, is missing from the uploaded file
explanations: Retryable: the information is on the page and a targeted error message tells the model where to re-read.
Retryable: the dates are present and legible, so feedback naming the conflict usually corrects the misread.
Correct. The value does not exist in the source; retrying invites fabrication. Represent it as absent and review.
Retryable: the date is present; feedback on the expected format fixes it.
Correct. The source itself is incomplete; no amount of re-reading recovers the missing page.

questions.stem: The contract-extraction pipeline uses structured outputs. A business rule says a contract's `end_date` must be after its `start_date`. Where should the pipeline enforce this rule?
options: In the JSON schema, so constrained decoding prevents an end date earlier than the start date
In a `dates_valid` boolean that the model sets itself after it has extracted both dates
In the prompt only, as a sentence telling the model that the end date always follows the start date
In code after the response is parsed, triggering a retry with the specific error or a review item
explanations: Structured outputs enforce shape and types; a cross-field comparison between two dates is not something to rely on the schema for.
A self-reported flag is not a check; the model can set it to true on a wrong extraction.
A prompt can lower the error rate but cannot guarantee the rule.
Correct. Semantic and cross-field rules are validated in code after parsing; failures feed a targeted retry or review.

questions.stem: The invoice pipeline's validation-and-retry loop (two retries with error feedback) works for most vendors. For one large vendor, about 300 invoices a week fail all retries with the same error: a "shipping and handling" summary row is extracted as a line item, so totals never reconcile. What is the BEST long-term fix?
options: Raise the retry limit for that vendor to five attempts so more of its invoices eventually pass
Send that vendor's retries to the most capable model tier while keeping the existing prompt, since a stronger model should read the layout correctly
Treat it as a systematic prompt gap: add an example of this layout (summary rows are not line items) and route this week's failures to review
Relax the totals check for that vendor so its invoices stop failing validation on every run
explanations: The same error on every attempt shows the retry message is not resolving the misunderstanding; more attempts add cost.
May fix some cases, but pays the premium on every retry and leaves the first-pass prompt wrong.
Correct. A failure that repeats identically across retries and documents points at the prompt, not at noise. Fixing it with a targeted example removes the failures at the first pass.
Disabling the check hides real errors for exactly the vendor that has them.

questions.stem: In the research system, the synthesis subagent returns a report as JSON in which each claim lists the `source_ids` that support it. Occasionally a claim cites an ID that does not exist in the findings the subagent was given. The report is then published with a broken citation. What is the BEST fix?
options: Remove `source_ids` from the output and let readers check the claims against the bibliography
Add "Only cite source IDs that appear in the findings you were given" to the synthesis prompt
Before returning, have the synthesis subagent re-check its own citations in the same conversation and correct any IDs it judges to be wrong
In the coordinator's code, check each cited ID against the findings set; on failure re-prompt with the invalid and valid IDs, then drop or flag claims still unsupported
explanations: Removing provenance hides the problem and makes the report less trustworthy.
A prompt-only rule reduces but does not guarantee correct citations; nothing catches the failures that remain.
Self-review in the same context tends to confirm its own output and is still not a deterministic check.
Correct. Existence of a cited ID is a cheap deterministic check in code; a targeted retry fixes most cases and a final fallback keeps unsupported claims out.

questions.stem: A CI job runs `claude -p --json-schema "$(cat fix-plan.json)"` to produce a plan of file edits for a failing build, and a later step applies the plan. The JSON always matches the schema, but sometimes the plan lists a file path that does not exist in the repo, and the apply step crashes. What should the pipeline do?
options: Validate every path before applying; on failure, re-run once with the error naming the missing paths, then fail the job with that message if it persists
Increase `--max-turns` so Claude has more turns to explore the repository with Read, Grep and Glob before it writes out the final plan of file edits
Add "Only reference files that exist in the repository" to CLAUDE.md so CI picks it up
Drop `--json-schema` and parse a free-text plan, so the model is not constrained by the schema
explanations: Correct. Schema-valid output still needs semantic validation in code. A capped, targeted retry with the specific error, then a clear failure, keeps bad plans from being applied.
More turns may help exploration but does not check the plan before it is applied.
A prompt-level rule can reduce the rate but nothing stops a bad path reaching the apply step.
The schema is not the cause; removing it loses the structural guarantee and adds parsing failures.

questions.stem: The extraction platform has two workloads: a customer portal where a user uploads one invoice and waits on screen for the extracted fields, and a monthly backlog of about 200,000 archived invoices from newly onboarded clients. To cut spend, a manager proposes routing all extraction through the Message Batches API. What should the architect recommend?
options: Keep both workloads on real-time calls and switch the backlog to the smallest model tier to save cost
Route everything through batches, and show portal users a "processing" message until their batch result arrives
Keep the portal on real-time Messages calls and send the monthly backlog through the Message Batches API
Batch the portal uploads every five minutes into small batches so users still get results quickly
